articles.title: "It's Just About Being with My Friends": Children's Perspectives on the Use, Risks and Benefits of Virtual Worlds Platforms
articles.authors: Cláudia Silva; Miguel Barreda-Angeles
articles.abstract: Despite the central role that virtual worlds based on user-generated content, such as Roblox, play in the digital lives of children and adolescents, research incorporating their first-hand experiences and perspectives of these platforms remains limited. Roblox is one of the world's largest virtual world platforms, used predominantly by children and adolescents, with most users estimated to be under the age of 16. Grounded in a children's rights perspective, this study adopts an arts-based qualitative approach that combines cognitive mapping through drawing with follow-up interviews to explore what children's and adolescents' perceptions of Roblox reveal about its risks and benefits. To address this aim, we engaged 29 children aged 10–16 in partnership with an international school in Italy. Our analysis identifies three key findings with theoretical and regulatory implications. First, rather than simply as a game, participants perceive and use Roblox primarily as a social platform where they play and communicate with friends, form new relationships, and maintain long-distance connections. Related to that, participants also perceive Roblox as operating in ways that resemble social media platforms.  Second, these social dynamics are closely intertwined with risks, including exposure to scams, toxic interactions, grooming, online dating practices, and monetisation pressures. Third, participants routinely migrate to platforms such as Discord and WhatsApp for communication, circumventing Roblox's age-based restrictions and complicating platform-specific safeguarding efforts. These findings highlight the need for adaptive safeguarding strategies and contribute to theoretical discussions of the increasingly blurred boundaries between digital games and social media and children’s online safety.

articles.title: Who Speaks When the Chatbot Answers? Generative AI as Institutional Speech
articles.authors: Bibhor Acharya; Sandesh Gupta; Himani Moktan
articles.abstract: When a branded chatbot answers a customer, the reply is often taken as the institution speaking. This paper treats that uptake as a media and communication problem rather than as a model-accuracy problem alone. Using Erving Goffman’s account of footing—the gap between who animates an utterance and who stands as its principal—and Austin and Searle’s account of commitments as speech acts, we read the British Columbia Civil Resolution Tribunal decision in Moffatt v. Air Canada (2024 BCCRT 149) as a public episode of institutional speech gone wrong. A website chatbot told Jake Moffatt that a bereavement fare could be claimed retroactively within ninety days; a different page on the same site, and later human staff, denied that path. Air Canada argued it should not be held liable for the chatbot; the tribunal disagreed and ordered damages. The case lets us follow authorization, utterance, uptake, contested repair, and the failed attempt to split the animator from the principal. While systematic reviews of AI disadvantages map privacy, displacement, and bias at a macroeconomic scale, they leave open this micro-communicative surface where an institution’s name is attached to a fluent reply. We argue that handoff to a named human is part of the speech act when commitment is at stake, not an optional engineering fallback.

articles.title: The Architecture of the Unreal: Translating Kandinsky’s "Inner Necessity" into a Cinematic Framework
articles.authors: Amirhossein Amini
articles.abstract: Modern narrative cinema frequently traps itself in a materialist cage, caught between the mechanical reproduction of mundane reality and the hollow calculation of digital spectacle. This paper resurrects Wassily Kandinsky’s 1911 philosophy of "inner necessity" (Kandinsky, 1977) and translates it into a structural framework for Unreal Cinema. Rather than accepting the "unreal" as a generic aesthetic, this theory demands reality-breaking. By establishing an exacting Subtraction Test, the methodology explicitly dismisses commercial franchise spectacle—where the impossible serves merely as digital decoration over a fundamentally materialist core—to isolate films whose dramatic engines strictly require impossibility. The paper constructs a comprehensive taxonomy divided into four categories of materialist escape: Autonomous Reality, The Impossible Intrusion, Historical Subversion, and The Subjective Fracture. Utilising a diverse roster of directors—including Guillermo del Toro, Peter Jackson, Hayao Miyazaki, Darren Aronofsky, Satoshi Kon, and Tomm Moore—as core case studies, the framework establishes a hierarchical gradient to map the remaining cinematic landscape. This gradient rigorously separates true structural rebellion from ambitious edge cases, such as expressionist exaggeration or rationalised psychological tethers. By expanding Kandinsky’s vision to the cinematic medium, this paper argues that true cinematic art demands the creativity and courage to project an internal reality, actively refusing to merely recapture the world as it is. Cinema reaches its highest generative threshold only when it requires the architectural invention to abandon the pre-existing scaffolding of the physical world. To achieve the profound spiritual weight Kandinsky demanded on the canvas, filmmakers must systematically shatter the physical laws of the baseline universe.

articles.title: Examining the Prevalence and Persistence of Data Implicated in Article Retractions
articles.authors: Ashvin Narayan; A.J. Million; John T Kubale
articles.abstract: Sharing study data has become a regular aspect of the research process, often required by journals, funding agencies, and other stakeholders to facilitate study replication and collaboration among researchers. However, while post-publication remedies—retractions, corrections, and expressions of concern—have long been used to flag ethical issues in scientific literature, their application to corresponding data is inconsistent, potentially contributing to the spread of dis- and misinformation. A lack of standardized corrective mechanisms to address problematic data hinders the identification of problematic datasets, researcher assessments of their impact, and associated determinations of data reliability. Using the Inter-University Consortium for Social and Political Research (ICPSR) and its catalog of social-scientific data as a case study, we seek to identify problematic datasets and establish workflows for evaluating the reliability of archived data. In this paper, we identify ICPSR datasets associated with publications requiring post-publication remedies. We examine editorial notices of post-publication remedies and data documentation to identify errors and/or ethical concerns affecting ICPSR datasets. Our work highlights how inconsistent documentation and communication about post-publication remedies inhibit the use of traditional corrective publishing mechanisms extended to the research data space. This work also seeks to identify resources and practices that may better facilitate processes of data re-evaluation and remediation, helping to mitigate the downstream impacts of data-related issues on scientific research.

articles_hidden.title: Moving Beyond Statistical Significance: How to Improve the Reporting and Interpretation of Medical Research
articles_hidden.authors: Alessandro Rovetta; Mohammed Ali Mansournia; Pavlos Msaouel; Winston Lin; Steven Stovitz; Alessandro Vitale; Anna Chiara Frigo; Richard Riley; Sander Greenland
articles_hidden.abstract: Many methodologists have warned against interpreting statistical estimates through dichotomous labels such as “significant” and “non-significant.” Yet, articles in medical journals still rely heavily on P-value thresholds and confidence interval boundaries to guide inference and communication of research findings. Here, Rovetta and colleagues discuss how such a focus on statistical “significance” obscures clinical relevance and uncertainty, whilst distorting evidence appraisals. Rather, they suggest P-values and confidence intervals should be interpreted as continuous measures of compatibility between data and hypotheses, which also reflect choices about how data are collected, modeled, and analyzed.

articles.title: Cerebellar contributions to social learning in autistic and nonautistic adolescents
articles.authors: Yen-Wen Chen; Shannon Cahalan; Nicole Grace Treece; Ann Clawson; Alyssa Verbalis; Christoph Korn; Gabriela Rosenblau; Allison Jack
articles.abstract:
The role of the cerebellum in social learning remains poorly understood. Although the cerebellar posterior lobe (CPL) has been implicated in social decision-making and autistic traits, its contribution to social prediction and prediction-error (PE) processing during learning is unclear. We focused on adolescence, a critical developmental period for social decision-making and learning. 71 autistic (AUT) and 75 non-autistic (N-AUT) participants completed social and non-social learning tasks during fMRI. Preregistered hypotheses predicted that the CPL would be involved in prediction and PE processing, with effects differing by diagnostic status and age.

We found no group differences in social learning. Across participants, PEs decreased more steeply during non-social than social learning; in the AUT group this difference between social and non-social learning was more pronounced. In the cerebellum, PE-related activity in the CPL (lobules Crus I/II, VI, and VIIb) showed group- and age-related differences. Contrary to our hypothesis, PE-related activity during social learning was greater in AUT than N-AUT participants in right Crus II. Across several other CPL regions, PE-related activity increased with age in N-AUT participants but showed the opposite pattern in AUT participants. Mirroring the marginally steeper behavioral PE reduction in the non-social condition in the AUT vs. the N-AUT group, PE-related brain activity was greater for non-social than social PEs in left Crus I and right lobule VI in the AUT group. Exploratory searchlight analyses showed greater PE-related connectivity between left Crus II and prefrontal cortex in AUT than N-AUT participants. 

These findings suggest that AUT adolescents may engage CPL differently during learning, particularly for social versus non-social information. Greater CPL activity and connectivity during social learning in AUT may reflect compensatory mechanisms supporting comparable behavioral performance to N-AUT youth.

articles.title: Understanding Medical Invalidation from the Patient Perspective: A Qualitative Interview Study Across Diseases and Healthcare Settings
articles.authors: Seraina Petra Lerch
articles.abstract:
Objective 
Research on patients feeling that their symptoms are not taken seriously (medical invalidation) has predominantly focused on individual diseases. This study explored patients' experiences across different medical conditions and healthcare contexts to identify common characteristics, contributing factors, consequences, and opportunities for prevention. 
Methods
The study was conducted in Germany between January and March 2025 using interviews undertaken remotely or in person. Data were analysed using qualitative content analysis following Kuckartz and Rädiker. Thirty-one adults (≥18 years) with self-reported experiences of not being taken seriously in healthcare were purposively recruited through patient organisations and social media to achieve maximum variation regarding symptoms and diagnoses.
Results
Participants described not being taken seriously as a cross-cutting healthcare phenomenon occurring across diverse symptoms, diagnoses, medical specialties, and healthcare settings. Experiences ranged from isolated encounters to cumulative processes that developed over repeated interactions with healthcare professionals (HCPs). Contributing factors were perceived at multiple levels, including healthcare system, HCPs, patient, disease, and interactional factors, which frequently interacted. Consequences extended beyond the initial consultation and included psychological distress, loss of trust, delayed or inappropriate diagnosis and treatment, reduced healthcare utilisation, occupational consequences, and impaired social well-being. Participants identified opportunities for prevention at different levels, highlighting structured feedback mechanisms. 
Conclusions
Medical invalidation is a multifactorial phenomenon that extends across diseases and healthcare settings. Patients emphasized that medical invalidation depends not only on clinical decision-making but on being heard, having their illness perceptions acknowledged, and receiving transparent communication. Strengthening these elements of patient-centred care may improve healthcare experiences.

articles.title: Caregiver prosody coincides with infant sustained visual attention
articles.authors: Manash Sahoo; Valerie Bambha; Chen Yu; Linda B. Smith; Jeremy Isaac Borjon
articles.abstract: Prosodic modifications in caregiver speech are related to infant attention, word learning, and long-term language development, yet how moment-to-moment caregiver prosody relates to infant attentional dynamics during naturalistic interaction remains unclear. Here, we used unsupervised learning to categorize 12,311 caregiver utterances produced during free play across the second year of life (12-24 months) into four prosodic contour types: fall, hill, rise, and valley. Infant visual attention was measured using head-mounted eye-tracking. Proportions of contour types were stable from 12 to 24 months. Despite this stability, specific contours were temporally coordinated with the onset and offset of infant sustained visual attention (SVA). Rise contours coincided with the initiation of SVA in older infants, beginning approximately one second before onset, and valley contours coincided with the period following SVA offset in both age groups. At the dyad level, two patterns emerged. Caregivers who produced higher levels of vocalizations that coincided with the onset or offset of SVA had infants with more SVA episodes and total SVA time overall. Further, caregivers who exhibited a specific prosodic pattern in the two seconds following SVA disengagement, a fall contour in the first second and a valley contour in the following second, had infants with longer average SVA episodes.  These results dissociate two facets of dyadic temporal coordination: a broad association between caregiver prosody and the quantity of SVA episodes, and a specific post-disengagement prosodic pattern linked to the duration of SVA.

articles.title: Orthographic retrieval unfolds in parallel with single-word production
articles.authors: Jens Roeser; Pablo Aros Muñoz; Markus Damian; Gary Jones; Mark Torrance
articles.abstract: Written word production is often assumed to begin after the relevant spelling has been retrieved. We challenge this pre-onset assumption by asking whether spelling-related processing can continue during output. Across four picture-word interference experiments (Ns = 60, 72, 96, 93), participants typed or spoke picture names while ignoring pronounceable non-word distractors. Distractors either preserved the target-compatible spelling pattern or introduced a phonologically plausible alternative spelling; only the latter should disrupt writing if phonology makes alternative spellings relevant during orthographic retrieval. Bayesian mixed-effects mixture models estimated the probability that response-onset latencies and post-onset intervals came from a longer-duration component. Spelling-mismatch distractors sometimes facilitated onset responses but increased long-duration probability at later timings and within typed words. These late mismatch effects disappeared for spoken responses. These time-course data challenge the classical assumption that written words are mentally prepared as complete spellings before output begins; instead, orthographic retrieval can remain vulnerable to phonologically plausible alternatives during written production.

articles.title: Iconicity and Age Make Distinct Contributions to Symbolic Correspondence in Early Childhood
articles.authors: Keyi Yang; Ruoxi Chen; Suizi Xue; Jiajia Zhou; anonymous; Juan Wang; Jingmei Wang; Jinliang Qin
articles.abstract: Iconicity has been proposed to support children’s symbolic understanding, yet it remains unclear when iconicity contributes to symbolic correspondence and how this contribution varies across early childhood. The present study examined semantic judgments in 204 Chinese preschool children (Mage = 5.36 years, SD = 0.78; 102 boys) across three representational formats: line drawings, Oracle Bone script, and simplified Chinese characters. Children judged whether sequentially presented picture–symbol pairs referred to the same objects or actions, allowing broad format differences to be distinguished from graded item-level iconicity within each format. Children were consistently more accurate when rejecting mismatches than when confirming matches. Iconicity was especially informative when children had to confirm that different forms shared a meaning. Diffusion decision modeling further showed that this advantage was expressed in the accumulation of decision-relevant evidence during confirmation. Older age was associated with more efficient evidence accumulation for establishing semantic correspondence across representational formats, but age did not systematically strengthen or weaken the iconicity-drift relation. These findings suggest that iconicity and age make distinct contributions to symbolic correspondence: iconicity functions as a task-dependent source of information, whereas age-related differences are characterized by broader gains in the efficiency of establishing correspondence across symbolic forms.

articles.title: Dissociable neural oscillations track subjective value under risk and ambiguity
articles.authors: Shuting Mei; Leyou Deng; Gökhan Aydogan; Christian Carl Ruff; Ya Zheng
articles.abstract: How the brain values uncertain prospects and translates them into choices is a central question in decision neuroscience. Current accounts propose that decisions under risk and ambiguity share a valuation process that integrates outcome with probability information, with ambiguity additionally requiring evaluation of the uncertainty about the probabilities themselves. Here we used computational modeling to estimate trial-wise subjective value and tested whether it was tracked by shared or distinct neural dynamics under risk and ambiguity. Participants accepted or rejected risky and ambiguous monetary gambles while we recorded neural activity using electroencephalography (Experiment 1) and magnetoencephalography (Experiment 2). Across both experiments, alpha-band (9–14 Hz) activity localized to the precuneus and superior parietal cortex tracked subjective value under both risk and ambiguity. By contrast, delta-band (1–3 Hz) activity localized to the ventromedial prefrontal and anterior cingulate cortices tracked subjective value only under ambiguity. These findings reveal dissociable neural signatures for the two forms of uncertainty and suggest that the brain resolves ambiguity by combining a shared valuation process indexed by alpha activity with an additional process indexed by delta activity that may reflect the motivational salience of options with ambiguous outcome probabilities.

articles.title: Consistency: A Critical but Often Overlooked Requirement for Causal Inference in Psychological Research
articles.authors: Lukas Junker; Michael P. Grosz
articles.abstract: Psychologists are often interested in specific causal quantities (“What is the effect of reducing social-media scrolling by 20 minutes on well-being?”) but tend to focus on vague questions (“Does ‘time spent on social media’ predict well-being?”). There is a mismatch between the causal effects researchers care about and the associations and correlations they compute. In this article, we highlight consistency as a foundational requirement for causal inference that can bridge this mismatch and make statistical estimates causally interpretable. Consistency shows how causal quantities are interpretable only when (a) the causal quantity of interest—the causal estimand—is described precisely enough that it does not bundle different versions of the treatment (e.g., passive scrolling, reading distressing news, or chatting with friends on social media) that have different effects, and (b) the way that the treatment variable changes in the data matches this causal estimand of interest. We clarify these requirements and illustrate how to state and assess them in settings common in psychological research, with a focus on indirect experimental manipulations and multidimensional constructs. Making this step explicit helps researchers articulate their estimands more transparently and is a prerequisite for other concerns such as confounding and model specification.

articles.title: Music as Emotional Regulation in the Climate Crisis: Relationships with Eco-Anxiety, Eco-Guilt, and Eco-Grief
articles.authors: Friederike Koehler; Dana Swarbrick; Suvi Saarikallio
articles.abstract:
Background: Climate change increasingly evokes complex emotional responses, yet little is known about how everyday practices, such as music listening, relate to these emotions. Given that music is one of the most common tools people use to manage affect in daily life, examining its role in the climate context offers huge potential for insights into eco-emotional experiences. 
Methods: 312 adults completed an online survey on music‑based mood regulation and eco‑anxiety, eco‑grief, and eco‑guilt. Associations were examined using structural equation modelling.
Results: Zero-order bivariate correlations indicated positive correlations between eco-emotions and all music-based mood regulation strategies except for entertainment. Structural equation models further revealed two distinct patterns: using music for mental work, discharge, solace, and strong sensation were associated with higher levels of eco‑distress, whereas entertainment, revival, and diversion were linked to lower distress. This suggests that when distressing climate emotions arise, individuals who experience them more intensely may immerse themselves more deeply in their emotional processing through music, while those who experience less distress may use music in lighter, recreational ways. Qualitative responses showed that individuals use music in diverse ways to navigate climate emotions, including calming listening, engaging with climate‑themed lyrics, creative expression, community, and nature‑evoking soundscapes, while others reported no connection. 
Conclusions: Findings highlight music as a meaningful yet heterogeneous context in which people relate to climate emotions, offering new insight into the emotional dimensions of the climate crisis. Through integrating music psychology and climate-emotion research, the study underlines the value of everyday cultural practices as part of individual and collective adaptation.

articles.title: Inhabiting digital ecologies: A qualitative approach to good digital practices
articles.authors: Esther Paniagua; Myriam Durán Vilches; Noemí Robles; Pepa Barral González; Manuel Armayones
articles.abstract:
The integration of digital technologies into everyday life has produced complex digital
ecologies in which platforms, algorithms, and social practices jointly shape experience,
identity, and emotional regulation. Although research on digital well-being has
increased significantly, little is known about how individuals reflect on their digital lives
and the practical criteria they develop to navigate these environments while preserving
well-being and autonomy.,This paper addresses these questions through qualitative
research conducted within a digital community of 100 adults residing in Spain whose
participation unfolded across four successive waves. Fieldwork combined individual
journals, thematic forums, and an open social space, generating a longitudinal corpus
on the everyday experience of inhabiting digital spaces. Results were interpreted
through discourse analysis to reconstruct shared patterns of meaning and discursive
positions.,Findings reveal an ambivalent relationship with digital environments: the
same tools that enable connection, communication, and access to information are also
described as sources of noise, overstimulation, attention fragmentation, and loss of
control. Alongside these discomforts, participants describe daily repertoires of
adjustment that crystallise into distinct discursive positions from which they inhabit
digital ecologies and develop good practices.,We propose that good digital practices
should not be understood as a universal list of self-regulatory norms, but as relational
competencies developed through reflection and experience. Methodologically, the
study shows that a digital community is a particularly suitable tool for examining
everyday, complex, largely automated phenomena, since it enables participants to
observe, compare, and transform their digital experience into practical criteria guiding
their relationship with digital ecologies.

articles.title: Made in the Culture, Not the Voice: Lyrical Camp, Production Texture, and the Queer Anthemization of Popular Songs
articles.authors: Logan Barrett
articles.abstract: Why do some popular songs become queer anthems while others, including many by openly queer artists, do not? We tested musical affordance and historical contingency accounts in a purposive corpus of 100 songs (69 artists) designed to dissociate queer authorship, explicit queer lyrical content, and community adoption. Adoption was measured as an evidence-coded anthemization score from URL-verified documentation of Pride, drag, ballroom, club, activist, and queer-media use. Anthemization was unrelated to whether artists were publicly queer (rs = −.02) and only weakly related to explicit queer lyrics (rs = .22). Among 16 language-model-coded lyrical themes, camp potential predicted anthemization after family-wise correction and controls for era, genre, authorship, and explicit content (partial r = .40, n = 55). The association replicated with masked lyrics, among songs the coding model could not identify, with a second coding model, and with two independent outcome coders (partial r = .45–.54, n = 46), although it was not robust when the model's own anthem judgements were also partialled out. Full-mix acoustic descriptors related to formant energy and voicing predicted anthemization (|rs| = .38–.43, family-wise p < .05) but vanished when computed on Demucs-separated vocal stems (n = 80), locating the acoustic signal in production texture rather than the singer's voice; spectral brightness was confounded by genre and era. Outcome reliability was moderate (weighted κ = .57). The results support reception-centred accounts of musical queerness. They implicate lyrical camp and production as affordances for queer adoption, not a characteristic queer voice.

articles.title: Using Artificial Intelligence to estimate how common alcohol references and alcohol-related brand references are among influencers on Instagram
articles.authors: Jack Delmenico; Dan Anderson-Luxford; Emmanuel Kuntsche; Jingda Du; Zhen Du; Megan Cook; Charlotte Jonhston; Paula O'Brien; Simone Pettigrew; Benjamin Riordan
articles.abstract:
Background: Young people spend hours on social media every day, where following influencers is the norm. Influencers post frequently about alcohol and alcohol brands and there has been a rise in influencer marketing. However, prevalence estimates rely on manual analyses of only a small number of posts. We used a large language model (LLM) to estimate at scale how often top Australian Instagram influencers reference alcohol and alcohol brands, and whether this varies by influencer type.
Methods: We identified 988 of the most-followed Australian Instagram influencers and retrieved all 667,531 of their posts that were visible to all users, including those under 18 (i.e., not age gated). An LLM classified whether each post referenced alcohol and these were screened manually to record brand references. Influencers were coded into 14 types (e.g., athletes, actors).
Results: Most influencers (87.45%) referenced alcohol and 47.10% referenced an alcohol brand in at least one post. Overall, 20,448 posts (3.06%) referenced alcohol and 2,869 (0.43%) a brand (14% of alcohol-related posts). Food influencers posted the most alcohol and brand-related content, while athletes posted the least alcohol-related content but had the highest proportion referencing a brand.
Conclusions: Influencer alcohol-related and alcohol-related brand content is pervasive on Instagram and reaches audiences of every age, including those under 18 who should not see alcohol advertising.
So what: Given the link between exposure and use, health promotion should aim policies and strategies at reducing alcohol-related content, particularly branded content that likely reflects influencer marketing.

articles.title: Color cues, developmental coupling, and the limits of the late-sighted model: A commentary on Vogelsang et al. (2024)
articles.authors: David Henry Peterzell
articles.abstract:
Vogelsang et al. (2024) report in Science that congenitally blind individuals who gain sight late in life rely disproportionately on color cues for object recognition, unlike normally sighted controls. They propose that this pattern reflects the adaptive value of neonatal color immaturity: because typical infants experience a period of degraded chromatic input, they develop object representations grounded in luminance rather than color.
The theoretical account, however, rests on an incomplete engagement with the developmental literature. Decades of research indicate that color and luminance sensitivity are developmentally coupled through shared photoreceptor immaturity: the same front-end bottleneck that degrades chromatic input in neonates simultaneously degrades luminance and spatial processing. If this coupling is real, there is no luminance-first window, because the bottleneck lifts for both dimensions together. The account's central premise is therefore undermined not by arguing independence, but by showing that color and luminance do not develop in the sequence the account requires.
I further identify methodological concerns: a small and unusual sample, a fixed order confound in the primary behavioral task, a computational model implementing a binary switch rather than the gradual chromatic cascade of normal development, and a color sensitivity test using non-equiluminant stimuli, leaving open the possibility that luminance rather than chromatic contrast sensitivity drove performance.
Together, these issues require qualification of the conclusions of Vogelsang et al. and reconciliation of the proposed account with classical findings in infant visual development. This broader question remains important, but the answer is unlikely to hinge on color alone.

articles.title: Interval-Dependent Effects of Action and Choice Availability on Temporal Binding
articles.authors: Lauren Claire Fong; Silvia Seghezzi; Paul Michael Garrett; Mia Nightingale; Philip L. Smith; Robert Hester; Daniel Feuerriegel
articles.abstract: Temporal binding research proposes that voluntary actions compress perceived time between actions and their outcomes, reflecting an implicit sense of agency. However, it remains unclear whether such effects are stable across action--outcome interval durations and whether they depend on the degree of decisional freedom, such as the availability of choice options. Here, we investigated whether action generation (action vs. no action) and choice availability (one vs. two options) influence interval estimation across multiple action-outcome intervals using a yoked action-baseline design. Across two experiments, action-baseline differences consistent with temporal binding were observed only at the shortest interval (300 ms), where action trials produced relatively shorter interval estimates than matched baseline trials. However, these differences did not generalise to longer intervals and reversed in direction at longer intervals in one experiment. Across the full interval range, baseline estimates shifted more steeply with interval duration than action estimates, producing a crossover pattern in which shorter intervals were overestimated and longer intervals underestimated across conditions. We did not find evidence that choice availability, operationalised as one versus two options, modulated interval estimates in either experiment. These findings suggest that action-related differences in interval estimation are temporally constrained and may arise from an interaction between action-related processes and general perceptual biases in temporal estimation, including regression toward the mean. More broadly, the results show that apparent temporal binding effects in interval-estimation tasks can depend strongly on where tested intervals fall within the broader interval range, highlighting the importance of accounting for interval-dependent estimation biases when interpreting temporal binding effects in interval estimation tasks as proxy measure of the sense of agency.

articles.title: How Adults in Spain Perceive Love:  Individual Differences in Cultural Attunement and Evaluative Style
articles.authors: Saida Heshmati; Lindy Williams; Dana Hussein; Jaymes Paolo Rombaoa; Royce Anders; Zita Oravecz
articles.abstract: Love is culturally universal in presence, yet highly variable in how people perceive it. The present study examined individual differences in cultural attunement and judgment styles related to love. Adults (N = 502) living in Spain rated 61 everyday scenarios according to how likely each would make most people feel loved. Using the Continuous Response Model within Cultural Consensus Theory, we captured individuals’ alignment with the shared understanding of love (i.e., their cultural attunement) in Spanish culture. Greater attunement was observed among women, individuals with higher perceived support from a significant other, those with lower anxiety, and those who valued benevolence. Weaker attunement, on the other hand, was associated with endorsement of power and traditional values. In addition, individuals differed in how they expressed their judgments: older adults and men used a narrower range of responses, whereas those higher in extraversion and conscientiousness showed greater differentiation across scenarios. More educated individuals were less likely to judge situations as loving overall, whereas those higher in agreeableness were more likely to do so. These findings highlight that judgments of love experiences reflect not only shared cultural knowledge but also systematic individual differences in how that knowledge is applied.

articles.title: Accounts Balanced: The Contingent Role of Rhetoric in Who Survives Political Scandal
articles.authors: Pierce D. Ekstrom; Marti Hope Gonzales; Allison Williams; Elliot Weiner; Rafael Aguilera
articles.abstract: When accused of misconduct in their private or public lives, people choose whether to apologize or to defend their character or reputation. Previous experiments have found that when misconduct is severe or offends outgroup members, transgressors may benefit by defending themselves and denying culpability for wrongdoing. In this study, we explore whether these tendencies can successfully reduce politicians’ accountability for wrongdoing in the context of a U.S. congressional election. We constructed a novel dataset documenting Representatives’ public remarks in response the 1992 House Bank Scandal, during which Representatives from both major parties were accused of misusing funds. Contrary to predictions, conciliatory remarks were not associated with electoral failure among more severe House Bank “offenders.” Consistent with predictions, defensive remarks (refusals) lost their typical association with electoral failure when the incumbent’s party controlled the district. Results suggest that groups may allow their leaders to escape blame for wrongdoing and retain power.

articles.title: Cultural and Personality Predictors of Attitudes Toward AI Chatbots: A Systematic Literature  Review
articles.authors: Michelle Ming Ertl; Katherine Moore
articles.abstract:
As AI chatbots are becoming increasingly relevant in our daily life, understanding what shapes
people’s attitudes toward them is becoming more important. This systematic literature review
brings together the findings of 34 articles (from across multiple countries) to examine how
personality traits and one’s cultural background predict attitudes towards AI chatbots. The
review suggests that culture works as a primary filter that sets a person’s starting position when
they encounter AI. Western users tend to approach chatbots with more skepticism and stronger
privacy concerns, while on the other hand East Asian users show higher comfort with social AI
interaction. Within each of these cultural settings, individual personality traits fine-tune these
responses, but which trait matters most changes depending on the culture. Agreeableness
drives trust in Western samples, while Conscientiousness drives trust in Arab ones. Technology
specific variables like Personal Innovativeness in Information Technology (PIIT) and AI
configuration anxiety turned out to be stronger predictors than broad personality traits overall.
The review also identifies a persistent global gender gap in AI adaptation that operates
differently depending on cultural setting. Limitations include the overrepresentation of young
university educated participants in existing research, the Western bias present in both study
samples and AI training data, and the ongoing confusion between physical robot findings and
text-based chatbot research. The paper concludes that effective chatbot design and AI policy
require culturally adapted approaches rather than one-size-fits-all solutions.

articles.title: Caregivers’ multimodal actions scaffold word learning in the preschool years
articles.authors: Antonia Jordan-Barros; Francesco Cabiddu; Ed Donnellan; Yan Gu; Gabriella Vigliocco
articles.abstract: Children learn language in face-to-face interactions with their caregivers where they are continuously exposed to multimodal input in which verbal content is combined with non-verbal signals (e.g., caregivers looking and pointing at an object while naming it). However, little is known about how caregivers’ use of the full range of multimodal behaviours is linked to children’s word learning. Using the ECOLANG Corpus, we examined how caregivers’ multimodal behaviours predict children’s word learning during a semi-naturalistic parent-child interaction. Thirty-seven caregivers (age: 29-48, 36 female; British and American English speakers) interacted with their child (age: 3-4, 19 female) talking about 12 unknown objects for 30 minutes. Caregivers’ verbal (e.g., label repetitions, speaking rate) and non-verbal (e.g., points, gaze, gestures) behaviours were annotated and used as predictors in regression analyses of children’s learning of the novel object labels along with child vocabulary scores. Results showed that, in the verbal domain, caregivers’ use of high pitch and more lexically diverse speech were associated with better word learning, while caregivers’ use of representational gestures was a significant non-verbal predictor. In particular, using more representational gestures when labelling unknown objects predicted better word learning specifically for children with lower vocabulary scores, suggesting that non-verbal cues such as manual gestures can provide additional support for children with less advanced linguistic abilities. This work presents the first comprehensive investigation of the combined role of verbal and non-verbal caregivers’ behaviours and provides robust evidence that multimodal caregiver communication can shape preschool-aged children’s lexical development.

articles.title: The Impasse Model: A Clinical Formulation Framework for Understanding Psychological Impasse and Restoring Movement
articles.authors: Clare Layhe
articles.abstract:
Psychological impasse is defined here as a state in which change, resolution or 
movement is experienced as necessary or desired, yet no sufficiently viable route can currently 
be perceived, accessed or enacted. The Impasse Model arose from collaborative clinical 
formulations in which people were often highly mobilised rather than passive. They had 
explained, repaired, problem-solved, pursued reassurance, withdrawn or protected themselves, 
yet their available field of action had progressively narrowed. Relational difficulty and 
mismatches in communication or understanding were recurrent, though not universal, pathways. 
The model identifies impasse as a clinically useful warning point before higher-cost coping or 
protective responses become necessary. Formulation then proceeds in two directions: backwards, 
to understand how viable movement became restricted and forwards, to identify the smallest 
change capable of reopening it. Existing literatures on entrapment, action crisis, psychological 
inflexibility, hopelessness, decisional conflict, uncertainty and systemic constraint overlap 
substantially with this territory. The proposed contribution is therefore not a new universal 
mechanism but a clinically organised formulation framework whose distinctiveness and utility 
are open to empirical test.
Keywords: psychological impasse, formulation, entrapment, trauma, dissociation, anxiety, 
systemic formulation, EMDR, therapeutic intervention

articles.title: Two sides of the same coin in memory: Speech and its accompanying gesture are remembered together
articles.authors: Yang Liu; Tilo Kircher; Luyao Chen; Yifei He; Benjamin Straube
articles.abstract: When a speaker gestures, speech and gesture form one multimodal event. Memory research mostly asks how gestures help people remember speech, not how the gesture is remembered or how the two relate. Participants watched videos of an actor speaking sentences with a related gesture or none (Experiment 1, N = 20), or a related or unrelated gesture (Experiment 2, N = 43). They recognized written sentences and, for each called old, judged whether a gesture had been present (Experiment 1) or related (Experiment 2), with confidence ratings. Recognition was better after related than unrelated gestures, but not better after related gestures than none. Gesture judgments were above chance and more accurate for confidently recognized sentences; for these, participants also tended to report non-matching gestures as matching (Experiment 2). Gesture reports thus appear partly retrieved with the sentence and partly inferred from it: memory for speech and gesture is closely coupled.

articles.title: Irregular Natural Environments Are Associated with Better Context-Supported Recall
articles.authors: Dylan Chau Huynh; Aja Khalid Hussein; Lars Brorson Fich; Zakaria Djebbara
articles.abstract: Natural environments are often treated as a relatively uniform category in cognitive research despite substantial variation in their spatial organization and regularity. This study examined whether episodic memory depends not only on environmental type but also on the internal structure of the environment. Sixty participants experienced four immersive virtual environments in a 2 × 2 within-subject design crossing environmental type (natural vs. urban) with structural regularity (rhythmic vs. irregular). Memory was assessed using free, cued, and delayed recall and analyzed using linear mixed-effects models controlling for presentation order. Immediate recall showed little evidence of environmental effects. In contrast, Cued Recall 1 showed a significant Environment × Regularity interaction, with the irregular natural environment producing the highest performance. Follow-up contrasts showed higher recall in irregular nature than in all three comparison conditions for Cued Recall 1 and Delayed Recall, with a more selective advantage during Cued Recall 2. Retention proportions did not differ across conditions, indicating that delayed differences reflected earlier memory advantages rather than differential forgetting. These findings suggest that episodic memory effects associated with natural environments cannot be understood through a nature–urban distinction alone. Instead, the internal organization of an environment may shape memory, with irregular natural environments potentially providing more distinctive contextual information that becomes particularly useful during context-supported retrieval.

articles.title: Noradrenergic influences on human thought
articles.authors: Claire O'Callaghan
articles.abstract: Neuromodulators help balance the trade-off between flexibility and stability that is needed for adaptive cognition and behaviour. Among the neuromodulators, the noradrenergic system plays a key role in balancing this trade-off: it helps shape whether we pursue a given behaviour or task, versus shifting our behaviour to pursue an alternate strategy. Put differently, the noradrenergic system drives the balance between a stable versus flexible engagement with the world around us. How might this capacity relate to human thought? In this chapter, we review the functional and organisational principles of the locus coeruleus–noradrenergic system, and consider how it might modulate different aspects of human thought. Highlighting examples from attention, belief-updating, spontaneous thought and stress. Together, revealing how the locus coeruleus–noradrenergic system helps shape the balance of flexibility and stability in human thought.

articles.title: When the brain can change: effects of neuroplasticity education on beliefs about brain-based mental disorders
articles.authors: Olha Guley; Elena Pasquinelli; Daniel Nettle
articles.abstract: Mental disorders are increasingly framed as brain-based, which can promote pessimism about recovery. We tested whether brief education about neuroplasticity, the brain’s capacity to change throughout life, can counter these beliefs. Across three preregistered vignette experiments with UK adults (Ns = 414, 411, and 418), participants viewed a brain-framed mental disorder after either a brief neuroplasticity video and text intervention or a matched control. The intervention increased the perceived possibility of recovery, but this effect was short-lived after a single exposure in Study 1 and more durable with a booster in Study 2. The effect in Study 3 was not significant, but a pooled analysis of data from Studies 2 and 3 confirmed the positive effect overall. The intervention did not affect perceived treatment efficacy, nor did it reduce desired social distance from people with mental disorders. In Study 3, higher familiarity with the disorder was associated with a higher perceived recovery and lower desired social distance. These findings suggest neuroplasticity education can increase public optimism about recovery from mental disorders, but changing treatment beliefs or social attitudes may require more targeted interventions.

articles.title: Coming of Age in Polarized Times: Affective Polarization Across Adolescence
articles.authors: Jakob Kasper; Gijs Schumacher; Lysanne te Brinke; Eveline Crone; Bert N. Bakker
articles.abstract: Concerns about affective polarization among young people have grown in political, media, and academic debate. Yet, despite adolescence being a crucial period of identity formation and young people’s central role in shaping the future of democratic societies, little is known about when affective polarization emerges, and how it varies across adolescence and political environments. Drawing on survey data from adolescents (N = 7,031; ages 11–25) and adults (N = 9,997; ages > 25) in the Netherlands, the United Kingdom, Austria, Poland, and Greece, we examine within-adolescence age differences in affective polarization, adolescent-adult differences, and temporal variation in affective polarization levels around a major political event. We find that affective polarization is already visible by early adolescence and differs remarkably little across adolescent age groups, challenging the expectation that affective polarization increases sharply around the transition to the legal voting age. Comparisons with adults in the Netherlands, the United Kingdom, and Austria show that adolescents are consistently less affectively polarized than adults. Further, our longitudinal panel evidence from the Netherlands suggests that adolescent affective polarization varies with the broader political environment, increasing around the 2023 parliamentary election and declining thereafter. This illustrates that adolescent affective polarization is not fixed but varies with political dynamics, highlighting adolescence as an important period for educational efforts that foster democratic engagement and constructive political disagreement.

articles.title: Data-Matrix-Based Overall Goodness-of-Fit Testing for Confirmatory Factor Analysis: In-Sample Prediction Error for Observed Variables
articles.authors: Young Ze Kim; Gyeongcheol Cho; Hanjoe Kim
articles.abstract:
Conventional χ²-based tests in confirmatory factor analysis assess overall fit through covariance reproduction and remain the standard inferential tools for overall goodness-of-fit testing. However, they do not directly quantify the magnitude of model misfit and may become unavailable when estimation fails to converge or produces improper solutions.
We introduce and evaluate two data-matrix-based alternatives within structured factor analysis: the in-sample prediction error for observed variables (IPEo) test for a single model and the ΔIPEo test for nested models. IPEo quantifies the proportion of variability in the observed data matrix left unexplained by the hypothesized model, while its bootstrap p value provides an inferential decision. Monte Carlo simulations showed that the IPEo-based tests controlled Type I error, gained power with increasing sample size, and remained available when conventional χ²-based tests frequently failed. An empirical illustration further showed that the IPEo value and its p value provide complementary information about the magnitude and statistical significance of model misfit. These findings support IPEo-based testing as a complementary inferential framework for evaluating CFA model fit directly at the level of the observed data matrix.

articles.title: Ostensive affective feedback and the emergence of the capacity to negotiate communicative content: the psychology of establishing agreement.
articles.authors: Wouter Wolf
articles.abstract: Inferring agreement, that is, inferring that mental content is mutually considered to be sufficiently aligned for the purposes of an interaction, is crucial for many facets of human sociality. Importantly, humans are highly skilled at facilitating such inferences through communication. Yet even within communicative interactions, agreement might fail for interpretive reasons (uncertainty or misunderstanding) or alignment reasons (disagreement). Solving either of these problems often requires iterative communicative interactions during which the content of mental states is negotiated until misunderstandings are repaired and/or disagreements are resolved through compromise. But what social cognitive mechanisms allowed humans’ successful negotiation capacities to emerge, even when conventionalized negotiation and communication systems were not available? Here, I argue that humans developed the capacity to directly negotiate the content of communication by understanding the interactive intent underlying ostension in a previously underappreciated way: To infer a lack of agreement in communicative interactions, a key piece of evidence lies in how the other reacts to one’s communicative act. However, this reaction is often ambiguous. I argue that ostension helps facilitate interpreting such reactions, not only through assumptions of mutual relevance, but in large part due to pragmatic tension that arises from ostensive non-affirmative affective feedback. This tension forces individuals to isolate content as a separate dimension of communicative acts that can be evaluated and negotiated. This facilitates the resolution of interpretive problems through boundary-setting and disagreement through compromise. As such, ostensive feedback has likely played a major role in the emergence of human sociality.

articles.title: Loneliness and Interpersonal Emotion Regulation in Everyday Life
articles.authors: Jasmin Bruna Stariolo; Anh Tran; Kristina Mei; Katharine Helen Greenaway
articles.abstract: Loneliness is a growing public health concern rooted in emotional distress and social disconnection. Interpersonal emotion regulation — managing ones’ own or others’ emotions — is a mechanism for strengthening social bonds and fostering emotional health. Their shared socio-emotional foundation raises the possibility that loneliness may be connected to how people regulate others and are regulated in turn. Accordingly, we investigated whether loneliness is associated with adaptive and maladaptive interpersonal emotion regulation strategies in the moment and over time. To address this question, we conducted a daily diary (N = 170, collected 2020; Study 1) and experience sampling study (N = 239, collected 2021; Study 2). Participants reported on global trait loneliness, then recorded momentary loneliness and use of four strategies as both regulator (regulating others extrinsically) and target of regulation (being regulated by others intrinsically) for seven days. State loneliness predicted greater invalidation as both regulator and target, and global trait loneliness predicted less physical support as regulator and target. Most consistently, the person-level average of momentary loneliness across the week predicted greater use of all strategies — responsiveness, invalidation, reappraisal, and physical support — both as regulator and target. Methodologically, our findings show the importance of assessing loneliness at different time scales. Theoretically, our findings suggest lonely individuals do actively attempt emotion regulation during interactions, yet they may be just as likely to use maladaptive strategies that undermine connection as adaptive strategies that enhance it. This work underscores the importance of interaction quality in understanding how loneliness persists and might be interrupted.

articles.title: Same Effect, Different Magnitude: How the Choice of Pre- or Post-Treatment Standard Deviation Shapes Standardized Effect Sizes in Psychological Clinical Trials
articles.authors: Matthias Pillny; Anika Buchholz; Anna Suling; Antonia Zapf; Tania Marie Lincoln
articles.abstract: Standardized mean differences (SMDs) are used to express treatment effects on a common metric, yet there is no consensus on whether mean differences should be standardized using the outcome standard deviation (SD) at baseline or follow-up. This study examined whether this choice systematically affects effect-size magnitude in a reproducible sample of 100 randomized psychological clinical trials. For each trial, SMDs were calculated using either the pooled baseline SD (SMDpre) or the pooled follow-up SD (SMDpost). The unweighted paired mean difference showed that |SMDpre| was, 0.11 SMD units larger than |SMDpost|, 95% CI [0.07, 0.14]. In a multilevel meta-regression |SMDpre| was 0.082 SMD units larger than |SMDpost|, equalling a 13% increase, 95% CI [0.042, 0.123]. Bland–Altman analysis indicated substantial between-study variation, 95% limits of agreement [−0.25, 0.46]. Secondary analyses including 2,228 effect sizes across all follow-ups mirrored this pattern, indicating a 7% increase of SMD magnitude associated to |SMDpre|, 95% CI [0.021, 0.044]. Moderator analyses suggested that discrepancies were larger in studies applying symptom-threshold eligibility criteria, and in secondary analyses, using the same measure both to determine eligibility and to assess the outcome and with longer follow-up. Importantly, 70% of included studies did not report how SMDs were operationalized. These findings demonstrate that the choice of standardizing SD systematically affects estimated treatment-effect magnitudes and that the discrepancy can become more pronounced under specific design conditions. Researchers should therefore carefully consider the choice of standardizer and explicitly report the time point and method used to derive the SD.

articles.title: Made in the Culture, Not the Voice: Lyrical Camp, Production Texture, and the Queer Anthemization of Popular Songs
articles.authors: Logan Barrett
articles.abstract: Why do some popular songs become queer anthems while others, including many by openly queer artists, do not? We tested musical affordance and historical contingency accounts in a purposive corpus of 100 songs (69 artists) designed to dissociate queer authorship, explicit queer lyrical content, and community adoption. Adoption was measured as an evidence-coded anthemization score from URL-verified documentation of Pride, drag, ballroom, club, activist, and queer-media use. Anthemization was unrelated to whether artists were publicly queer (rs = −.02) and only weakly related to explicit queer lyrics (rs = .22). Among 16 language-model-coded lyrical themes, camp potential predicted anthemization after family-wise correction and controls for era, genre, authorship, and explicit content (partial r = .40, n = 55). The association replicated with masked lyrics, among songs the coding model could not identify, with a second coding model, and with two independent outcome coders (partial r = .45–.54, n = 46), although it was not robust when the model's own anthem judgements were also partialled out. Full-mix acoustic descriptors related to formant energy and voicing predicted anthemization (|rs| = .38–.43, family-wise p < .05) but vanished when computed on Demucs-separated vocal stems (n = 80), locating the acoustic signal in production texture rather than the singer's voice; spectral brightness was confounded by genre and era. Outcome reliability was moderate (weighted κ = .57). The results support reception-centred accounts of musical queerness. They implicate lyrical camp and production as affordances for queer adoption, not a characteristic queer voice.

articles.title: Cultural Differences in Emotion Regulation May Not Be Unique to Expressive Suppression
articles.authors: Sooyeon Kim; Katharine Helen Greenaway; Peter Koval
articles.abstract: Controlling emotion expression is theorized to be more valued and thus more frequently used and beneficial among Easterners than Westerners. However, existing evidence relies on global self-reports capturing culturally informed beliefs about suppression rather than moment-to-moment suppression. Moreover, whether cultural differences are specific to suppression or reflect broader emotion-regulation patterns remains unclear. Using three experience-sampling datasets, we tested cultural differences in suppression across global and momentary self-reports and their specificity. Easterners reported greater suppression at both global and momentary self-reports. Cultural differences were specific to suppression at global levels but generalized to reappraisal and rumination at momentary levels. We found less support for cultural differences in the affective correlates of emotion regulation. However, there was moderate evidence that momentary suppression, reappraisal, and rumination were less strongly associated with negative affect among Easterners than Westerners. We provide the first comprehensive test of cultural differences in suppression and suggest they may reflect broader emotion-regulation patterns.

articles.title: Multi-party simulations with human participants and role-based LLM conversational agents: A design framework and validity evidence for organizational research
articles.authors: Yuki Nozaki; Naho Fujisawa; Yoshinobu Kano
articles.abstract: Dynamic organizational phenomena often unfold through ongoing communication among multiple interdependent actors, yet studying them involves trade-offs among realism, controllability, and scalability. We propose a methodological framework for using role-based conversational agents powered by large language models (LLMs) as multi-party interaction partners in organizational research. It specifies how to create standardized but contingent interaction environments through scenario design, persona prompts, interaction protocols, and iterative testing. In a preregistered illustrative study of leadership communication, we analyzed 394 employees’ text-based simulations powered by GPT-5.2, Gemini 2.5 Flash, or Claude Sonnet 4.6. Across models, participants perceived the agents as anthropomorphic and animate, and as acting consistently with their assigned backgrounds, personalities, and linguistic styles. Behavioral coding corroborated and extended these perceptions, with deviations from assigned persona prompts in 2.59% of utterances. Participants’ utterances also yielded codable indicators of theoretically relevant behavior, in this case leadership communication. These findings provide initial validity evidence that multi-party LLM-agent simulations can create plausible interaction environments, deliver persona-consistent stimuli, and elicit behaviorally analyzable responses. We also offer practical guidelines on model selection, replicability, and ethics.

articles.title: Unsupervised transfer in relational category learning
articles.authors: Hilary Don; Micah Goldwater; Kit S Double; Evan James Livesey
articles.abstract: Abstraction of relational structures beyond surface features is essential for transfer of learning across contexts. However, learners often fail to apply relational knowledge outside the original learning setting. Our prior work shows that inference-learning can promote relational abstraction and supervised far transfer, but it remains unclear whether such learning supports spontaneous transfer without feedback. This study tested whether inference learning improves unsupervised far transfer across tasks with distinct surface characteristics. Participants learned to categorise stimuli based on monotonic versus non-monotonic relations among line lengths, under classification or inference-learning conditions. Transfer was assessed for luminance-based dot arrays and digit sequences, presented in counterbalanced order. Inference-learning led to stronger relational responding during training and significantly improved far transfer performance overall, even in the absence of feedback. Transfer accuracy was higher for digit sequences than dot arrays, particularly among participants who demonstrated strong relational learning. Moreover, an unexpected finding was that completing the digit task first selectively improved subsequent transfer to the dot task, suggesting that symbolic representations may scaffold relational alignment. These findings provide evidence that inference-learning fosters abstract relational representations that support far transfer, while also highlighting the role of representational format and task sequencing in enabling effective generalization.

articles.title: Echoes of Thought: Task Complexity, Inner Speech Analogs, and Prompt Design Shape LLMs' Response
articles.authors: Franziska Usée; Daniel Schad
articles.abstract:
Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown impressive performance across a wide range of tasks, yet
the mechanisms behind theirresponse behaviorremain poorlyunderstood. Drawing on insights from
cognitive science and the computational framework of model-free and model-based reinforcement
learning (RL), we examined conditions under which GPT-3.5 and four open-weight LLMs can exhibit
behavioral signatures of model-based RL in the two-step task, a well-established paradigm for
studying human learning and decision-making. Across nine simulation studies, we varied the task
complexity and prompt design to examine conditions under which previously reported model-based
RL signatures could be replicated. We found that GPT-3.5 showed model-based RL signatures in
simplifiedtasksettings,butthattheseeffectsdisappearedunderde-simplifiedtaskversions.Crucially,
model-based reasoning signatures could be re-established when incorporating an inner speech-
analog prompt, requiring the LLM agent to reflect on previous trials and anticipate consequences of
future actions. For the open-weight LLMs tested, diminished signatures of model-based reasoning
evolved under both de-simplified and facilitative task conditions. Our fine-grained analyses of
behavioral learning dynamics highlight the role of structured reflective and anticipatory linguistic
processes in enabling complex response patterns in LLMs and reveal both similarities and differences
to human decision-making patterns.

articles.title: Christian Nationalism as a Unique Predictor of Policy Attitudes and Voting Behavior: The Christian Nationalism Scale
articles.authors: Jason Michael Miller
articles.abstract: Christian Nationalism (CN) is a unique political ideology that has long been prominent in U.S. politics. Current measures of CN have poor psychometric properties (Davis, 2023). Study 1 (n=237) shows that CN predicts voting behavior and policy attitudes when controlling for established religious and political measures and provides an initial test of the Christian Nationalism Scale. Study 2 (n=603) replicates findings that CN is the best predictor of voting behavior and policy attitudes when accounting for established religious and political measures. A CFA shows excellent psychometric properties of the scale, and invariance testing shows similar factor structure across Christian denominations and racial groups. Study 3 (n=313) finds CN best predicts support for politicians who will restrict individual freedoms on topics related to traditional Christian values. These studies demonstrate that CN explains unique variance in voting (past and anticipated) and policy attitudes. This work provides a validated scale for future research.

articles.title: The Ultimate Tutorial for AI-driven Scale Development in Generative Psychometrics: Releasing AIGENIE from its Bottle
articles.authors: Lara Lee Russell-Lasalandra; Hudson Golino; Luis Eduardo Garrido; Alexander P. Christensen
articles.abstract:
Psychological scale development has traditionally required extensive expert involvement, iterative re-
vision, andlarge-scalepilottestingbeforepsychometricevaluationcanbegin. TheAIGENIE Rpackageim-
plementstheAI-GENIEframework(AutomaticItemGenerationandValidationwithNetwork-Integrated
Evaluation), which integrates large language model (LLM) text generation with network psychometric
methods to automate the early stages of this process. The package generates candidate item pools using
LLMs, transforms them into high-dimensional embeddings, and applies a multi-step reduction pipeline
— Exploratory Graph Analysis (EGA), Unique Variable Analysis (UVA), and bootstrap EGA — to
produce structurally validated item pools entirely in silico. This tutorial introduces the package across
eight parts: installation and setup, text generation, embeddings, item generation, the full AI-GENIE
pipeline, the GENIE pipeline for researcher-supplied items, advanced prompt engineering, and fully lo-
cal operation. Two running examples illustrate the package’s use: the Big Five personality model (a
well-established construct) and AI Anxiety (an emerging construct). The package supports multiple
LLM providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Groq, HuggingFace, and local models), offers a fully offline mode
with no external API calls, and provides the GENIE() function for researchers who wish to apply the
psychometric reduction pipeline to existing item pools regardless of their origin. The AIGENIE package
is freely available on CRAN at https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=AIGENIE.

articles.title: mlstats: An R package for multilevel descriptive statistics and data preparation
articles.authors: Felix Dietrich
articles.abstract: Mobile research methods such as experience sampling, smartphone logging, and daily diary designs produce nested data, in which within-level fluctuations must be distinguished from between-level differences. Yet, there is no established convention for preparing and descriptively reporting such multilevel data. This paper introduces mlstats, an open-source R package that computes multilevel descriptive statistics — including intraclass correlation coefficients and within- and between-group correlations — in a single call, exports publication-ready tables, and decomposes variables for random effects within-between (REWB) modeling. Supporting both frequentist and Bayesian estimation, mlstats is freely available on CRAN with extensive online documentation at https://felixdidi.github.io/mlstats/.

articles.title: The Male Evaluator Penalty: How Participant Sex and Relationship Context Shape the Perceived Credibility of Male Sexual Violence Victims
articles.authors: Martina Giorgio; Robyn Mooney
articles.abstract: Male victims of female-perpetrated “forced-to-penetrate” sexual violence experience significant psychological harm and stigma shaped by traditional gender scripts. However, research is scant regarding how such victims are perceived by others. This study investigated how participant sex (male vs. female), perpetrator-victim relationship context (intimate partners vs. strangers), and male rape myth acceptance affect the perceived credibility of male sexual violence victims. Using an experimental vignette design, 300 participants (50.3% male, aged 18-35) living in the Netherlands were asked to read a description of a female-perpetrated sexual assault and complete self-report measures of perceived victim credibility and male rape myth acceptance. Results of a moderated multiple regression analysis indicated that higher myth acceptance universally predicted lower credibility ratings for the male victim. Furthermore, male evaluators displayed significantly higher myth acceptance and rated the victim as less credible overall than female evaluators. Crucially, male victims assaulted by an intimate partner were perceived as significantly less credible than those assaulted by a stranger, but this penalty was applied exclusively by male evaluators. These results highlight the urgent need for targeted education for legal professionals and gender-inclusive legal reforms to ensure equitable justice for male victims of female-perpetrated sexual violence.

articles.title: Dyadic Theory of Mind profile shapes verbal cooperation and the trajectory of non-verbal cooperation
articles.authors: Roksana Markiewicz; Ali Mazaheri; Katrien Segaert
articles.abstract: Theory of Mind (ToM) is thought to support cooperation, yet it is studied as a property of individuals, even though cooperation is achieved by two people together. We examined whether cooperation depends on the ToM profile of a dyad: the pair's average ToM and the mismatch (absolute difference) between partners. Unacquainted pairs completed two cooperation tasks. In a verbal task, each partner held information needed to solve a shared problem, and partners had to talk to combine it. In a non-verbal task, partners synchronised button presses without communicating, adjusting their timing based on feedback. ToM was assessed using the Movie for the Assessment of Social Cognition (MASC; Dziobek et al., 2006); fluid intelligence was controlled. Across both paradigms, we found converging evidence that cooperative performance was shaped by the interaction between partners’ ToM abilities, beyond individual ToM ability in isolation. In the verbal task (N=171 pairs), larger ToM mismatches were associated with poorer cooperative performance in pairs with relatively low average ToM, whereas higher average ToM attenuated this detrimental mismatch effect. In the non-verbal task (N=175 pairs), the same pattern emerged only over time: pairs with large ToM mismatches and relatively low average ToM improved their synchrony more slowly, so that their disadvantage was most pronounced late in the task, when cooperation depends more on anticipating the partner’s adjustments. Taken together, our findings suggest that ToM operates not only as an individual socio-cognitive capacity but also as a dyadic resource that shapes how partners establish shared representations in cooperative settings.

articles.title: Selective reductions amid global increases in neural information dynamics jointly track self-dissolution in meditation
articles.authors: Daniel Andrew Atad; Pedro A. Mediano; Fynn-Mathis Trautwein; ‪Yair Dor-Ziderman‬‏; Henrik Röhr; Yoav Schweitzer; Ohad Nave; Stephen Fulder; Aviva Berkovich-Ohana
articles.abstract: The sense of self is fundamental to experience, yet its neural basis remains unresolved. Contemplative traditions and empirical evidence suggest it can be voluntarily dissolved while retaining awareness, offering a window onto this question. We combined magnetoencephalography with in-depth phenomenology in long-term meditators (N=45, mean 3,832 practice hours) who reliably modulated self-boundaries across rest, self-maintenance and self-dissolution. Meditation broadly increased entropy and information transfer, yet selective reductions characterized self-dissolution. Reduced posterior-medial high-beta entropy and within-cingulate information transfer differentiated dissolution from maintenance. Information transfer reductions from occipital, cingulate, limbic, and subcortical regions, alongside orbitofrontal entropy stabilization, correlated with dissolution phenomenology. Combined with posterior-medial high-beta power reductions, these correlates explained 52% of dissolution depth variance, yet only information transfer predicted held-out participants. We propose selfhood relies on distributed processes that can be reconfigured in meditation through relaxed priors, gated bottom-up evidence, and stabilized evaluative dynamics, distinct from global disruption during psychedelic ego-dissolution.

articles.title: Aligning how we measure and support social media addiction with young people's lived experience
articles.authors: Lukas J. Gunschera; Jamil Adjallah; ioanna fokas; Gabriel Mackie; Jo Hickman Dunne; Alice Roe; Jade Davies; Camilla Nord; Margarita Panayiotou; Amy Orben
articles.abstract: Social media use is widely conceptualised as a potential addiction. However, the instruments used to index it are reformulations of criteria developed for established addictions, presuming pathology rather than establishing it. We inverted the direction of inference, integrating lived experience from adolescents who feel addicted to social media and experienced substantial life impairment as a consequence. We conducted eight in-person workshops with 44 adolescents (contributors) to discuss experiences constituting social media addiction, their perceived harms, and how those experiencing it could best be supported. We examined correspondence between lived experiences and features of established addictions, such as conflict (interpersonal struggles and loss of self-control), salience (preoccupation with social media), and tolerance (needing more to get the same effect). Discussions of how, by whom, and through what means adolescents could be supported were analysed using framework analysis. Correspondence between lived experience and the prevailing addiction model was partial and asymmetric. Of 121 experiences, 58.7% described conflict or salience, none described tolerance, and few described withdrawal (2.5%) or relapse (7.4%). A fifth (20.7%) fell outside the model. Effects on sleep, attention, mental health, and time displacement were ranked as most harmful, while impaired control and social comparison ranked lower. Discussions of support revealed a strong sense of individual responsibility, alongside agreement that platform redesign, provision of alternative activities, and shifts in social norms would be most effective. Clinical addiction intervention was rarely raised, despite frequent use of medical addiction language and analogies. These results raise questions about current addiction models and the assumption of pathology applied to social media use. Future work should move beyond these frameworks and ground conceptualisation and measurement in lived experience rather than predefined notions of disorder.

articles.title: Do People Think ChatGPT Is Conscious? Evidence from a Large Polish Sample
articles.authors: Hubert Plisiecki
articles.abstract:
Large language models (LLMs) like ChatGPT are increasingly treated by the public as if they
possess subjective experience, with multiple studies probing the popular opinion on the matter. The
present study provides the first large-scale measurement of this phenomenon in Poland. A
nationally distributed online survey panel (N = 1,736) rated ChatGPT’s capacity for conscious
experience on a 1–100 scale. "Most respondents (74%) attributed ChatGPT at least minimal
consciousness on the continuous rating scale, closely mirroring prior U.S. findings; because this
figure is sensitive to question format, however, we conservatively estimate that more than 10% of
respondents would affirm ChatGPT's status as an experiencer under a stricter, categorical framing.
Small exploratory associations suggested that older and more highly educated participants were
slightly more skeptical, whereas right-leaning respondents attributed slightly more consciousness.
A multivariate regression confirmed that these associations were not simply artifacts of
confounding among demographic variables, though together they explained less than 3% of the
variance in consciousness attributions. These effects, though modest, indicate theoretically relevant
variation. Interpreting these results through Epley’s three-factor anthropomorphism model, the
work argues that limited mechanistic understanding of LLMs, highly human-like behavior, and
unmet social needs likely contribute to widespread phenomenal consciousness attribution. Given
ethical concerns about over-trust, parasocial attachment, and responsibility misperception, these
beliefs matter for AI deployment and governance. Our findings highlight the need for evidence-
based educational strategies that improve public understanding of how LLMs work while allowing
beneficial use of the technology

articles.title: Morphological analysis when morphemes are hard to detect: evidence from infixation and reduplication
articles.authors: Dave Kenneth Tayao Cayado; Kathleen Rastle
articles.abstract: There is substantial psycholinguistic evidence that skilled reading involves morphological analysis, whereby morphologically complex words like teacher are recognised via constituent morphemes {teach}+{-er}. The ability to recognise morphemes is vital as it allows readers to interpret both familiar and unfamiliar words. However, over 50% of the evidence for this claim comes from studies of suffixation in English, where morphemes typically have a relatively consistent surface form across exemplars (clean in cleaner, cleanliness; -ed in walked, jumped).
