It remains unclear whether morphological analysis is also robust when morphemes lack a consistent surface form. Using the morpheme interference paradigm in Tagalog, we test whether infixes and reduplicants are detected during prelexical processing. Infixes are inserted within a stem and therefore reduce the consistency of its surface realisation (e.g., tawag → t-in-awag ‘called’), while reduplicants involve partial or full copying of a stem and therefore lack a consistent surface realisation (e.g., tawag and lundag become tatawag ‘will call’ and lulundag ‘will jump’, where ta- and lu- are instances of the same reduplicant morpheme). We found robust morpheme interference effects in both accuracy and RTs. Specifically, nonwords with morphological structure induced significantly lower accuracy and longer RTs than nonwords without. Our findings show skilled readers’ acquired sensitivity to these sophisticated morphological structures and motivate refinements to theories of morpheme learning.

articles.title: Can You Read Me Through the Screen? Only Extraversion Shows Distinctive Personality Accuracy in Face-to-Face and Videoconferencing Interactions
articles.authors: Valentina Andreeva; Maxim Likhanov; Elina Tsigeman
articles.abstract: Existing theories yield competing predictions regarding personality perception accuracy in face-to-face versus videoconferencing. While cue-reduction frameworks suggest videoconferencing deceases accuracy, social presence perspectives argue decreased constraints facilitate self-expression, leaving the impact of videoconferencing unresolved. This study examined personality perception accuracy following face-to-face and videoconferencing interactions. Previously unacquainted participants (N = 168; 40 videoconferencing and 44 face-to-face dyads) engaged in 40-minute interaction. Pre- and post-interaction Big Five self- and partner-ratings were analyzed via the Social Accuracy Model, partitioning accuracy into distinctive and normative components and controlling for assumed similarity. Results demonstrated that videoconferencing neither impaired nor enhanced distinctive personality accuracy relative to face-to-face. Trait-level analyses revealed only extraversion exhibited significant distinctive accuracy across both formats. These findings indicate perceptual accuracy is driven less by communication modality and more by diagnostic behavioral cues and trait observability.

articles.title: Measuring Multimodal Social Skills in the Digital Age: Development and Validation of a Questionnaire
articles.authors: Aike Horstmann
articles.abstract: As inherently social beings, humans possess specialized communicative capacities, that are essential for fostering social connection and supporting both personal and collective well-being. In an increasingly technology-driven social landscape, a psychometrically sound instrument is crucial for assessing these evolving social skills, identifying individuals experiencing interpersonal difficulties, and evaluating targeted interventions over time. This paper reports the development and validation of the Multimodal Social Skills Questionnaire (MSSQ), an instrument designed to assess social skills across diverse interaction modalities, including both online and offline environments. Multimodal social skills comprise six core dimensions: Assertiveness, Receptivity, Flexibility, Authenticity, Appreciativeness, and Resilience. Across two studies, the aim was to establish the scale’s factor structure, reliability, and construct validity. In Study One (N = 322) an initial pool of 120 items was subjected to exploratory factor analysis (EFA) and iterative item reduction, resulting in a preliminary six-factor solution. In Study Two (N = 260), confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) supported the refined six-factor structure. Construct validity was supported by expected patterns of convergent and discriminant correlations with established measures. Across both studies, the MSSQ showed strong internal consistency. Overall, the findings support the MSSQ as a reliable and valid instrument for assessing multimodal social skills in the evolving digital age.

articles.title: Slips of Action in Everyday Life: Capturing Habitual Smartphone Checking with a Decoy App Paradigm
articles.authors: Tim van Timmeren; Jonas Dano; Michael J. Moustaka; Lukas J. Gunschera; Sanne de Wit
articles.abstract: The study of habit has long faced a trade-off between experimental control and ecological validity. We translated a core laboratory test of habit to daily life: whether people continue responding despite knowing it no longer produces its outcome. For one week, participants (N = 74) replaced a frequently used social media app with a nonfunctional decoy icon. The original app was either removed (Detox) or relocated (Switch). Taps on the decoy were recorded as action slips. Nearly all participants slipped (97%), with mean daily slips dropping from 9.76 on the first day to 1.08 on the last across both groups. Slips correlated with baseline app openings (rs = .61) and self-reported automaticity (rs = .40), but not with motivation to reduce usage, problematic use, perceived control, or well-being (|rs| ≤ .09). Decoy slips thus capture a key behavioural signature of habit and reveal how strong app-checking habits can be.

articles.title: Seeing good and bad for what they are: Preverbal infants discern valence in geometric-agent interactions
articles.authors: Yaying (Tiffany) Bai; Hiromichi Hagihara; Yasuhiro Kanakogi
articles.abstract: Animated shapes have informed much of what is known about early sociomoral cognition, but concerns have been raised about this approach and the interpretations based on it. In particular, whether infants perceive interactions between geometric agents as socially and affectively meaningful has received little direct attention, despite being a prerequisite for moral evaluations. Two preregistered experiments conducted between 2025 and 2026 addressed this gap in infants aged 6.5 to 10.5 months (N = 92; 43 girls), recruited from middle-socioeconomic-status families living in urban and suburban areas of [city name], Japan (all Japanese or other East Asian). In Experiment 1 (n = 28; 13 girls), infants preferentially attended to agent-directed, relative to perceptually matched object-directed, caressing (prosocial) and hitting (antisocial), which indicates sensitivity to social structure. In Experiment 2 (n = 64; 30 girls), infants attended more when caressing and hitting were preceded by affectively congruent rather than incongruent music (i.e., prosocial-positive, antisocial-negative), suggesting that they attributed corresponding valence to these interactions. The results substantiate the use of geometric-agent paradigms and provide evidence that foundational evaluations of good and bad emerge within the first year of life, extending prior findings beyond simple approach-avoidance responses to prosociality and antisociality.

articles.title: Memory precision fluctuates with theta rhythmicity in humans
articles.authors: Troy Houser; Riley Acker; Dagmar Zeithamova
articles.abstract: Rodent research indicates that the hippocampus naturally oscillates between memory encoding and retrieval phases at theta rhythm, indicating that the timing of when information reaches the hippocampus can determine encoding success. However, non-invasively probing such oscillations is challenging in humans. Here, we employed a recently developed dense sampling approach to construct a time course of memory encoding success. Using an attention-grabbing cue expected to reset theta phase, we varied the delay between the cue and to-be-remembered stimulus. Experiment 1 replicated recent finding that human associative memory performance fluctuates with theta rhythmicity, with the best fitting frequency at 8 Hz. Experiment 2 tested and confirmed a new prediction that memory precision also fluctuates with theta rhythmicity, consistent with hippocampal models postulating oscillations in the relative engagement of alternative processing pathways. Together, these findings suggest that the rapid neural fluctuations underpinning memory processes are robust enough to be observed using the dense behavioral sampling approach. Moreover, this work substantiates models of episodic memory and provides new avenues to study models of hippocampal function in humas noninvasively, providing evidence from a purely behavioral approach that human mnemonic discrimination fluctuates with theta rhythm.

articles.title: Embodied mirroring increases interpersonal synchrony of movement and social connection established in subsequent conversations
articles.authors: Yasemin Abra; Christine Falter-Wagner; Irene Sophia Plank
articles.abstract: Interpersonal synchrony, the alignment of behaviours between individuals, is thought to facilitate social connection and rapport. However, less is known about whether synchrony can be intentionally fostered and whether its effects extend beyond the context in which it is established. We examined whether participation in the Mirror Game, a fundamental exercise from theatre where two players nonverbally imitate each other’s movements, influences subsequent interactions between previously unacquainted strangers. Using recordings of facial expressions, gaze patterns, and movement, we captured multi-modal conversational dynamics during a conversation. In line with our preregistered hypothesis, dyads who played the Mirror Game before conversing exhibited greater interpersonal synchrony of movement than those who performed a non-social movement exercise, suggesting a carry-over effect of instructed to emerging interpersonal synchrony. Furthermore, playing the Mirror Game prior to the conversation also increased positive social connection and rapport. However, increased interpersonal synchrony of movement on the level of the dyad did not account for these social benefits, challenging straightforward accounts linking synchrony to social connection. By contrast, exploratory analyses further revealed that behavioural patterns capturing interpersonal adaptation at the individual level predicted participants’ positive social experiences and feelings of connection emerging in the conversation. Together, these findings demonstrate that a brief shared embodied activity can shape the quality of a subsequent interaction and provide new insight into the processes through which positive social connections emerge between strangers.

articles.title: Expertise Shapes the Multidimensional Perception of Stories
articles.authors: Qingzhi Ruby Zeng; Derek Lilienthal; Coraline Rinn Iordan; Aaron Steven White; Elise A. Piazza
articles.abstract: Storytelling is a primary means of human connection and creative expression, but it is unclear how mechanisms of story perception may vary across people with differing expertise. Here, we examined how expertise in creative storytelling shapes ratings of five dimensions of story quality (creativity, imagination, novelty, complexity, cohesiveness), as well as how these ratings are influenced by four linguistic feature categories (language productivity, lexical predictability, semantic similarity, and lexical composition). Online storytellers (N=18) improvised six spoken stories each (for a total of 108 stories). The transcript of each story was rated by both novices (N=10-31) and creative writing/storytelling experts (N=15) on the five story dimensions and analyzed using the four linguistic feature categories above. Overall, experts and novices provided similar average ratings, and their rating spaces both showed two distinct underlying principal components–essentially, creativity and cohesiveness–which were, in turn, predicted by distinct linguistic features. However, experts perceived the five dimensions as more differentiated, and their ratings were less driven by linguistic features than novices’. These findings indicate that experts’ judgments are more nuanced but also may rely less on fine-grained structural features of narratives, highlighting the importance of capturing individual differences and multidimensionality in story perception.

articles.title: Everyday use of AI for emotion regulation depends on the person and the situation
articles.authors: Simon M. Li; Junkang Averi Lin; Shufang Sun; Shanshan Xu; Bin Yu; Mark S. Chen
articles.abstract: Young adults increasingly use AI to seek support and manage their feelings. Understanding when and where they use AI for emotion regulation (ER) and its effectiveness can provide evidence needed for research, practice, and policy. In a 13-day ecological momentary assessment study, 3,048 Chinese university students reported emotional situations, ER strategies, and affect four times daily. AI use for confiding, advice, or emotional support was reported on 2.0% of 134,275 prompts and by 17.3% of participants at least once. In person-level logistic regression, use was concentrated among students with greater lifetime AI use (OR up to 3.12); in multilevel logistic regression, it was more likely during digital, academic, and interpersonal situations (OR 1.22-2.56). AI use did not predict next-prompt affect overall, but was followed by lower positive affect when neither stressors nor positive events had occurred, weakening as more events co-occurred. AI has entered everyday ER as a context-dependent resource.

articles.title: Does Parent-Rated Neurocognitive Functioning of Children with ADHD Moderate the Effects of Different Behavioral Parent Training Techniques?  A Randomized Controlled Microtrial
articles.authors: Dominique Petra Amadee Doffer; Barbara van den Hoofdakker; Tycho Dekkers; Rianne Hornstra; Marjolein Luman; Saskia van der Oord
articles.abstract: The effectiveness of behavioral parent training (BPT) techniques for children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) may vary across individuals. Using a microtrial, we studied whether parent-ratings of child “hot” and “cool” executive functions moderated effects of stimulus-control (antecedent-based) versus contingency-management (consequent-based) techniques on child behavioral difficulties. Parents of 92 children with ADHD were randomly assigned to antecedent-based training, consequent-based training or waitlist. Results indicated that consequent-based techniques were particularly effective for children with lower arousal regulation and higher reward responsivity, while antecedent-based techniques were most effective for children with lower sensitivity to aversive stimuli. Possible explanations for these findings are discussed.

articles.title: Inhabiting digital ecologies: A qualitative approach to good digital practices
articles.authors: Esther Paniagua; Myriam Durán Vilches; Noemí Robles; Pepa Barral González; Manuel Armayones
articles.abstract:
The integration of digital technologies into everyday life has produced complex digital
ecologies in which platforms, algorithms, and social practices jointly shape experience,
identity, and emotional regulation. Although research on digital well-being has
increased significantly, little is known about how individuals reflect on their digital lives
and the practical criteria they develop to navigate these environments while preserving
well-being and autonomy.,This paper addresses these questions through qualitative
research conducted within a digital community of 100 adults residing in Spain whose
participation unfolded across four successive waves. Fieldwork combined individual
journals, thematic forums, and an open social space, generating a longitudinal corpus
on the everyday experience of inhabiting digital spaces. Results were interpreted
through discourse analysis to reconstruct shared patterns of meaning and discursive
positions.,Findings reveal an ambivalent relationship with digital environments: the
same tools that enable connection, communication, and access to information are also
described as sources of noise, overstimulation, attention fragmentation, and loss of
control. Alongside these discomforts, participants describe daily repertoires of
adjustment that crystallise into distinct discursive positions from which they inhabit
digital ecologies and develop good practices.,We propose that good digital practices
should not be understood as a universal list of self-regulatory norms, but as relational
competencies developed through reflection and experience. Methodologically, the
study shows that a digital community is a particularly suitable tool for examining
everyday, complex, largely automated phenomena, since it enables participants to
observe, compare, and transform their digital experience into practical criteria guiding
their relationship with digital ecologies.

articles.title: Digital Reflections of Social (Dis)connectedness: A Snapchat Data Donations Study
articles.authors: J. Loes Pouwels; Milou Tilstra; Lara Vreeswijk; Nienke Prot; Michelle Alexandra Pingel
articles.abstract: By linking self-reported psychosocial experiences to actual Snapchat interactions, the present study aims to provide a nuanced understanding of how social experiences are reflected in digital contexts. Specifically, the study investigates how adolescents’ experiences of friendship closeness, peer belongingness, loneliness, and social exclusion are related to adolescents’ online interactions with friends by combining real-time experience sampling methodology (ESM) with objective social media data from Snapchat. Participants were 123 adolescents (M age = 13.33 years; SD = 1.10; 58.50% girls). Adolescents with higher disconnectedness (i.e., greater loneliness and social inclusion) had more unanswered friendship requests and spent relatively more time on messaging. After controlling for multiple testing, social (dis)connectedness was not associated with the actual number of sent or viewed messages in the past two months, the number of friendships, Snapscore, or Snapchat AI usage. These findings do not provide clear evidence for either the social enhancement hypothesis or compensation hypothesis.

articles.title: Displacement and Compensation: How Online and In-Person Interactions Relate to Adolescents’ Social and Emotional Connectedness
articles.authors: J. Loes Pouwels; Marlies Maes; Daan Hulsmans; Maaike Verhagen
articles.abstract: By proposing that superficial online interactions displace deeper, in-person connections, displacement theory has given rise to widespread societal concerns about adolescents' use of social media. However, previous research only showed limited evidence for the displacement theory. Therefore, this study aims to provide a more nuanced understanding of how both online and in-person interactions shape adolescents' sense of connectedness. A total of 335 adolescents in Grades 7-9 participated in a 4-week Experience Sampling Methodology study. Three times a day, they reported on their in person and online interactions with friends and peer groups, as well as the quantity and quality of these interactions and their perceived connectedness to their friends and peer groups. Multilevel analyses will be used to examine how the occurrence of in-person and online contact, as well as the quantity and quality of these interactions, are related to adolescents’ social and emotional connectedness.

articles.title: Not “born that way”: Homophobic social preferences and non-essentialism of sexual orientation in childhood
articles.authors: Rebecca Peretz-Lange
articles.abstract: Although prejudice begins early in development, very few studies examine the developmental roots of homophobia. We explored the onset and developmental timecourse of homophobic social preferences as well as the cognitive and environmental factors predicting these preferences. We were particularly interested in whether children would essentialize orientation (e.g., consider it inborn and uncontrollable), since essentialism often positively correlates with prejudice but negatively correlates with adolescents’ and adults’ homophobia. As environmental predictors, we explored parents’ anti-prejudiced values and children’s LGBTQ contact. A diverse sample of participants from across the United States (n = 128 six- to nine-year-olds, 60 girls & 68 boys, 42% White & 58% of color) selected between heteroparental and homoparental peers in a Playmate Preference Task and then completed an essentialism assessment. Parents reported their anti-prejudiced values and children’s LGBTQ contact. Homophobic social preferences were present by age seven and increased across childhood. Moreover, despite children’s pervasive essentialist tendencies, participants overwhelmingly rejected the idea that being in a same-gender vs. other-gender marriage reflects any internal uncontrollable characteristic. Instead, children viewed this as a matter of choice. Essentialism was very low overall and did not predict social preferences. Instead, parents’ values and children’s LGBTQ contact predicted these preferences. In sum, children view orientation as reflecting a choice rather than an intrinsic nature, and then rely on the adults in their lives to determine how to feel toward that choice. Homophobic social preferences therefore emerge early and in the context of behavioral views of orientation. Social, cognitive, and developmental implications are discussed.

articles.title: The Not So Illusory Truth Effect: Source Credibility and the Effect of Repetition on Belief
articles.authors: Reed Orchinik; David Gertler Rand; Rahul Bhui
articles.abstract: The illusory truth effect, in which repetition increases belief, is often seen as a cognitive bias. Here, we argue that it may reflect a rational adaptation to generally high-quality information environments. A formal model shows that increasing belief in repeated statements improves accuracy when a source usually tells the truth but sometimes errs. The model captures previous findings and, unlike existing accounts, predicts that repetition should do little to increase belief when the source is not credible. In a large (N = 4,947) preregistered experiment with a quota-matched U.S. sample, the effect was substantially smaller when headlines appeared in a mostly false rather than mostly true newsfeed. In a second preregistered experiment (N = 2,484), repetition increased partisans' belief only in claims from the 2024 U.S. presidential candidate they trusted. Repeated misinformation may therefore be most persuasive when it comes from sources people trust.

articles.title: Forging ahead, pulling back, and acting strategically: Climate activists’ responses to criminalisation and repression in the UK
articles.authors: Peter Gardner; Sunniva Davies-Rommetveit; Jenny Douch; Anna Aretha Sach
articles.abstract: In response to the post-2018 rise in climate protest, many liberal democratic countries have witnessed the criminalisation and repression of environmental activists. Instead of assessing macro-level effects of repression on activism, this paper explores the micro-level responses to surveillance, arrest, fines, and imprisonment. Drawing on socio-legal scholarship that understands the law as socially constructed rather than objective and external, this paper delves into the black box of political repression, offering an examination of how climate activists respond to state sanctions. Analysing a survey of 1,375 Extinction Rebellion UK activists through thematic analysis and quantitative coding, we demonstrate that individual biography and narrativisations of the law lead activists to forge ahead, pull back, or act strategically in response to repression.

articles.title: Felt but Not Detected:  Salience Versus Detectability of Affective Change in Ambulatory Assessment
articles.authors: Aleksandra Kaurin; Mario Wenzel; Paula Philippi; Jonas Dora
articles.abstract: Ambulatory assessment (AA) captures within-person fluctuations in daily life, yet not all observed change exceeds measurement error, and not all reliable change is subjectively experienced. We propose a preregistered dual-threshold framework distinguishing statistical detectability (smallest detectable change, SDC) from experiential salience (minimal important change, MIC). Adults (N = 250) completed a 14-day AA protocol with twice-daily and event-contingent assessments (5,982 observations), rating momentary stress, positive affect, and negative affect (0–4) and perceived change since the previous assessment. SDC₉₅ estimates ranged from 1.56 to 1.92 scale points, so roughly three-quarters of consecutive changes fell below reliable detection. Anchor-based MICs, in contrast, were 1 point for all constructs. Correspondence between detectable and perceived change was asymmetric: sensitivity was high (.77–.87), but specificity (.46–.56) and positive predictive values (.24–.31) were low, as participants frequently reported change without reliable change; directional reversals were rare. Reliable change strongly predicted perceived change (ORs 4.6–12.5). Event-contingent assessments, higher prior states, and person-level characteristics (e.g., impulsivity, emotion regulation) increased the general propensity to report change but did not moderate this link. Felt change thus precedes measurable change: detectability and salience are distinct thresholds that intensive longitudinal research must evaluate separately.

articles.title: Cross-Lagged Panel Analysis Using Structural Equation Modeling: Trends and Suggestions Based on a Literature Review of 111 Studies
articles.authors: Asuka Nishida; Satoshi Usami
articles.abstract:
Cross-lagged panel analysis based on structural equation modeling (SEM) has been widely used in the behavioral sciences. The present study provides a literature review based on 111 studies published in major psychology journals that conducted cross-lagged panel analysis. Through this review, we offer an overview of current trends in study design, analytical methods (e.g., estimation method, missing data handling), and model selection, and discuss practical challenges and implications for future applications. A major finding is that the use of the random intercept cross-lagged panel model (RI-CLPM) has increased substantially (41% of the studies) over the past few years. At the same time, most studies rely on longitudinal data with a small number of measurement occasions (e.g., T = 3 − 4). Studies that employed the RI-CLPM on the grounds that it enables inference about within-person relations tended to conduct only limited comparisons with potential alternative models, and only 3% of the studies evaluated model fit from the perspective of local fit (i.e., residual correlations). Although many studies using psychological scales relied on sum scores, only 40% of the studies examined longitudinal measurement invariance, suggesting that there is
still room for improvement.

articles.title: Questionable mediated effect of adolescent neuroticism on short-form video overuse: A comment on Liu and Wu (2026)
articles.authors: Kimmo Sorjonen; Bo Melin; Marika Melin
articles.abstract: Drawing on the covariance matrix reported by Liu and Wu, we reassessed the empirical basis of their mediation model linking adolescent neuroticism to short-form video overuse (SVO). We demonstrate that the observed covariance structure can be reproduced by a theoretically different latent-variable model that does not rely on the directional mechanism proposed in the original article. In this alternative account, self-reported neuroticism, depression, anxiety, and SVO are conceptualized as indicators of a broader construct, core self-evaluation. The results illustrate a broader inferential problem in psychological research: multiple theoretically plausible models may provide equally adequate explanations of the same correlational pattern. Consequently, observational associations alone offer limited grounds for preferring one explanation over competing alternatives. Researchers should therefore routinely evaluate alternative models when drawing inferences about psychological mechanisms from nonexperimental data.

articles.title: Is GenAI Helpful for Writing? A Re-Analysis Using Robust Bayesian Meta-Analysis (RoBMA)
articles.authors: Shawn Hemelstrand
articles.abstract: A recent meta-analysis showed that genAI has a strong impact on writing. The current analysis instead shows that the effects are negligible after correcting for heterogeneity and publication bias.

articles.title: Assessing resurgence as persistence in the Valproic Acid rat model of Autism Spectrum Disorder
articles.authors: Ana J O Cerveira; Eldereis de Paula; Andréia Schmidt; Fernando Eduardo Padovan-Neto
articles.abstract: Behavioral persistence poses a clinical challenge in patients with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD), as targeted problematic behaviors resist elimination and reemerge upon treatment discontinuation (resurgence). Prenatal exposure to valproic acid (VPA) has been proposed as a rat model of ASD that would increase behavioral persistence, but findings in this model have been inconsistent. This study investigated whether prenatal VPA exposure increases persistence by assessing the persistence of target responding on a three-phase resurgence procedure: Training (target response reinforced), Elimination (target response placed on extinction while an alternative response is reinforced), and Testing (alternative response also placed on extinction, producing resurgence of target responding). Male and female Sprague-Dawley rats prenatally exposed to saline (SAL) or VPA were compared. Target and alternative response rates did not differ between SAL and VPA animals in either sex at any phase, nor did the proportional change from target to alternative responding during Elimination or the magnitude of resurgence at Testing. Males did, however, display higher resurgence magnitudes than females in both prenatal conditions. Together, these findings indicate that VPA-exposed rats do not behave more persistently, but contribute to the investigations of potentially ASD-related traits in this animal model in a behavioral analytic perspective.

articles.title: Rethinking Spaced Practice Under Limited Instructional Time: The Benefits of Repetition Depend on Spacing
articles.authors: Meng Cao; Paulo F. Carvalho
articles.abstract: Spacing and repetition are two fundamental principles of learning, yet under limited instructional time, increasing repetitions necessarily shortens the intervals between encounters. Prior research found that more repetitions with shorter spacing produced better learning than fewer repetitions with longer spacing, but the respective contributions of spacing and repetition remained unclear. The present study sought to disentangle these contributions and replicate prior findings. Data were collected in 2026 from 120 English-speaking U.S. adults. Participants learned Indonesian-English word pairs three or six times under both massed and spaced schedules within a fixed instructional time. Retention was assessed immediately, one day, and three days later, and forgetting curves were used to estimate initial memory strength and forgetting rate. We replicated the advantage of more repetitions with shorter spacing. Spaced practice produced greater initial memory strength and slower forgetting than massed practice, whereas additional repetitions increased initial memory strength only when practice was spaced. These findings suggest that, under time constraints, additional repetitions benefit learning primarily when spaced, indicating that the advantage of repeated practice depends on the accumulation of learning across spaced encounters.

articles.title: Development and Accuracy Evaluation of an LLM-Assisted Workflow for Screening and Data Extraction in Large-Scale Syntheses
articles.authors: Vsevolod Scherrer; Franzis Preckel; Moritz Breit
articles.abstract:
Large-scale research syntheses are labor-intensive and prone to human error, and large language models (LLMs) could support their screening and data extraction. Building on current recommendations, we developed an integrated workflow for title and abstract screening (Step 1), full-text screening (Step 2), and data extraction (Step 3), and evaluated it in a preregistered proof-of-concept study.
The study updated a meta-analysis on the rank-order stability of cognitive abilities, in which records may report several nested coefficients. Every step used ensembles of five LLM-instances, and we evaluated 2,960 workflow configurations against a human gold standard of 892 records, of which 692 records with 102 coded effect sizes formed the evaluation set. Without human review, Steps 1 and 2 retained 96.72% and 100.00% of eligible records. At Step 3, the LLMs missed 35.05% of gold effect sizes in rule-based extracted text but none in text from machine-learning-based parsing, which also lowered their coding error from 10.16% to 2.61%. In the recommended configuration, human review was confined to Step 3, where checking effect sizes of 5 of 40 records and 16.43% of the cells raised specificity to 100.00% and coding accuracy from 97.39% to 99.24%.
We derive five recommendations: (1) refine criterion-specific prompts on a calibration set, (2) use machine-learning-based PDF parsing for data extraction, (3) aggregate ensemble ratings leniently at screening and strictly at data extraction, (4) focus human review on data extraction, targeted via flags and ensemble disagreement, and (5) identify nested effect sizes in a separate stage with unique identifiers.

articles.title: On Color and Emotion: What Can Vision Science Learn from the Rorschach?
articles.authors: David Henry Peterzell
articles.abstract: For a century, clinicians have recorded how people use color when they interpret inkblots, rank colored cards, or draw. They believed that how a person handles color reveals how that person handles feeling. Vision science has rarely read this literature, and the most complete modern review of color and emotion research excluded it. This paper introduces the projective color literature to vision scientists in plain language. Three conclusions follow. First, the tradition’s central belief, that chromatic color stirs emotion directly, was tested from the 1940s onward and largely failed. Second, narrower findings survived. The degree to which a person lets color lead over form in an ambiguous image is modestly related to several independently assessed clinical, behavioral, and biological outcomes. Some indices that set color in balance with other responses, such as coping versus overload, are also supported. What these scores measure is disputed. Third, the findings concern how color is weighted against form, which vision science already studies, yet only one study has linked that weighting to an object-recognition task, and none has used calibrated stimuli. I then read both literatures through a constructivist model of color in which the percept and the wider event it belongs to determine each other reciprocally. On this reading, the question is not only whether color influences emotion but also whether emotion influences color. The projective tradition raised the second question. Modern color-emotion science has mostly set it aside. Five studies are proposed that would join the two fields.

articles.title: The multidimensional structure of perceptual and aesthetic evaluation: Independent features, interacting feature values, and perceptual unity
articles.authors: Eline Van Geert; Nori Jacoby
articles.abstract: Subjective appearance and aesthetic appreciation are inherently multidimensional, arising from the combined influence of a variety of visual features such as color, shape, and size. Yet, how multiple feature dimensions jointly shape perceptual and aesthetic evaluations remains poorly understood. Most previous studies either employ multidimensional stimuli without precise parametric control or use parametrically controlled stimuli that vary along only one dimension, limiting our understanding of the multidimensional structure underlying subjective evaluations. To address this challenge, we combined two methodological advances: the Order & Complexity Toolbox for Aesthetics (Van Geert et al., 2023), which enables the generation of parametrically controlled multidimensional stimuli, and Gibbs Sampling with People (Harrison et al., 2020), which efficiently characterizes subjective evaluations in high-dimensional stimulus spaces. Our stimuli consisted of visual displays containing multiple elements that varied in color, shape, and size and were arranged according to different organizational structures. Across nine experiments involving more than 1,000 participants and over 125,000 evaluations, we estimated multidimensional probability distributions underlying perceptual evaluations of order and complexity and aesthetic evaluations of pleasure and interest. Three main findings emerged. First, evaluations depended on both absolute feature values and relative differences between elements for each feature dimension, indicating that observers are sensitive not only to the characteristics of individual elements but also to the relations among them. Second, the influence of these relative differences depended on the overall perceptual organization of the display. Preferences for simplicity — operationalized as small differences in feature values between elements — varied systematically across evaluation criteria and with the degree of perceptual unity within the display. Third, despite these contextual effects, different visual features (color, shape, and size) conributed largely independently to the evaluations, suggesting that their influences on subjective evaluations are relatively separable. Together, these findings provide a multidimensional account of how visual features and their relations jointly shape perceptual and aesthetic evaluations.

articles.title: Inhabiting digital ecologies: A qualitative approach to good digital practices
articles.authors: Esther Paniagua; Myriam Durán Vilches; Noemí Robles; Pepa Barral González; Manuel Armayones
articles.abstract:
The integration of digital technologies into everyday life has produced complex digital
ecologies in which platforms, algorithms, and social practices jointly shape experience,
identity, and emotional regulation. Although research on digital well-being has
increased significantly, little is known about how individuals reflect on their digital lives
and the practical criteria they develop to navigate these environments while preserving
well-being and autonomy.,This paper addresses these questions through qualitative
research conducted within a digital community of 100 adults residing in Spain whose
participation unfolded across four successive waves. Fieldwork combined individual
journals, thematic forums, and an open social space, generating a longitudinal corpus
on the everyday experience of inhabiting digital spaces. Results were interpreted
through discourse analysis to reconstruct shared patterns of meaning and discursive
positions.,Findings reveal an ambivalent relationship with digital environments: the
same tools that enable connection, communication, and access to information are also
described as sources of noise, overstimulation, attention fragmentation, and loss of
control. Alongside these discomforts, participants describe daily repertoires of
adjustment that crystallise into distinct discursive positions from which they inhabit
digital ecologies and develop good practices.,We propose that good digital practices
should not be understood as a universal list of self-regulatory norms, but as relational
competencies developed through reflection and experience. Methodologically, the
study shows that a digital community is a particularly suitable tool for examining
everyday, complex, largely automated phenomena, since it enables participants to
observe, compare, and transform their digital experience into practical criteria guiding
their relationship with digital ecologies.

articles.title: Facial evidence matters less for stereotype-consistent judgments: Weaker formidability-aggression associations in Black vs. White faces
articles.authors: Kirstan Brodie; Brandon Cohen; Youngki Hong
articles.abstract: Facial characteristics are reliably associated with social judgments, but these relationships may depend on whether a judgment is consistent with stereotypes of the target’s social group. Across four studies with adult participants, we tested this possibility using perceived aggression and threat in Black and White faces. Perceived dominance (Study 1, N=117) and physical strength (Study 2, N=626) predicted aggression judgments less strongly for Black than White faces. Dominance also predicted perceived threat less strongly for Black than White faces after controlling for several threat-related covariates (Study 3, N=380). Furthermore, machine learning analyses found less overlap in dominance- and threat-predictive facial information for Black faces. Finally, face morphing that matched featural variation across race while manipulating apparent race showed a weaker dominance-aggression relationship for Black-appearing faces (Study 4, N=467). Together, these findings are consistent with the possibility that facial evidence has reduced influence on judgments of stereotype-consistent traits.

articles.title: Characterizing deaf and hard-of-hearing language experiences as arousal-regulation processes
articles.authors: Christina Kim; Laurel Aichler; Onudeah Nicolarakis; Shilpa Hanumantha Lacy; Rachel Sortino; Rachel Pizzie
articles.abstract: Empirical language research with deaf and hard-of-hearing (DHH) groups often includes proficiency, age of acquisition, or language background measures but excludes people’s socioemotional context. Measuring socioemotional context depends on characterizing the socioemotional experiences associated with DHH language development and use. We used the biopsychosocial model of arousal regulation as a theoretical lens to explore 11 qualitative interviews with DHH participants. Using reflexive thematic analysis, we developed three characteristic themes: 1) Deafness is not a monolith, 2) Name it to tame it – Language Anxiety, and 3) Positive roots for resilient shoots. These themes show that DHH language experiences are heterogeneous, that negative experiences can represent language anxiety, and that positive experiences modulate arousal regulation. Our study highlights new socioemotional considerations for language processing research like how emotions influence language use, how motivations support language skills, and how communication strategies impact social interactions within DHH communities.

articles.title: Bridging Psychophysics and Psychometrics to Address Dyslexia Screening Floor Effects: An Adaptive-Timing Approach
articles.authors: Wanjing Anya Ma; Benjamin Domingue; Guilherme Lichand; Karine Votikoske Roncete; Lucas Iantorno Klotz; Carrie Townley-Flores; Adam Richie-Halford; Jason D. Yeatman
articles.abstract: As children learn to read, two skills develop in parallel: the complexity of words they can decode and the speed of word recognition. Reading assessments capture these processes with timed and untimed tasks, yet it remains unclear whether word processing speed and word difficulty are separable dimensions of reading ability or two manifestations of the same skill. The distinction has practical stakes: beginning readers decode too few words to be measured precisely, producing floor effects that limit early dyslexia screening. Here, we independently manipulated word difficulty and presentation time in a lexical decision task to test whether they constitute distinct axes of reading development. Through a research--practice partnership, we collected large-scale developmental data from 3,147 students spanning Grades 1--12 in the United States (English) and Brazil (Portuguese). Items presented with infinite presentation time were systematically less difficult but required longer response times than items under fast conditions, for students across development in both language contexts. Importantly, word processing speed and word difficulty were characterized by a unidimensional framework, indicating that presentation time extends a single difficulty continuum rather than measuring a second construct. We leveraged this result to design and validate a multistage adaptive-timing screener for dyslexia (N = 14,393 calibration; N = 841 validation). A K--2 validation study showed that adaptive timing reduced floor effects and improved screening precision and efficiency for beginning readers. By integrating the experimental precision of psychophysics with scalable psychometric frameworks, this work shows how basic science can be translated into universal school-based dyslexia screening.

articles.title: Life Control: A Psychological Theory
articles.authors: Leonardo Bonneti
articles.abstract: Life Control is the capacity to remain an active and effective director of one’s life under changing and constrained conditions. Existing psychological theories explain important elements of agency, motivation, self-regulation, resilience, and flexibility, but do not integrate the broader patterns through which people direct different parts of their lives. This article proposes Life Control as a framework of ten dimensions organised across four domains: Self, Growth, Others, and Life Organisation. The dimensions describe distinct but interacting tendencies involving emotional regulation, self-understanding, effort, responses to adversity, practical responsibility, relationships, and the allocation of personal and material resources. The theory also proposes four connecting claims. Self-direction is recursive because present actions shape both later capacities and future conditions. Rationality keeps action responsive to evidence, while a spark of delusion permits action before success is assured. Psychologically formative activities develop or maintain capacities through participation, and the Non-Outsourcing Principle predicts that assistance supports Life Control when it preserves such participation but may weaken it when it repeatedly replaces it. The framework generates testable predictions concerning the dimensions, their combinations, development over time, and the consequences of different forms of assistance.

articles.title: Dawdling at Dusk: Affect and Bedtime Procrastination
articles.authors: Yijun Lin; Erin Corwin Westgate
articles.abstract: Why don’t people go to bed on time? Most research on bedtime procrastination has focused on individual differences (e.g., self-regulation, chronotype), potentially conflating between-person patterns with within-person processes. To address this, we examined whether affective valence and arousal predict bedtime procrastination within people, between people, or both. In Study 1, we replicated cross-sectional associations between negative affect and bedtime procrastination in a Chinese community sample. In Studies 2–3, we attempted to manipulate valence and arousal in separate week-long diary experiments; the manipulations produced limited shifts in affect and did not significantly change bedtime procrastination. Across both diary studies, however, analyses of self-reported affect revealed a consistent pattern: people who generally felt less positive were more likely to procrastinate, whereas evening-to-evening fluctuations in affect did not predict whether they procrastinated on a given night. Exploratory analyses in Study 2 suggested that this between-person association was partly indirect through feeling less able to go to bed. Taken together, these findings suggest that whether people put off going to bed may be more closely tied to how they typically feel than to how they feel on a given evening, highlighting the importance of separating between-person and within-person levels.

articles.title: Growing Beyond Traits: A Skill-Based Approach to Volitional Personality Change
articles.authors: Christopher J. Soto; Christopher Napolitano; Madison Nicole Sewell; Heejun Roy Yoon; Tommaso Feraco; Nathan W. Hudson; Brent Roberts
articles.abstract: Recent research suggests that individuals can intentionally change their personality traits. This article proposes a complementary, skill-based approach to volitional change, arguing that social, emotional, and behavioral (SEB) skills—defined as learned capabilities rather than dispositional tendencies—represent more direct and intuitive targets for intentional development. We introduce the Cumulative Practice Model (CPM), a framework that integrates principles from the personality development, clinical intervention, managerial coaching, and cognitive science literatures. This model proposes that the volitional development of SEB skills can occur most effectively through a repeating cycle of motivation, instruction, opportunity, practice, feedback, and skill change. We then review preliminary evidence supporting this model. This evidence indicates that individuals generally find developing SEB skills to be more desirable and feasible than changing personality traits. It further shows that skills exhibit plasticity across the lifespan, with both normative age trends and individual-level changes linked to relevant life experiences. Crucially, it suggests that interventions centered on deliberate practice can facilitate SEB skill development, and that gains in these skills are linked with positive life outcomes including academics, occupational interests, social relationships, health, and well-being. Thus, the Cumulative Practice Model offers a promising framework for individuals who wish to improve their SEB skills, practitioners who wish to facilitate skill development and growth, and researchers who wish to better understand the antecedents, process, conditions, and outcomes of volitional change. This skill-based approach to volitional change also highlights open questions and promising directions for future research.

articles.title: The 2024 U.S. Election, Sexual and Gender Minority Adults’ Moving Plans, and Mental Health Symptoms: A Mixed-Methods Analysis
articles.authors: Briana Shiri Last; Nguyen Tran; Dane Rivas-Koehl; Devin Hursey; Juno Obedin-Maliver; Mitchell Lunn; Annesa Flentje
articles.abstract:
Introduction: Since the 2024 U.S. Presidential election, the rights of sexual and gender minority (SGM) people have been at risk. The purpose of this mixed-methods study was to describe SGM people’s thoughts, plans, and decisions to move following the election and to examine whether these thoughts, plans, and decisions differed by participants’ sociodemographic characteristics and mental health symptoms. 
Methods: Participants completed an online survey between November 5, 2024 and September 20, 2025 for The PRIDE Study, a national, prospective, community-engaged cohort study of SGM adults. Participants responded to closed-ended questions about their: thoughts, plans, and decisions to move; sociodemographic characteristics; and mental health (anxiety, depression, and posttraumatic stress disorder) symptoms. Participants responded to open-ended questions about their moving destinations and moving reasons. 
Results: The sample included 3,301 participants (48.1% identified as transgender or nonbinary [TNB]). Most participants (85%) thought about, planned to, or decided to move to another state or country. Moving considerations differed by participants’ sociodemographics (e.g., participants with moving thoughts, plans, and decisions were more likely to be TNB than cisgender, ps<.05) and mental health symptoms (e.g., participants with moving thoughts, plans, and decisions had more symptoms than those with no moving thoughts, ps<.05). Participants’ reasons for moving included the increasingly hostile and anti-SGM sociopolitical conditions in their states and the country. 
Conclusions and Policy Implications: Following the 2024 election, many SGM U.S. adults made plans to or decided to move due to the changing policy environment. Psychological distress from anti-SGM policies may be driving individuals to move.

articles.title: Characterizing deaf and hard-of-hearing language experiences as arousal-regulation processes
articles.authors: Christina Kim; Laurel Aichler; Onudeah Nicolarakis; Shilpa Hanumantha Lacy; Rachel Sortino; Rachel Pizzie
articles.abstract: Empirical language research with deaf and hard-of-hearing (DHH) groups often includes proficiency, age of acquisition, or language background measures but excludes people’s socioemotional context. Measuring socioemotional context depends on characterizing the socioemotional experiences associated with DHH language development and use. We used the biopsychosocial model of arousal regulation as a theoretical lens to explore 11 qualitative interviews with DHH participants. Using reflexive thematic analysis, we developed three characteristic themes: 1) Deafness is not a monolith, 2) Name it to tame it – Language Anxiety, and 3) Positive roots for resilient shoots. These themes show that DHH language experiences are heterogeneous, that negative experiences can represent language anxiety, and that positive experiences modulate arousal regulation. Our study highlights new socioemotional considerations for language processing research like how emotions influence language use, how motivations support language skills, and how communication strategies impact social interactions within DHH communities.

articles.title: Perceived error climate in elementary school classrooms: A multidimensional perspective
articles.authors: Jana Spear; Donna Bryce; Cara-Sophie Enste; Robert Grassinger; Markus Dresel
articles.abstract: The error climate in the classroom captures the extent to which errors are positively perceived and treated as constructive learning opportunities by teachers and students. It has been conceptualized as comprising eight subdimensions organized under a single second-order factor among secondary school students (Steuer et al., 2013). However, this structure has not yet been investigated in younger students. Consequently, we examined the error climate’s structure in elementary school classrooms while additionally proposing a novel and more differentiated second-order structure distinguishing between emotional and instructional support following errors. Among 2,628 elementary school students from 187 classrooms across two domains (maths and German), multilevel multigroup confirmatory factor analyses at the individual and classroom level were conducted. Results revealed a multifaceted error climate perception already in elementary school, with eight subdimensions loading onto the two proposed second-order factors. These, in turn, were also positively related to students’ individual adaptive reactions to errors.

articles.title: Gaze semantics: A scoping review of how gaze conveys and constrains meaning in social contexts
articles.authors: Nikol Figalová; Anne Böckler; Lynn Huestegge
articles.abstract: Humans rely on gaze to encode information and signal to others. Gaze may indicate where someone is attending, but its contribution extends beyond spatial orientation. Evidence is scattered across different research traditions. This scoping review synthesises 361 publications on gaze as a meaningful social cue. Gaze semantics describes the systematic contribution of gaze to conveying and constraining social meaning. A cross-domain synthesis identified four recurrent operations: gaze orients by making objects, people, or locations socially relevant; addresses by positioning people as recipients or interaction partners; qualifies by modifying how other cues are interpreted; and coordinates by organising participation and unfolding action. These functional contributions can co-occur within a single gaze event. Gaze interpretation is inferential, shaped by five categories of contextual factors: signal properties; interactional availability; multimodal and sequential embedding; cultural, social and activity frame; and gazer and observer states and interactional history. We propose a Gazer-Observer Model of Gaze Understanding that integrates these findings to describe the dynamic relation between gaze production and interpretation. The same gaze pattern may support different interpretations across situations yet allow a relatively specific interpretation within a particular encounter. Gaze can therefore systematically affect social interpretation while remaining semantically underdetermined to varying degrees.

articles.title: Neural Racing Accumulator Model Estimation With Lightweight Monotonic Flows
articles.authors: Malte Lüken; Stefan T. Radev; Lourens Waldorp; Andrew Heathcote
articles.abstract: Race models describe speeded decision-making as a race between competing runners that accumulate evidence in favor of available choice options. Their parameters can be estimated through the model likelihood that combines the probability and cumulative density functions of each runner. However, estimating parameters of complex race models whose runners have intractable densities with (hierarchical) Bayesian inference has been challenging: Numerical density approximations tend to be slow and amortized neural posterior estimation methods require complex network architectures that can be expensive to train and, in classical settings, tie the trained estimator to a specific prior distribution and generative model. We propose a flexible neural estimation method that decouples training from the choice of prior distribution or model parameterization. We train a small neural network together with a monotonic neural spline flow to simultaneously learn the runners' conditional probability density and cumulative density functions. We then combine both functions to efficiently estimate race model likelihoods that can be used in combination with modern samplers. We demonstrate the utility of our approach on both tractable and intractable versions of the popular racing diffusion model. Based on our results, we argue that, when flexibility in choosing prior distributions or model parameterizations is needed, learning the model likelihood with lightweight neural density estimators is advantageous.

articles.title: Children and adults infer traits from observed immoral behavior, but children preferentially use emotional expressions to predict future moral violations
articles.authors: Sophia Thierry; Rebekah Gelpi; Denise Arefhaghi; Jessica A. Sommerville
articles.abstract: Learning which characteristics of another person are reliable and relevant for predicting how that person is likely to behave in the future is fundamental to social cognition. This is particularly true of moral behavior given the importance of anticipating potential harm. Across three experiments (data collected between December 2020 and May 2022), we investigated how six- to eight-year-old children (total N = 94; 50 girls; predominantly Canadian) and adults (N = 48; American) weighed a character’s prior behavior and emotional expressions to infer whether that character would commit a future moral violation. Both children and adults used a character’s prior behavior and their emotional expressions to inform their predictions; however, children relied on emotional expressions to a significantly greater degree than adults. Further, children and adults attributed a negative trait (meanness) and state (anger) to characters who committed a prior moral violation. However, whereas trait attributions mediated adults’ predictions of future violations, neither trait nor state attributions mediated children’s predictions. These findings reveal developmental differences in both the cues used to predict others’ moral behavior, and in the representations underlying these predictions.

articles.title: Problematic Internet Use and Anxiety in Adolescents: A Scoping Review of Mechanisms and Contextual Influences
articles.authors: Cleo Albertus; Freda Scheffler; Sibeko; Dan J. Stein; Christine Lochner; Nynke A. Groenewold
articles.abstract: Problematic internet use (PIU) and anxiety are prevalent, co-occurring difficulties during adolescence, yet their shared psychological mechanisms remain insufficiently mapped. This scoping review investigated evidence on the PIU-anxiety relationship in adolescents aged 13-18 years, following Arksey and O’Malley’s framework and PRISMA-ScR guidelines. PubMed, EBSCOhost, and Web of Science were searched from January 2014 to December 2025, supplemented by hand-searching of reference lists. Ninety-six studies from 20 countries were included. Across all modalities, PIU was associated with elevated anxiety. Longitudinal studies indicated suggestive but not definitive bidirectional associations with symptoms of anxiety. Avoidance-based coping and cognitive-emotional dysregulation emerged as primary mechanism clusters, with emotion dysregulation as a central transdiagnostic process. Co-occurring internalising phenomena including depressive symptoms and loneliness were included where they provided relevant context for interpreting the association between PIU and anxiety in adolescents. Family functioning, social support, and environmental stressors moderated associations. These findings indicate that PIU and anxiety should be assessed concurrently. Interventions may benefit from targeting shared transdiagnostic mechanisms, particularly emotion dysregulation, while taking family and environmental contexts into account.

articles.title: Epistemic Stances in Humanoid Robot Evaluation: Evidence from the Frankenstein Syndrome Questionnaire and Morph-Based Perceptual Judgements
articles.authors: Ilaria Maria Antonietta Benzi; Francesca Ciardo
articles.abstract: Humanoid robots occupy an ambiguous position between social partners and artefacts, and people differ markedly in how they evaluate them. Research on individual differences in human–robot interaction has focused on personality, anthropomorphic tendencies and technology acceptance, leaving largely unexamined the processes by which people decide whether an artificial agent can be treated as a credible source of social information. The present study introduces epistemic stances, as conceptualised within the mentalizing tradition, to this literature. Seventy adults completed the Epistemic Trust, Mistrust and Credulity Questionnaire, along with measures of generalized attitudes toward robots (Frankenstein Syndrome Questionnaire, Negative Attitudes toward Robots Scale, Robotic Social Attributes Scale), and a morph-based task in which robot faces varying in human likeness were rated for likeability, eeriness and human likeness. Epistemic stances were selectively associated with generalized social evaluations: Epistemic Trust predicted higher Robot Anxiety and lower attributed Warmth, whereas Credulity predicted higher attributed Warmth, with no associations for perceived Competence. At the stimulus level, morph condition strongly shaped all three judgements, whereas epistemic stances added little. Rather than a failure to extend person-level effects, this dissociation follows from the claim that epistemic stances operate on socially communicated information rather than on perceptual appraisal. Epistemic functioning may therefore shape the social meaning attributed to artificial agents, offering a testable framework for the design of robot communication.

articles.title: Beyond Virtue: Courage's Associations with Aversive Intentions and Behaviors and Dark Triad Traits
articles.authors: Grzegorz Pajestka; Katarzyna Skałacka
articles.abstract: Individual differences associated with aversive behavior have been linked primarily to antagonistic personality traits. Less is known about whether characteristics typically regarded as adaptive also contribute. Courage is traditionally viewed as a virtue, yet theoretical accounts suggest it may also facilitate socially aversive behaviors. This study tested whether two operationalizations—psychological courage (PC) and courage as a character strength (VIA-C)—predict aversive intentions and behaviors beyond Dark Triad traits (Machiavellianism, narcissism, psychopathy). A community sample of 711 Polish adults completed measures of PC, VIA-C, the Short Dark Triad, and aversive intentions and behaviors. Variable-centered analyses (hierarchical regressions, two-part models) controlling for age, gender, and Dark Triad traits revealed domain-specific effects: both courage measures predicted higher aggressive intentions and greater frequency of aggressive behaviors; VIA-C additionally predicted aggressive and sex-/drug-related behaviors. Neither courage measure related to theft, reckless driving, or self-destructive behaviors, and PC showed a small protective association with self-destructive intentions. Latent profile analysis identified four classes defined primarily by Dark Triad levels rather than courage; no high-courage/low-antagonism profile emerged. Overall, findings challenge unqualified valorization of courage and underscore the need to pair courage-building with ethical frameworks, empathy training, and prosocial goal setting to reduce iatrogenic risk.

articles.title: Psychiatric Overdiagnosis as Diagnostic Stretching in Response to Clinical Need
articles.authors: Awais Aftab
articles.abstract: I define psychiatric “overdiagnosis” as the observation that there has been a rapid rise in the rate of mental health diagnoses in recent decades, combined with the suspicion that a substantial proportion of these diagnoses are illegitimate or unwarranted. I propose that a major and under-recognized contributor to both the rise and the suspicion is diagnostic stretching: the application of a specified diagnostic category to a presentation that does not meet its official criteria but is accompanied by clinically significant distress or impairment, to make that presentation legible to the institutions that organize care. Since the 1990s, specified categories such as major depressive disorder, ADHD, bipolar disorder, and autism have been stretched in clinical practice to cover patients who have the relevant symptoms and clinically significant distress or impairment but whose presentations are subthreshold or phenomenologically adjacent. Increased awareness of mental health problems has lowered the help-seeking threshold, so that the population that comes to clinical attention is converging on the population that meets a burden threshold independent of help-seeking. Stretching is a response to genuine clinical need interacting with official classifications that are too narrow, not too broad. The overdiagnosis backlash correctly perceives a mismatch between official criteria and diagnostic practice but misidentifies its source, reading as laxity what is better understood as unmet need routed through official categories that are not adequate to the task.

articles.title: Hybrid Consciousness and the Cultural Evolution of Leadership
articles.authors: Rebekah Sēnānāyaka
articles.abstract: Ninety percent of human societies practise institutionalised alterations of consciousness. Across independent traditions, communities that develop governed protocols for sustained engagement with non-human organisms produce practitioners whose hybrid consciousness becomes the basis of social authority. Drawing on 27 months of apprenticeship-based fieldwork in the Peruvian and Colombian Amazon and comparative analysis of the 2,300-year Buddhist Bodhi tree tradition in Sri Lanka, I argue that inter-species contact protocols function as culturally evolved adaptive technologies that solve a recurrent problem in human social complexity: producing leaders whose authority is corruption-resistant and community-verifiable. The prestige these protocols generate is metabolically costly to acquire, continuously verified through public diagnostic performance, and resistant to capture because it depends on ongoing relationship maintenance with non-human agents rather than a one-time credential. Framed within cultural group selection, the convergence of this protocol structure across independent traditions suggests selective pressures on human sociality rather than local cultural production. The argument carries implications for cultural evolution theory, the study of religion and ritual, and contemporary encounters with non-human intelligence.

articles.title: An inverted U-shape association between mind health and generative AI-use frequency
articles.authors: Jerzy Bala; Tara Thiagarajan
articles.abstract: Generative AI chatbots such as ChatGPT and Claude have rapidly become part of how we work and live, yet there is little systematic understanding of what they do to the human mind. Here we use a global Internet-enabled sample of 176,198 adults aged 18+, collected in 2025-2026, to examine how frequency and type of generative AI use relate to mind health. Respondents completed a 47-item assessment of emotional, social, cognitive, and physical capacities and problems, aggregated into an overall mind health score, the MHQ, alongside questions on AI use, lifestyle, and life context. Mind health rises with low to moderate GenAI use and then falls sharply with daily use, an inverted U most pronounced among adults aged 18-34. The pattern holds for both cognitive and emotional purposes, although those using GenAI for emotional support or companionship have markedly lower MHQ at every frequency, reflecting higher levels of suicidal thoughts, confused or slow thinking, hallucinations and other problems linked to psychosis. These associations are cross-sectional and cannot be considered causal, but they persist after adjustment for education, trauma, exercise, nature exposure, and sleep. As GenAI becomes part of daily life, these results suggest a downward trajectory of collective global mind health.

articles.title: Holding up a mirror: The mental health and well-being of academic psychologists
articles.authors: Andrew Devendorf; David Disabato; Maya Nauphal; Jonathan Rottenberg; Sarah E. Victor
articles.abstract: The profession of psychology aims to improve societal mental health and well-being. Ironically, psychologists have neglected the study of mental health within the profession. We conducted the first comprehensive assessment of mental health difficulties across psychology disciplines in a sample (N = 1,261) of faculty and graduate students affiliated with U.S. doctoral degree granting institutions. Over 84% of respondents reported a lifetime history of mental health difficulties; 54% reported a lifetime diagnosis; 15% had clinically elevated current depression symptoms; 16% reported clinically elevated current anxiety symptoms; and 51% met Keyes’ “flourishing” criteria. The most common mental health concerns were depression, generalized anxiety disorder, panic attacks, suicidal thoughts, and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder. Across all outcomes, graduate students reported significantly greater frequency and severity of difficulties. Clinically elevated current depression and anxiety were 3-4 times higher in graduate students (21% and 22%, respectively) compared to professor-level faculty (6% and 7%, respectively). Rates of flourishing were lower in graduate students than faculty (OR = 2.65, p < .001). Clinical-area respondents (92%) were more likely to report a lifetime mental health difficulty than non-clinical area respondents (83%). Interestingly, while there were no field-level differences in rates of current elevated anxiety, clinical-area respondents had lower rates of clinically elevated depression. Academic psychology is not an exception to the mental health crisis in higher education. Particularly urgent action is needed to improve graduate students’ mental health. We discuss both systemic and practical recommendations for the profession of psychology.

articles.title: Peer Transmission of Mental Health Information Increases ADHD Self-Diagnosis
articles.authors: Tanay Katiyar; George Gillett; Adam Hunt; Amanda M Ferguson; Alessia Pascale; Alberto Acerbi; Nikhil Chaudhary; Amy Orben
articles.abstract: Increased sharing of mental health information online has intensified public concern that social media may amplify mental health self-diagnosis rates. While much work has examined the types of mental health information available online, little attention is paid to the mechanisms governing how this information is created and consumed. Taking a cultural evolutionary perspective, we posit that social media facilitates peer-to-peer transmission of psychiatric information in novel formats and provides new motivations to transmit such information; this alters the information people see and their reactions to it. We investigate this through an adapted transmission chain paradigm where participants sequentially modify and transmit Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) explanations amongst each other, allowing us to examine how self-diagnostic tendencies evolve during this process. Across four studies, we find that such transmission increases participants’ tendency to diagnose themselves, and another individual with subclinical traits, with ADHD. Participants’ tendency to recommend this other individual to seek professional help also increases. Transmission format (i.e. generating an example list versus narrative summary) and motivation (i.e. making an explanation for maximising likes versus accuracy) moderate some effects. These results indicate that peer-to-peer transmission may play a key role in determining psychiatric diagnostic trends and shaping the public understanding of mental health.

articles.title: Usage frequency predicts lexicalization across languages
articles.authors: Temuulen Khishigsuren; Francis Mollica; Ekaterina Vylomova; Charles Kemp
articles.abstract: Languages are more likely to have lexical items for some concepts (e.g. CHILD and SUN) than others (e.g. PARENT and WEATHER). We present a large-scale quantitative analysis of factors that predict lexicalization across languages, and test in particular the hypothesis that usage frequency predicts lexicalization. We consider 854 concepts and demonstrate that average usage frequency across 46 languages from the Language Documentation Reference Corpus is a relatively good predictor of the typological prevalence of lexicalization across the 41 languages in the World Loanword Database (β = 0.25, 95% CI = [0.16, 0.33]) and across 262 languages from the Intercontinental Dictionary Series (β = 0.30, 95% CI = [0.23, 0.38]). This finding implies that cross-linguistic regularities in lexicalization can be attributed in part to shared usage patterns across cultures.

articles.title: Multimodal Dynamics in Learning and Explaining Abstract and Concrete Concepts: A Triadic Interactive Task with Families
articles.authors: Chiara De Livio; Claudia Mazzuca; Francesca Bellagamba; Alessandro Gennaro; Giuliana Mazzoni; Silvia Mazzoni; Julian Zubek; Anna M. Borghi
articles.abstract: Studies have shown that learning abstract concepts (e.g., freedom compared to table) may be particularly challenging. To address concept learning, most studies use paradigms involving a single participant, such as lexical decision, match to sample, induction, and rating tasks. Here, we use an interactive task involving three family members—mother, father, and a 5-year-old child—and examine how concepts differing in abstractness are explained by the parents, either individually or together, and how the child learns and employs them. We investigate multimodal dynamics in interaction, studying gestures, movements of bodily parts, and movement coordination among interactors, in an effort to capture different embodied signatures characterizing concepts differing in abstractness. Results reveal that people gesture differently with abstract and concrete concepts, but in both cases tend to instantiate the conceptual referent, either metaphorically or iconically. Subtle differences in head movements and social touch suggest that people struggle more to understand the meanings of abstract concepts than concrete ones. Finally, with abstract concepts, coordination episodes are longer. Overall, the results provide support for the view that, with abstract concepts, people use more communicative signals and tend to converge more than with concrete concepts.

articles.title: Object Details Persist in Visual Working Memory Regardless of Category Sufficiency for Search
articles.authors: Ryan Williams; Joseph M. Saito; Keisuke Fukuda; Susanne Ferber
articles.abstract: When searching for objects in complex environments, performance often improves with more specific target representations. Yet, sometimes a more general representation may be preferable. For example, when repeatedly searching for unique exemplars from the same object category, a shared category-based representation could help alleviate the cognitive burden of constantly encoding and maintaining new exemplar representations. We therefore examined whether the format of target representations used for search is sensitive to the sustained preservation of object-category membership. Across two experiments, observers searched consecutively for images of real-world objects from the same basic-level category. We recorded contralateral delay activity (CDA), an electrophysiological marker of visual working memory (VWM) maintenance, to assess whether the encoding of object-specific details diminished across category repetitions in favor of more generalized representations. In Experiment 1, we manipulated whether object-category membership alone sufficiently differentiated each unique target from nontargets in the search array. In Experiment 2, we preserved category sufficiency but allowed the targets to additionally repeat at the level of the exemplar to examine how repeatedly searching for the same object differs from repeatedly searching for the same kind of object. We found that while fewer object-specific details were maintained in VWM when category membership was sufficient, the amount of detail only diminished across repetitions of the exact same object. Moreover, observers exhibited sensitivity to the sustained preservation of the target category in the form of perceptual and semantic expectancy violations following category switches, as indexed by N2pc and N400 ERP components. Together, we show that, even though the sustained preservation of a target object category does not continuously reduce the encoding of object-specific details, categorical information is nonetheless represented in parallel. We speculate that object-specific representations principally serve attentional guidance, while categorical representations benefit target-match decisions.

articles.title: Identifying Windows of Developmental Susceptibility to Media Emotion Regulation with Associations to Children’s Internalizing and Externalizing Behaviors, Problematic Media Use, and Emotional Development
articles.authors: Jane Shawcroft; McCall Booth; Peter Joseph Reschke; Sarah Ashby; Rachel J. Munk; Ali Young; Sarah Coyne; Chris L. Porter
articles.abstract: Research has consistently found that media emotion regulation processes are negatively related to several developmental outcomes in early childhood. Using longitudinal data from N  = 451 children, we examined how the association between media emotion regulation processes and children’s problematic media use, internalizing and externalizing behaviors, and social-emotional functioning fluctuated across early and middle childhood, spanning from 2 to 9 years of age.
