Using a Time-Varying Effects Model (TVEM), we found evidence that the association between media emotion regulation and children’s development is not static across childhood and fluctuates across different ages and stages. Specifically, we identified windows of developmental sensitivity to media emotion regulation processes during early childhood in terms of internalizing and externalizing behaviors, and an increasing sensitivity to the effects of media emotion regulation on problematic media use across early childhood. These findings point to the need for developmentally-sensitive research approaches, interventions, and parenting practices around the use of technology to calm young children.

articles.title: The structure and degree of social connection is associated with the structure and idiosyncrasy of emotion perception
articles.authors: David Dodell-Feder; Tamar Galvin; Tara Augenstein
articles.abstract: Social connection is associated with broad aspects of social cognition. Here, we probe the nature of this association in two studies (Ns=305, 759) with college-aged samples in which we measured different aspects of social (dis)connection (e.g., loneliness) and performance on a measure of emotion perception. We find that intersubject differences in social connection mirrored intersubject differences in emotion perception, suggesting a shared fingerprint between the experience of one’s social relationships and the perception of emotion information. Further, greater levels of social disconnection were associated with greater idiosyncrasy in emotion perception, which was largely driven by task inaccuracy. This finding suggests that social disconnection may distort internal models of affective states in a way that pulls individuals from a canonical understanding of how emotions are expressed in faces. Although findings were specific to Study 2, these results provide important context to how social connection relates to emotion perception and highlights emotion perception as a potential intervention target for social disconnection.

articles.title: Using Large Language Models to Contextualize Smiling in Psychotherapy Research
articles.authors: Martin Lund Trinhammer; Stella Grasshof; Jana Volkert; Pia Rasche; Anna-Maria Weiland; Sami Sebastian Brandt; Uwe Altmann
articles.abstract:
The meaning of a smile during conversation depends on what is being
said, yet psychotherapy research has historically analyzed facial movements independently of
context. We introduce a methodology that links both partners’ smiling in a dyadic setting to
the sentiment of a speech turn (positive, neutral, negative). Using open-weight models on local
hardware only, we transcribed and diarized attachment interviews, annotated the sentiment of
the participant’s speech turns with a large language model (LLM), and analyzed individual smiling
 and smile synchrony as a function of that sentiment. We applied linear mixed models to
test for differences in smiling according to sentiment. Across 70 interviews and 1,294 speech
turns, only the interviewer’s smiling differed significantly according to the sentiment of what
the participant was saying (interviewer d = .51, q < .001; participant d = .05, q = .165); the
pair smiled simultaneously more often during positive than negative turns (d = .21, p < .001).
By conditioning smiling on what is being said — sentiment annotated from the conversation
as it unfolds rather than created by experimental instruction — our method enables the kind of
context-sensitive analysis contemporary theories call for. The pipeline is open and reproducible,
runs entirely on local hardware so that no data leave the site, and can be easily modified for any
annotation scheme or clinical setting.

articles.title: Abstract concepts map differently onto the body in humans and generative AI
articles.authors: Kyoshiro Sasaki; Yuki Yamada
articles.abstract: Abstract concepts are systematically associated with body-centered space, yet it remains unclear how they are represented across the body itself. Here, we used Body Mapping to characterize the bodily organization of four conceptual dimensions—time, length, quantity, and physical size—in humans and generative artificial intelligence (AI). In Experiment 1, human participants reported significant increases in bodily activity for “future”, “long”, “more”, and “large”, whereas no significant activation or deactivation survived correction for their conceptual opposites. “Future”, “more”, and “large” were primarily associated with the head and central torso, whereas long showed a distinct limb-centered pattern. In Experiment 2, six image-generation models were tested; five produced sufficient valid samples for the main comparison and yielded statistically reliable body maps whose organization differed markedly from the human pattern and across model families. GPT Image models showed either strongly lateralized or widespread activation patterns, whereas Nano Banana models more clearly expressed conceptual opposition through complementary activation and deactivation. These findings show that bodily organization of abstract concepts cannot be inferred directly from conventional spatial compatibility effects and that sensitivity to conceptual polarity does not imply human-like bodily organization. More broadly, Body Mapping provides a common representational framework for comparing conceptual organization across human and artificial systems, opening a route from behavioral comparison toward representation-level comparison—and potentially training—using human-derived bodily data.

articles.title: Growing Up With Conversational AI: A Developmental Framework for Adolescent Agency Over Conversational AI Use
articles.authors: shanting chen; Mary Kate Koch; Renkai Ma; Cindy Liu; Natalie C. Ebner
articles.abstract: Conversational generative AI has rapidly reached majority adoption among U.S. adolescents. These systems now provide advice, emotional support, academic assistance, simulated social interaction, and opportunities for identity exploration at a critical phase in development when mental health needs are rising and capacities for self-regulation, autonomy, and social competence are still developing. Scholars and clinicians have raised urgent questions about what these systems do to adolescents, and early findings point to both benefits and risks. In this article, we ask what adolescents do with AI and introduce the concept of adolescent agency over conversational AI use: the degree to which adolescents purposefully direct, critically evaluate, and set limits on their engagement with conversational AI. Existing constructs such as AI literacy and AI self-efficacy describe what young people know or believe about AI and the risks associated with its use, but they do not capture how adolescents exercise agency across areas of their lives. We identify nine processes that arise at the intersection of conversational AI’s features and key developmental tasks during the period of adolescence, which we label AI-ERA: autonomy, identity, emotion regulation, relationships, and achievement. We distinguish this agency from existing constructs, including agentic engagement with AI and AI overreliance, and then propose how it is shaped by adolescents’ developing capacities, adult scaffolding, and peer influence. We conclude with implications for families, schools, clinicians, and researchers, as well as considerations regarding the design, regulation, and ethics of AI systems.

articles.title: Emotional and Well-being Consequences of Discrimination and Collective Action Engagement
articles.authors: Shahrzad Goudarzi; Riana M. Brown; Ashley L Berkebile-Weinberg; Maureen A. Craig
articles.abstract: Inequality and collective struggles against it are psychologically taxing. Yet to be successful, social movements must persist through sustained action despite their toll on the participants, and many do. While the negative affective determinants of collective action, particularly outrage, are extensively studied, less is known about the accompanying positive psychological states. Using cross-sectional and experience-sampling methodologies, we find that engaging (and intending to engage) in collective action is marked by heightened subjective well-being and a range of positive feelings. Nonetheless, the positive consequences of engagement (but not mere intention) may only emerge when action is coupled with experiences of discrimination targeting outgroups (but not the self, personally, or ingroups) or in the absence of discrimination. This suggests that some psychological distance from discrimination supports the psychological benefits of collective action in grappling with inequality. Overall, this work can provide insight into a psychological mechanism contributing to sustained mobilization.

articles.title: Co-STARS: A Participatory Action Research Approach to Co-Producing Culturally Responsive Mental Health Literacy Training with Young Black People
articles.authors: Milan Antonovic; Megan A. Pope; Gerald Jordan; Balachandran Kumarendran; Luke Brown; Nadia; Ayan Mahamud; Lowri Griffiths
articles.abstract:
Objective: Young Black people in the UK face disproportionate mental health inequalities driven by stigma, racism, and structural exclusion. Although mental health literacy can promote early recognition and help-seeking, most interventions do not reflect Black communities’ lived realities. This study used Participatory Action Research (PAR) to co-produce a peer-led community mental health literacy training package with young Black people, alongside an e-learning resource to support culturally responsive practice among mental health and allied professionals.

Method: Eight young Black participants (M age = 24.5; five female) with lived experience of mental ill health from diverse cultural, religious, and gender backgrounds took part in four peer-led workshops and three refinement sessions. Guided by an anti-oppressive framework, participants identified priorities, developed content, and shaped the training. Data were audio-recorded, transcribed, and analysed using reflexive thematic analysis.

Results: Four interconnected themes emerged: (1) Navigating Cultural Silences and Systemic Exclusions (stigma, cultural taboos, intergenerational trauma, and racialised experiences in education and healthcare); (2) Fighting to Be Heard (dismissal, misrecognition, and delayed care); (3) Reimagining Care Through Cultural Proximity and Community Anchoring (relational, culturally grounded, community-based models); and (4) Embedding Accountability and Cultural Reflexivity in Training (youth-led recommendations for train-the-trainer programmes emphasising structural competency, experiential learning, and supervision).

Conclusions: Co-production elevated young Black people’s expertise and produced a culturally responsive training package grounded in lived experience and structural realities. The findings highlight the need for preventative, relational, and equity-focused mental health approaches and support community-led, culturally grounded interventions to reduce disparities among Black and racialised youth.

articles.title: People With Lower Well-Being Show Longer and Less Stable Smartphone Use: A Large-Scale Analysis of 12 Datasets
articles.authors: Anna M Langener; Philip Chow; Aurelio Fernández; Nicholas C. Jacobson; Martien Kas; Anne Milek; Rüdiger Pryss; Theda Radtke; Ramona Schoedel; David de Segovia Vicente
articles.abstract: Debate over whether smartphone use relates to poorer well-being is limited by self-reports, small single-country samples, and a focus on average use. We harmonized objective app-use from 12 studies  (2,945 participants; 37,229 person-days; 851,865 person-hours) across five countries to examine associations of well-being with smartphone use and its variability. Additionally, we examined variations in smartphone use across age, gender identity, and time-of-day and day-of-week. Daily, participants averaged 3.27 hours of use (SD = 2.28), accessed 15.9 apps (SD = 6.16), and were unstable (40.6% of the total variation accounted for by within-person changes). Poorer well-being was associated with longer, more variable use; a depressive symptom increase of 10% of the scale range corresponded to 7 additional minutes of daily use and 7.5% higher within-person variance. Overall, younger persons and women used their phones more frequently, and higher wellbeing was related to consistently lower smartphone usage.

articles.title: Remembering how events unfold: Emotion and memory consolidation for naturalistic events
articles.authors: Charline Colson; Arnaud D'Argembeau
articles.abstract: Although emotional content is known to strengthen memory consolidation, its influence on how the unfolding of events is retained over time has received little attention. Building on the finding that negative events are remembered with less temporal compression and richer detail than neutral events, this study examined whether this emotional advantage changes over time, as would be expected if consolidation contributes to it. Participants viewed a series of negative and neutral videos and, either immediately or after a 24-hour or 72-hour delay, mentally replayed each event and verbally described it. Temporal compression was indexed by the ratio of video duration to replay duration, memory richness by narrative length and linguistic measures of episodic detail, and the preservation of event content by embedding-based similarity to descriptions produced during viewing. At immediate recall, negative events were replayed with less compression and described with more words and episodic detail than neutral events, replicating prior findings. After a delay, the emotional advantage in narrative length and episodic detail increased, and similarity to the video descriptions declined for neutral but not for negative events, whereas evidence for a corresponding increase in the emotion effect on temporal compression was less conclusive. These findings show that the emotional advantage in memory content for naturalistic, dynamic events is not fixed at encoding but increases over time, pointing to a role for consolidation.

articles.title: Enrichment of weak free associations in the aging mental lexicon and the limits of methodological inference
articles.authors: Dasol Jeong; Thomas Hills
articles.abstract: Older adults’ lexical networks often appear sparser than those of younger adults, a pattern typically interpreted as evidence of cognitive decline. The enrichment model instead proposes that lifelong experience creates richer lexical representations in which associative strength is distributed across more weak connections. Across two stimulation studies, we examine this model and the limits of methodological inference when studying free association networks. Study 1 reproduced empirical aging data, showed that lifelong learning enriched networks with age, leading to more distributed free associations that appear as an enrichment of weak associations with age. Study 2 demonstrated that these patterns depended on participant sample size and lexicon size. In particular, increasing the number of participants reduced or reversed apparent age-related sparsity by revealing weak and infrequently observed associations. This also follows the logic of ecological studies that call for increased sampling when rare species may be undersampled. Overall, these findings suggest that aging enriches and redistributes associative strength across a broader lexical network and that observed sparsity may reflect methodological limitations rather than a genuine loss of lexical connectivity.

articles.title: How AI chatbots shape political attitudes when they are not prompted to persuade
articles.authors: Sayeh Yousefi; Jens Koed Madsen
articles.abstract: People increasingly turn to AI chatbots to find information, including information about politicians and political issues. Given evidence that Large Language Models (LLMs) have high persuasive capacities, this has raised concerns about their potential to have undue influence on political attitudes. However, most existing research on AI persuasion explicitly prompts the LLM to persuade the user, which is not representative of how people typically engage with LLMs. Whether undirected political conversations with LLMs shift political attitudes, and whether personalisation amplifies any such effect, remains unclear. We address these questions across two studies. First, in a quota-matched survey of UK adults (N = 2,137), we find that political use of AI is already widespread and its outputs are generally perceived as being politically neutral. Second, in a pre-registered randomised controlled trial (N = 2,081), participants conversed with an LLM about either a politician or political issue, with the LLM not being prompted to persuade. We find that conversations about politicians increased favourability toward them, while conversations about policies modestly reduced support. Conversation personalisation did not amplify these effects. Our findings show that AI chatbots are already a meaningful source of political information in the UK, and that undirected chatbot conversations can influence political attitudes.

articles.title: Battling Bots and Combating Fraud in Digitally Mediated Social Science Research: A Typological Toolbox of Countermeasures
articles.authors: Bradley E. Cox; Yilun Jiang; Brett Ranon Nachman; Karly Ball Isaacson
articles.abstract: As social science researchers increasingly use online mechanisms to recruit participants and collect data, they must also defend against the growing threat of fraudulent submissions from autonomous bots and bad-faith human respondents. This paper describes such threats and outlines conditions that make some studies particularly vulnerable. It also provides explicit guidance for researchers by introducing a typology of 30 protective countermeasures designed to deter, prevent, track, and detect fraudulent responses.

articles.title: Mesmer’s error: Beliefs reverse the rubber hand illusion (a Registered Report)
articles.authors: Peter Lush; Zoltan Dienes
articles.abstract: In the rubber hand illusion (RHI), participants report ownership of a fake hand which is stroked in synchrony with their own concealed hand, with lower ownership ratings for asynchronous stroking. This effect has been historically attributed to multisensory integration. However, such a pattern of results is consistent with experimental demand characteristics, and an alternative theory proposes that the RHI is an effect of phenomenological control (the trait ability to change experience to satisfy goals). To date, support for a phenomenological control theory of the RHI has been limited to correlational evidence. Here we conduct a pre-registered causal test of the relative contribution of these two proposed mechanisms in RHI effects. 25 high phenomenological control participants (top 15%) were tested in an RHI procedure and the classic effects of greater response for synchrony than asynchrony were replicated. The procedure was then repeated following imaginative suggestions for a reversal of the classic effect (i.e. greater synchrony than asynchrony effects). Ratings of ownership and proprioceptive drift were modulated by suggestion. Effects for ownership and drift were reversed. Exploratory analysis showed the same pattern of results for referred touch ratings. Participant beliefs arising from demand characteristics dominated over multisensory mechanisms in RHI ownership of a fake hand and proprioceptive drift. Multisensory synchrony was not necessary to produce the classic effects, falsifying the theory that the illusion requires multisensory integration. Claims of an illusion beyond that attributable to demand characteristics and phenomenological control require experimental evidence from controlled experiments.

articles.title: Beyond Turing Equivalence:  The Human Premium in Human–AI Interaction
articles.authors: Ophelia Deroy
articles.abstract: Asking whether we can know whether a given text or output is coming from a machine or a human, which was at the core of the Turing test, is being progressively retired. This opens a new and no less interesting question: what happens when we know? This paper reviews evidence that when humans encounter exactly the same content, presented here as coming from a human and there from an AI, they do not behave similarly. The evidence across different kinds of interaction, advice giving, compliance, reciprocal interaction, and preferential choice, is that humans respect other humans more than they respect machines. This difference is often described as a 'machine penalty' where we distrust machines or lack familiarity with them, and predicted to decrease as AI becomes more prevalent. The paper offers a different interpretation, showing that we treat humans better for good reasons, including utility calculations, and that this human premium is likely to stay.

articles.title: The Effects of Group-Based Community Interventions on Social Reintegration of Marginalized Adults with Mental Illness: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
articles.authors: Nina Thorup Dalgaard; jakob Kaarup Jensen; Jasmin Sami Adada; Maya Christiane Flensborg Jensen; Elizabeth Bengtsen; Mikkel Helding Vembye; Elizabeth Tipton
articles.abstract:
Background 
Adults with mental illness who also experience social marginalization face interconnected clinical and social challenges, yet scalable interventions addressing both dimensions of recovery remain limited.

Aims 
To evaluate the effects of group-based community interventions on social reintegration and mental health among socially marginalized adults with mental illness.

Methods 
We conducted a preregistered systematic review and meta-analysis of interventions delivered in OECD countries. Searches identified 28,980 records; 62 studies met the inclusion criteria and 49 studies, contributing 349 effect sizes, were included in the meta-analysis. Outcomes were classified as social reintegration or mental health. Meta-analytic models accounted for dependent effect sizes within studies.

Results 
Group-based community interventions improved social reintegration (g = 0.195, 95% CI [0.122, 0.268]) and mental health (g = 0.215, 95% CI [0.090, 0.340]) relative to control conditions, corresponding to effects approximately 2.3 and 1.4 times larger, respectively, than the typical improvements under treatment as usual. Effects varied substantially across studies and outcomes, while measured moderators explained little of this heterogeneity. Effects on social reintegration and mental health were positively associated. Findings were robust across sensitivity analyses and showed little indication of publication bias. Nearly half of studies were preregistered and contributed approximately two-thirds of all effect sizes. Preregistered studies yielded smaller social reintegration effects than non-preregistered studies, although the average effect remained statistically significant and substantively meaningful.

Conclusions 
Group-based community interventions can improve both social reintegration and mental health among marginalized adults with mental illness, suggesting that they may support multidimensional recovery. Their potential value therefore extends beyond scalability and lower delivery costs to substantively meaningful improvements in outcomes. However, substantial unexplained heterogeneity indicates that benefits are unlikely to be uniform across populations, interventions, and settings.

What is already known on this topic
Adults experiencing both mental illness and social marginalization face interconnected clinical and social challenges, while existing systematic reviews on group-based interventions have largely focused on specific diagnoses, intervention types, or psychiatric symptoms.

What this study adds
Across 49 studies contributing 349 effect sizes, group-based community interventions produced positive average effects on both social reintegration and mental health. Effects in the two domains were positively associated, but substantial heterogeneity remained largely unexplained.

articles.title: What Makes a Child Go Bad? Genes, Choice, and Punishment in Original Sin
articles.authors: Madelief Isabel Kuijper; Kassandra Pomper; Josefina Benita Bernardo; Selim Sametoğlu; Elsje van Bergen
articles.abstract: This review reflects on Kathryn Paige Harden’s Original Sin through discussions in our Educational Genetics lab. We consider the book’s treatment of behavioural genetics, responsibility, punishment, religion, and parenting, highlighting both the power of Harden’s personal perspective and the limitations of its strongly American Evangelical framing. We conclude by reflecting on what science can, and cannot, tell us about why individuals behave badly.

articles.title: What Fifty Years of Research on the Misinformation Effect Can Tell Us: A Meta-Analytic Review
articles.authors: Björn Alfons Edmar; Nathalie Shekila Anna Enquist; Timothy John Luke
articles.abstract: This meta-analysis examines the impact of misleading or incorrect information on subsequent reports of witnessed events, with the aim of identifying key moderators of the misinformation effect – defined as reduced accuracy following exposure to misinformation. We synthesized experimental studies using the three-phase misinformation paradigm published between 1975 and 2025. A three-level mixed-effects meta-regression model was used to account for effect size non-independence and to examine moderators, including retention interval, warnings, overall test performance, and study characteristics. Across 480 studies and 1,998 effect sizes (N = 59,079), the average misinformation effect was substantial (g = 0.694, 95% CI [0.259, 1.128]) and highly heterogeneous (σ2 = 0.697, I2 = 92.21%). Control condition accuracy was positively associated with the magnitude of the effect, and post-misinformation warnings significantly reduced it. In contrast to prior findings, post-event testing did not significantly moderate the effect. These findings support the robustness of the misinformation effect and suggest that it reflects a combination of memory-related and strategic processes. Given the substantial heterogeneity observed, the misinformation effect may be better conceptualized as a constellation of related phenomena rather than a single unified effect, with important implications for theory and applied settings such as eyewitness testimony.

articles.title: Latent Profiles on the Intelligence and Development Scales – 2 and their Relationship with Classifications of Dyslexia and ADHD
articles.authors: Linda Visser; Selma Anne José Ruiter; Marieke Timmerman
articles.abstract: Objectives: The aim of the current study was to get insight in intelligence and executive functioning profiles and their relation with gender and dyslexia and ADHD classifications. Methods: We performed a latent profile analysis on IDS-2 data from 3,954 Dutch, German and Italian children (7 – 21 years). Results: The results showed six profiles differing in overall cognitive level. Three profiles were relatively balanced (below-average, low-average, and average), one showed high-average scores with a clear strength in visual short-term memory and two showed only slight strengths and weaknesses. There were large gender differences between the profile, amongst which a clear overrepresentation of boys in the profile with balanced below-average scores. This profile, along with the one with low-average scores, had relatively high rates of classifications for both ADHD and dyslexia and scholastic skills in the low-average range. For the other profiles, the scholastic skills scores were largely comparable to those on intelligence and executive functioning. Conclusion: Our results do not support the idea that ADHD or dyslexia classifications are related to specific weaknesses in a cognitive profile. This highlights the need for individualized assessment that takes into account both acquired academic competencies and innate cognitive capacities.

articles.title: Development and Preliminary Psychometric Validation of the Guna-Based Social Media Consumption Questionnaire: Associations with Social Networking Addiction and Nomophobia
articles.authors: Divyansh Pandey; Arnav Bhavsar; Alok Bajpai
articles.abstract:
Objective: This study aimed to develop and conduct preliminary psychometric validation of the Guna-Based Social Media Consumption Questionnaire (G-SMCQ) and examine its associations with social networking addiction (SNA) and nomophobia (NMP) using the Triguna framework from Indian psychology.
Method: Participants were 106 Indian undergraduate students (86 males, 20 females; aged 16–20 years, M = 18.05, SD = 0.72). A cross-sectional design evaluated the preliminary psychometric properties of the G-SMCQ and its relationships with the Social Networking Addiction Scale and the Nomophobia Questionnaire.
Results: MCA provided some preliminary evidence that the G-SMCQ response patterns were characterised by a multidimensional structure. Mean scores for the three Gunas indicated that Sattvic consumption was 9.86 (SD = 4.24), Rajasic consumption was 5.97 (SD = 3.66), and Tamasic consumption was 1.17 (SD = 1.75). Internal consistency reliability coefficients for the three Gunas were reported to be .840, .776, and .697, respectively. The relationship between Sattvic consumption and social networking addiction and nomophobia was negative (SNA: ρ = −.530, p < .001; NMP: ρ = −.295, p = .002), while Rajasic consumption was positively correlated to both constructs (SNA: ρ = .463, p < .001; NMP: ρ = .284, p = .003). However, Tamasic consumption was correlated to SNA (ρ = .270, p = .005) only, but not with nomophobia (ρ = .157, p = .109).
Conclusion: The results provided some preliminary psychometric evidence that suggests the potential of the G-SMCQ as a culturally-grounded measure of the Triguna-based social media consumption patterns.
Keywords: Social Media Consumption; Social Networking Addiction; Nomophobia;
Triguna Theory; Digital behavior

articles.title: Self-identity in anorexia nervosa
articles.authors: Stephen Gadsby
articles.abstract: Anorexia nervosa is widely characterised as a disorder of the self, in which sufferers come to identify with their illness. Yet what such identification amounts to remains poorly understood. I argue that there are two distinct forms of self-identity involved, individual identity and group identity. These emerge at different time points, stem from different factors, and bear different clinical consequences. By unpacking this distinction, I provide a pluralistic and psychologically plausible account of self-identity in anorexia—one that illuminates the disorder’s tenacity and points to new ways of understanding it.

articles.title: Day-to-day fluctuations in craving and the value of drugs and food in daily life
articles.authors: Sergej Grunevski; Emmanuel E. Alvarez; Emma M. Schweitzer; Julia Kong; Sahar Hafezi; Anna B. Konova
articles.abstract: Craving is a powerful urge for a specific target (e.g., food, drugs) that prompts decisions directed at satisfying craving. While prior laboratory studies suggest craving biases behavior by amplifying target-specific value, the real-world generalizability of this mechanism remains unknown. We validate and extend these findings in a 28-day naturalistic smartphone-enabled study in patients with opioid use disorder (N=67) and community controls (N=49) who reported on their food (savory, sweet) and drug (opioid) urges and willingness-to-pay values. Despite person-level (mean) covariation, food and drug urges fluctuated largely independently within individuals while maintaining target-specific relationships with value. Using dynamics in drug urge and value and computational modeling, we isolated a distinct, ecologically relevant craving “state” tied to drug cue exposure and drug use in daily life. This research shows craving acts on normative valuation processes in real-world decision making and offers a novel approach to infer clinically vulnerable moments for behavior change.

articles.title: Explicit affective inferences enhance behavioral sensitivity to naturalistic expressions
articles.authors: Doron Atias; Maria Gendron
articles.abstract: Emotion theories highlight the fundamental function of emotional expressions in regulating social behavior. Yet, this basic premise relies mostly on studies using posed expressions that may fail to capture the diversity of real-life emotional signals and invite explicit affective inferences due to their salient symbolic nature. Across three studies (N=1,529), we tested how naturalistic emotional expressions differentially shape affective judgments and prosocial behavior. Participants watched videos of distressed individuals expressing typical crying, atypical crying, typical laughter, or no vocalization, and either inferred the targets’ affect (Study 1) or donated real money to help them from a provided budget (Study 2). Perceivers were sensitive to the vocal crying variation when explicitly inferring affect, but not when making donation decisions. Importantly, when perceivers explicitly inferred affect before donating (Study 3), they donated nearly 40% more and showed increased sensitivity to vocal cue variation. These findings suggest that inferring other people’s affect when making behavioral decisions is not routine and can facilitate helping behavior and the sensitivity to others’ emotional signals. This also highlight the important role of explicit inferential processes in linking real-life emotional expressions to prosocial behavior in everyday life.

articles_hidden.title: Intentional Forgetting of Autobiographical Memories: Current Neuroimaging Evidence and Moving Towards an Integrationist EEG-fMRI Approach
articles_hidden.authors: Dhruv Aggarwal; Palmer Smith
articles_hidden.abstract:
Intentional Forgetting (INF) is one of many human memory processes which has gathered academic intrigue in emergent literature. Understood as a conscious and voluntary cognitive effort to suppress the recall of, or remove certain memories, INF has been extensively studied in associative paradigms. However, its application to autobiographical memory (AM) remains under-investigated, especially within neuroimaging studies. First, we summarize existing neuroimaging literature on intentional forgetting of autobiographical memories (INF-AM). Upon reviewing, we found evidence to be fragmented, providing no clear consensus around the neural bases of INF-AM. We argue this fragmentation is, in part, a result of a reliance on single-modality applications of electroencephalograph (EEG) and functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) methodology. 
EEG and fMRI, however, are complementary in their respective temporal and spatial superiority. Subsequently, we propose the application of an EEG-fMRI integrationist approach to INF-AM. We discuss how its application may help address conceptual, paradigm-level, and methodological concerns. Since human AM and the process of forgetting are inherently longitudinal, we contrast the popular cross-sectional design with a longitudinal alternative. We then present the application of the integrationist approach to longitudinal INF-AM designs. Though cognizant of the limitations that may accompany such an approach, we present the integrationist approach as a much needed and promising way forward in decoding the neuroscience of INF-AM.

Keywords: intentional forgetting, autobiographical memory, neuroimaging, EEG-fMRI, integrationist

articles_hidden.title: How to Select, Retain, Delete and Replace Items in IRT-Based Scale Development: A Multi-Criteria Framework for Psychometric Optimisation
articles_hidden.authors: Enoch Oluwatomiwo Oladunmoye
articles_hidden.abstract: Decisions about which items to keep, delete or replace shape the validity, precision and fairness of a scale, yet they are still often made with single statistics, such as the lowest discrimination parameter or the change in Cronbach’s alpha after deletion. This study proposes a multi-criteria framework for item decisions under Item Response Theory (IRT) and examines by simulation how single-criterion rules compare with it. Evidence is organised into six domains (information and targeting, model fit, local dependence and redundancy, differential item functioning, response categories, and content representation) and combined through a flag, investigate, compare and decide sequence. Counterfactual deletion and replacement are formalised as a purpose-weighted, constrained optimisation, and an Item Utility Profile is proposed as a decision aid rather than an index. A Monte Carlo study (500 replications) generated 60-item, six-domain two-parameter logistic pools containing locally dependent pairs and items labelled as functioning differently across groups. Five strategies for choosing 24 items were compared under two measurement purposes. Classical and slope-based rules each retained about four DIF-labelled items among the 24 chosen, and kept between 2.8 and 3.8 of six redundant pairs intact on average. An information-only rule left a content domain empty in 33% of replications when precision was needed near a screening threshold. The multi-criteria strategy kept about one DIF-labelled item, fewer than one redundant pair and every domain, at a cost of 13% to 17% of nominal weighted information. Conclusions. Item deletion is better handled as a documented measurement-design decision than as a statistical filter. The simulation is illustrative and uses known item parameters, so its findings need confirmation with estimated parameters and empirical data.

articles_hidden.title: Developmental and social variation in spatial behavior among BaYaka hunter-gatherers
articles_hidden.authors: Sarah Pope-Caldwell; Lee Gettler; Adam Boyette; Yann R. Ouamba; Alyssa N. Crittenden; Sheina Lew-Levy
articles_hidden.abstract: Effectively choosing between exploring alternative strategies versus exploiting familiar ones is a keyaspect of adaptive behavior. Previous research suggests that exploration in early life gives way tomore targeted exploitation with age. Further, group composition can shape one’s propensity forexploration   and   exploitation.   Yet,   few   studies   have   investigated   how   individual   cognitivedevelopment and collective intelligence articulate to help resolve the explore-exploit dilemma in real-world contexts. Here, we investigated spatial behavior in BaYaka hunter-gatherer children and adultsfrom the Republic of the Congo. We used 337 foraging GPS tracks collected across 42 days toinvestigate how individual age and group composition (child-only, mixed-age, adult-only) predictedsix spatial behaviors during real-world foraging bouts. We found that children's foraging paths weremore sinuous—that is, most exploratory—when travelling with peers than with adults. In contrast,mixed-age groups travelled further and covered more unique ground than child-only groups. Wesuggest that this may be indicative of distinct learning goals across foraging social contexts. Wefurther propose that child-only exploration alongside more adult-like exploitation may operate ascomplementary components of an age-graded division of cognitive labor, with discoveries made bychildren during exploratory foraging informing adults' subsequent resource exploitation.

articles_hidden.title: A Taxometric Analysis of the Three-Item UCLA Loneliness Scale in the National Social Life, Health, and Aging Project
articles_hidden.authors: Savannah M. Boyd; David Sbarra
articles_hidden.abstract: Loneliness is a well-established risk factor for physical and mental health in later life. This work responds to recent calls to examine the dimensionality of the UCLA Loneliness Scale among older adults. In a preregistered secondary analysis using three measurement occasions from the publicly available National Social Life, Health, and Aging Project (NSHAP), we applied taxometric analyses (i.e., mean above minus below a cut, maximum eigenvalue, latent mode factor analysis, and comparison curve fit index) to examine the latent structure of the 3-item UCLA Loneliness Scale. Results supported the preregistered hypothesis, showing the mean comparison curve fit index (CCFI) was below 0.45 on each measurement occasion (CCFI range: 0.23 – 0.35). Therefore, loneliness, as measured in this sample, likely follows a continuous rather than categorical distribution, with no clear cut point. These findings inform statistical decision-making regarding loneliness classification and use of this scale in this sample.

articles_hidden.title: Morpho-phonetic adaptation is realised in multiple cues: evidence from articulography
articles_hidden.authors: Motoki Saito; Jessie S. Nixon
articles_hidden.abstract: A critical issue in models of speech production concerns the modularity of processing: for example, can information from morphology influence the articulation of phonologically identical segments? A phenomenon that has the potential to help shed light on this question is what we term morpho-phonetic adaptation: systematic phonetic differences in identical segments patterning with morphological differences. Previous studies have been largely inconclusive, finding longer (enhancement) and shorter (reduction) duration of affixes, as well as null effects. The occurrence of morpho-phonetic adaptation for affixes suggests that morphological information can indeed influence segment articulation. However, to date, most studies have involved acoustic realisations in English. If it is the case that morphology interacts with phonetics, such morphological effects should also be observed in languages other than English. We also hypothesise that effects should also occur in articulatory realisations such as tongue movements. In the present study, we compared acoustic duration and tongue movements between two German suffixes -er [ɐ] and -t [-t]. We found that the suffixal -er [ɐ] was significantly longer in duration and significantly lower in tongue positions than its segmentally identical non-suffixal counterpart, and the lower tongue position could not be simply attributed to longer duration. Importantly, however, no effect of morphological status was found for -t [-t] for either duration or articulatory trajectory. These findings show that morpho-phonetic adaptation manifests in multiple cues and may depend on segment identity, with implications for models of speech production.

articles_hidden.title: The limits of ensemble perception: Hierarchical grouping and object-based encoding
articles_hidden.authors: Sabrina Hansmann-Roth; Bilge Sayim
articles_hidden.abstract:
The visual system can efficiently summarize information by extracting ensemble statistics such
as the average of visual features. However, it remains unclear how ensemble perception
operates when individual features are grouped into meaningful objects. In the present study,
we investigated whether ensemble statistics of local features can still be extracted when
oriented line segments form letters. Across two experiments, observers estimated the average
orientation of line elements either as unconnected lines in a typical ensemble display, arranged
into intact letters, or transformed into pseudo-letters. Although the number and orientation of
line elements were identical across conditions, grouping into meaningful letters systematically
impaired performance. Grouping interfered with observers’ ability to estimate average
orientation when intact letters did not provide a useful global orientation cue, leading to larger
errors and greater response variability than pseudo-letters or ungrouped lines. However, when
the average orientation coincided with the mirror-symmetry axis of a letter, observers could
rely on this global structure, resulting in improved performance. Crucially, these effects
replicated in peripheral vision, indicating that ensemble extraction is constrained by perceptual
organization even when access to local feature information is limited. Together, these results
show that ensemble perception is modulated by object-based grouping and perceptual
organization.

articles_hidden.title: Do ‘tortured phrases’ exist in the psychology literature, and are there psychology-specific ‘tortured phrases’?
articles_hidden.authors: Patrick Nebl; Mark G McCoy; Jaime A. Teixeira da Silva
articles_hidden.abstract: Objectives: The psychology literature is occasionally quoted as being in a replication crisis due to the inability to replicate key findings caused by either integrity issues, or weak scientific protocols. This paper focuses on an unexplored topic in psychological science, ‘tortured phrases’, first to appreciate whether any psychology literature might contain such ambiguous terms, even if they are not related to psychology per se. Methods and Results: The Tortured Phrases Detector (TPD) of the Problematic Paper Screener revealed 36 journal articles (including one proceedings paper) with tortured phrases, 14 of which have been retracted to date (10 October 2025). We then induced, using a free online paraphraser, a novel methodology for detecting ‘tortured phrases’, by converting 50 standard psychological terms that started with the letter “A” into purposefully created ‘tortured phrases’. We employed Google Scholar to detect whether any of these created ‘tortured phrases’ might actually exist in published literature. The second method, with only 50 terms, was able to detect at least one potential ‘tortured phrase’ (“evaluation utensil” used to represent “assessment instrument”). Conclusions: The exploratory nature of the methodology was prone to false positives but had success. It is our hope that this study will inspire further attempts to detect tortured phrases in psychology literature in order to further increase the scientific and ethical rigor in the field of psychology.

articles_hidden.title: Assessing psychological, neural and AI-based representational geometries across multiple similarity properties
articles_hidden.authors: Johan Alejandro Gamba; Megan A. K. Peters; Vincent Taschereau-Dumouchel; Brian Odegaard
articles_hidden.abstract: Assessing similarity between objects is a fundamental cognitive process, and similarity judgments can assess many different attributes, including objective properties (color, shape) or subjective appraisals (preference, scariness). Here, we investigated how psychological similarity across eight different properties relates to neural representational geometries and artificial models. We first collected large-scale pairwise similarity ratings for 280 objects. Using representational similarity analysis (RSA) and multidimensional scaling, we identified three mental representational spaces: one defined by multiple object features and general similarity, a second by affective evaluations, and a third by color. Combining fMRI and RSA in 80 participants, we found that object feature ratings significantly correlated with representational structures in visual and prefrontal cortices. Unexpectedly, affective ratings also correlated with patterns in visual cortices. Crucially, regional variability strongly shaped these correspondences: visual cortices exhibited high noise ceilings and consistent alignment with behavior, whereas associative regions showed greater across-subjects variability and weaker correlations. Finally, algorithms and neural networks with high classification performance on specific properties strongly correlated with behavioral and fMRI RSA matrices. Together, these results demonstrate that similarity is a multidimensional construct that comprises multiple representational spaces whose neural correspondence is shaped by representational content, regional variability, and modeling methodology.

articles_hidden.title: Vision and body representation: Insights from blindness
articles_hidden.authors: Dominika Radziun; Luke E. Miller
articles_hidden.abstract: Body representations arise from the integration of multiple sensory signals that provide information about the body’s size, posture, and internal states. Vision often plays a dominant role, calibrating and aligning signals from touch, proprioception, and interoception. Yet, individuals born without sight still construct coherent and functional body representations, suggesting that the role of vision in building these representations may be more flexible than previously thought. Here, we synthesize recent behavioral and neuroimaging findings on body representations in blind individuals. We argue that blindness offers a powerful case study in how body representations can emerge through non-visual pathways, revealing the brain’s capacity to flexibly reorganize the sensory inputs supporting its internal models of the body. In doing so, we highlight the broader relevance of visual loss for understanding the plastic and multisensory nature of body representation.

articles_hidden.title: Feasibility and acceptability of smartwatch-delivered micro-ecological momentary assessment (µEMA) during in situ exercise among breast cancer survivors
articles_hidden.authors: Elizabeth Webb Lampe; Aislinn E. Mitcham; Paget E. Chung; Carly Bobak; Hannah C. Edmonds; Sivakumar P. Kandasamy; Calie S. Sorenson; Hollin R. Hakimian; Kathleen Doyle Lyons; Amanda J. Emerson
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objectives. Micro-ecological momentary assessment (µEMA) facilitates in-real-time data capture using succinct prompts delivered to a smartwatch. µEMA overcomes limitations of smartphone-based EMA for activities where carrying a smartphone would be burdensome/impractical. To date, µEMA during exercise has only been conducted with younger, non-clinical samples. We evaluate the feasibility and acceptability of µEMA during in situ, self-directed exercise among breast cancer survivors within 5-years of completing cancer treatment.

Method. A µEMA app was installed on Fitbit Versa 3 smartwatches. N = 27 stage 0-III breast cancer survivors enrolled and 22 (81.5%) submitted ratings of affective response (via modified Feeling Scale) and physical effort (via modified Rating of Perceived Exertion Scale) during exercise sessions completed over 10 consecutive days. Feasibility was assessed as µEMA app response rates. Acceptability was assessed via User-Friendliness Scale ratings from daily dairy surveys as well as System Usability Scale (SUS) scores and exit interviews collected at end-of-study.

Results. Participants (Mage = 60.8 years, SD = 11.5) completed M = 4.7 (SD = 2.4) exercise sessions (walking most common) while responding to µEMA. The overall µEMA response rate across all exercise sessions was 77.7% (SD = 19.5). SUS scores (M = 82.9, SD = 15.5) exceeded the threshold for adequate usability (i.e., ≥ 68) and overall average person-weighted user-friendliness was ‘satisfactory’—‘good,’ M = 4.7 (SD = 1.1). Interviews revealed preference for µEMA over smartphone-based EMA during exercise. Notably, some technical issues were common. 

Conclusions. Results support the feasibility and acceptability of µEMA during in situ exercise among breast cancer survivors.

articles_hidden.title: Synthometricon: A search engine to identify conceptual overlap in measures in the behavioral sciences
articles_hidden.authors: Björn Erik Hommel; Annika Iris Külpmann; Ruben C. Arslan
articles_hidden.abstract: Every month, scores of new measures and constructs enter the behavioral science literature. Researchers struggle to keep an overview of their subfields, let alone the wider field, with an estimated number of allegedly different constructs now exceeding 30,000. Proposing constructs is easy, finding redundancies and overlaps is not. The effort of finding redundancies using participant responses grows quadratically with the number of measures. This cost motivates the use of language models, which can simplify and speed up the process without requiring new data collection. Earlier work employed latent semantic analysis (LSA) to make use of the textual nature of questionnaires in the social and behavioral sciences. However, LSA treats sentences as bags of words and ignores word order, syntax, and negation, all of which shape how respondents interpret items. Recent advances demonstrate that transformer-based sentence embedding models offer a more viable solution for predicting empirical relatedness between survey items. In the presented work, we use a fine-tuned language model, the SurveyBot3000, to introduce the Synthometricon, an open-access web application for systematic detection of conceptual overlap. The application indexes over 570,000 items across more than 97,000 scales from approximately 28,000 instruments in the APA PsycTests database and other sources.

articles_hidden.title: Congenital visual impairment does not impede the development of infants’ ability to reach to the self
articles_hidden.authors: GIULIA CAPPAGLI; Matej Hoffmann; Lisa K Chinn; Jason A.M. Khoury; Jeffrey J. Lockman; Sabrina Signorini; gori monica
articles_hidden.abstract: While early visual deprivation can hinder some spatial skills, it can also lead to sensory enhancements. Evidence from visually impaired infants is sparse but suggests preserved unisensory orienting and greater reliance on touch alongside reduced multisensory spatial integration and delayed spatially guided action.1,2 Reaching to touch on the body is a spatial task requiring touch to be remapped relative to body posture. Visual impairment could therefore delay this ability if vision calibrates spatial representations, or preserve or enhance it if attention to somatosensory input supports compensation. We tested sighted, low-vision, and blind infants (6–24 months) reaching to vibrotactile targets. Reaching success was comparable across groups and increased with age. Low-vision infants reached more slowly than sighted infants, whereas blind infants did not differ from sighted infants. Thus, body-centered tactile localization can develop without typical visual experience, although degraded visual input may selectively slow somatosensory guidance of action.

articles_hidden.title: More Than a Keypress: Continuous Key-Actuation Dynamics for Decomposing Speeded Responses
articles_hidden.authors: David Levi Tekampe; Philip Samuel Santangelo
articles_hidden.abstract: Conventional keypress measurement reduces a continuous motor action to a discrete event, typically represented by reaction time (RT) and accuracy. The present study evaluated continuous analogue key-actuation as a method for characterising the unfolding response while retaining a conventional two-choice keypress format. Seventy-seven adults completed the Attention Network Test-Revised (ANT-R) while response-key depth was recorded continuously. We derived target- and press-locked waveforms together with pre-specified measures of response timing, morphology, variability, preparation, and bilateral coor-dination. Established ANT-R manipulations served as experimentally controlled tests of measurement sensitivity. Target-locked waveforms differentiated six of the seven planned ANT-R contrasts after Holm adjustment; location conflict was not significant, and the alerting effect was less robust in sensitivity analyses. No exploratory press-locked contrast survived mul-tiplicity correction. Initiation time and peak-actuation time showed reliable effects across multiple attentional contrasts, whereas ramp time (the initiation-to-peak interval) showed no reliable modulation. Effects in the morphology, coordination, and preparation/control families were more selective and were confined to flanker conflict. Exploratory models further showed that ramp, rise-to-maximum, and return durations and hold jitter predicted trial-level accuracy after controlling for RT, whereas initiation time did not. These findings show that continuous key-actuation can decompose when a speeded re-sponse begins and how it unfolds, while selected key-actuation measures provide response-quality information beyond con-ventional RT. Continuous key-actuation therefore provides an experimentally sensitive measurement approach for extending standard keypress responses, although reliability and cross-device generalisation remain to be established.

articles_hidden.title: The Association Between SES and Students’ Achievement Motivation in Secondary School: An Individual Participant Data Meta-Analysis Spanning Two Decades of PISA Data
articles_hidden.authors: Sarah Grünthal; Lena Keller; Julia Kretschmann; Hanna Dumont; Martin Brunner
articles_hidden.abstract: Major theoretical frameworks of achievement motivation link family socioeconomic status (SES) to students’ achievement motivation in school settings. However, systematic evidence on this association remains limited. This study presents the first meta-analysis on this topic, using representative individual participant data (IPD) from the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA). The analysis included 485 student samples comprising a total of 3,576,278 15-year-old students, spanning four SES indicators, eight achievement motivation components, four academic domains, 92 countries, and eight assessment cycles across more than two decades (2000–2022). The average meta-analytic association between SES and achievement motivation was small (r = .10, 95% CI [.09, .11]), indicating slightly higher achievement motivation among students from higher-SES families. The magnitude of the association varied meaningfully across SES indicators and motivational components, but only marginally across academic domains. Educational home resources (e.g., books, educational materials) showed stronger associations with achievement motivation than parental education or occupational status, and self-efficacy exhibited the largest association among motivational components. The association increased over historical time but declined following the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic. After controlling for academic achievement, the meta-analytic average association between family SES and achievement motivation remained statistically significant, but its magnitude was attenuated. These nuanced findings highlight the complex association between family SES and students’ achievement motivation, emphasizing the multidimensionality of both constructs and providing an important empirical foundation for evaluating, refining, and advancing psychological theories that address the link between family SES and students’ achievement motivation.

articles_hidden.title: Calling Development: A Systematic Review of Longitudinal Evidence
articles_hidden.authors: Sophie Gerdel; Anna Dalla Rosa; Bryan Dik; Michelangelo Vianello
articles_hidden.abstract: Although career calling is linked to many beneficial outcomes for both individuals and organizations, knowledge on how a sense of calling develops is limited and, in some ways, controversial. To clarify this issue, we conducted a systematic review of longitudinal studies that analyzed the temporal relation between calling and other variables in its nomological network. Across 14 studies, the strongest longitudinal evidence suggests that calling is more often an outcome of career development processes rather than an initiating cause. Specifically, vocational self-definition, agency, and career feedback and appraisal appear to precede calling, whereas personal resources more often follow calling, and life meaning and values appears reciprocally linked with calling. On this basis, we propose a preliminary integrative developmental framework of calling in which calling emerges through recursive cycles of career clarification, agentic engagement, contextual feedback and appraisal, and life meaning- and value-based integration.

articles_hidden.title: La Pirámide del Sueño: desarrollo y difusión nacional de una herramienta de comunicación basada en hábitos para promover un sueño saludable
articles_hidden.authors: Manuel Armayones; Sílvia Gismera; Laura Armayones-Carranza
articles_hidden.abstract: La Pirámide del Sueño es una herramienta de educación para la salud que ordena las recomendaciones de higiene del sueño en cuatro niveles: ritmos y horarios; hábitos y rutinas que ayudan a desconectar; ambiente óptimo para el sueño, y estrategias en la cama. Se desarrolló en la Alianza por el Sueño combinando el formato, ya familiar, de las pirámides alimentarias con el enfoque de diseño de conducta y formación de hábitos de Fogg, que convierte cada recomendación en un pequeño hábito asociado a una rutina. Se presentó en mayo de 2025 con 26 organizaciones colaboradoras y, según el seguimiento de medios, generó 210 impactos informativos y 26 entrevistas, con una audiencia acumulada de 69,9 millones, además de 260 menciones en redes sociales. Unir una metáfora visual conocida y un modelo sencillo de formación de hábitos es una estrategia viable y de bajo coste para promover el sueño saludable; su efecto sobre la conducta está por evaluar.

articles_hidden.title: Questionable mediated effect of artificial intelligence anxiety on academic burnout: A comment on Long et al. (2026)
articles_hidden.authors: Kimmo Sorjonen
articles_hidden.abstract: Drawing on the covariance matrix reported by Long et al., I reassessed the empirical basis of their mediation model linking artificial intelligence anxiety to academic burnout. I demonstrate that the observed covariance structure can be reproduced by a theoretically different latent-variable model that does not rely on the directional mechanism proposed in the original article. In this alternative account, self-reported artificial intelligence anxiety, perceived stress, rumination, and academic burnout are conceptualized as negative indicators of a broader construct, core self-evaluation. The results illustrate a broader inferential problem in psychological research: multiple theoretically plausible models may provide equally adequate explanations of the same correlational pattern. Consequently, observational associations alone offer limited grounds for preferring one explanation over competing alternatives. Researchers should therefore routinely evaluate alternative models when drawing inferences about psychological mechanisms from nonexperimental data.

articles_hidden.title: Spatial Aspects of Felt Presence and the Phenomenon of Childhood Imaginary Companions: Peripersonal Space, Embodied Perspective, and Continuity of Agent Propensity
articles_hidden.authors: Burak; Bigna Lenggenhager
articles_hidden.abstract:
Felt presence (FP) refers to the experience of sensing another agent nearby despite the
absence of corresponding sensory evidence, and has been reported across neurological,
psychiatric, and non-clinical populations. However, its potential phenomenological similarity and
continuity with the common childhood experience of imaginary companions (ICs) have received
little attention. The present study characterizes the spatial and perspectival features of
retrospectively reported childhood IC experiences, evaluates their parallels with the
phenomenology of FP, and interprets these convergences within the theoretical framework of
bodily self-consciousness (BSC) and peripersonal space (PPS). Three theory-driven predictions
were tested using retrospective self-reports from a healthy adult sample (N = 185; IC+ = 45; IC−
= 140) excluding participants with psychiatric or neurological diagnoses. First, we examined
whether IC representations were spatially anchored within PPS (Peripersonal Anchoring). Second,
we assessed whether IC experiences were predominantly reported from an embodied, first-person
or third-person perspective. Third, we tested whether individuals reporting childhood ICs show a
greater adult propensity for presence-related experiences (Continuity of Agent Propensity).
Results supported all three predictions. Most spatial distance reports (76.1%) fell within 70 cm of
the body, with an overall median distance of 12 cm, consistent with PPS anchoring. IC experiences
were primarily reported from a first-person perspective (55.6%) and referenced to the body
(88.9%). Furthermore, individuals with childhood ICs reported higher scores on the Sensed
Presence Questionnaire (SenPQ; 15 items, excluding Item 7 due to cross-loading) during
adulthood, whereas dissociative tendencies did not differ between groups. Exploratory logistic
regression identified perceived presence proneness as the only significant predictor of IC history.
Together, these findings suggest that both adult FP and childhood IC experiences may be grounded
in the spatial organization of the bodily action field and reflect a stable disposition for internally
generated social-agent representations.

articles_hidden.title: Cognitive reserve differently impacts cognition and metacognition across domains
articles_hidden.authors: Audrey Mazancieux; Lucile Meunier-Duperray; Coline Grégoire; Christine Bastin; Céline Souchay; Chris Moulin; Lucie Angel
articles_hidden.abstract: Preservative effects of cognitive reserve on age-related decline have been widely studied in episodic memory, however less is known about how cognitive reserve influences other domains such as semantic memory or visual perception. Similarly, recent studies suggest that the decline of metacognition observed with age might be reduced by cognitive reserve in the memory domain, but the domain-generality of such effect remains unexplored. This study is part of a published study investigating the effect of age on cognition and metacognition in episodic memory, semantic memory, executive functioning, and visual perception (Meunier-Duperray et al., 2025). Here, we focused on cognitive reserve measured by the CRIq on cognition (i.e., task performance) and metacognition in a subsample of 319 participants (aged from 18 to 79). We expected an effect of cognitive reserve only on tasks sensitive to age-related decline: episodic memory, executive functioning, and visual perception for task performance and episodic and semantic tasks for metacognition. Overall, these results suggest evidence for the null hypothesis for the effect of cognitive reserve on the age-related decline in cognition and metacognition. Only anecdotal to small evidence was found for an effect of cognitive reserve on episodic memory performance across the lifespan suggesting that reserve reflects earlier individual differences rather than differences in the rate of decline. However, the low variability of our high-reserve sample may have masked some effects.

articles_hidden.title: When attention turns inward: Mind wandering reduces perceptual sensitivity across visual fields
articles_hidden.authors: Bianca de Haan
articles_hidden.abstract: We all mind wander from time to time, where instead of being focussed on our task, we start thinking about task-unrelated personal events or concerns. In daily life, however, mind wandering is often associated with reduced processing of external information. This is commonly explained by the decoupling hypothesis, which posits that processing of external sensory information is attenuated when attention turns inward. However, it remains unclear whether perceptual decoupling reflects a global, uniform attenuation of sensory processing, or a spatially-specific reduction linked to lateralised attentional mechanisms. In the current, pre-registered study, we used an online signal detection task to assess the impact of mind wandering on perceptual performance in the left and right visual fields. While performing the task, participants periodically reported whether they were mind wandering or on task. Consistent with the decoupling hypothesis, perceptual sensitivity (d′) was significantly reduced on trials during which participants reported mind wandering compared to on-task trials. However, this reduction in sensitivity did not differ between stimuli presented in the left and right visual field. These findings suggest that perceptual decoupling during mind wandering reflects a global attenuation of sensory processing, and that attentional systems involved during mind wandering may be distinct from those associated with slower fluctuations of attentional resources such as reductions in alertness.

articles_hidden.title: Exploring the Role of Physical Effort in the Rewarding Value of Sedentary Behavior
articles_hidden.authors: Silvio Maltagliati; Pam ten Broeke; Philippe Sarrazin; Ryan Rhodes; Erik Bijleveld; Genevieve Fridlund Dunton; Cedrick Bonnet; Benjamin Gardner; David A. Raichlen; Matthew W Miller
articles_hidden.abstract: Objective: Sedentary behavior is commonly studied based on the value of the higher-order task being performed, such as watching TV, using a phone, or playing video games. However, it is possible that the low physical effort associated with these behaviors also contributes to their appeal. That is, individuals may be drawn not just to the task but to the low effort it is paired with. This study aims to test this possibility by manipulating body position (sitting vs. standing) while participants engage in a familiar sedentary task (i.e., playing Tetris). Methods: To test this hypothesis, we manipulated body position during a smartphone video game task to examine how sitting versus standing affected the rewarding value assigned to the game. Results: Our results (two independent studies, N = 228 and N = 129) show that the rewarding value of this sedentary behavior also stems from the low effort cost associated with sitting. Conclusions: These findings suggest that the perception of effort may contribute to influencing sedentary preferences and provide valuable insights for interventions aimed at reducing excessive sedentary behavior, such as targeted strategies to increase the valuation of physical effort.

articles_hidden.title: Sampling Thoughts During Music Listening: A Systematic Comparison of Probe-caught, Self-caught and Retrospective Thought Reporting Methods
articles_hidden.authors: Nao Toyama; Kelly Jakubowski
articles_hidden.abstract: Music listening experiences dynamically unfold over time. However, as previous research has relied predominantly on short music excerpts and retrospective post-listening self-reports, how qualitative thought content unfolds during extended listening remains underexplored. Crucially, addressing this requires effective real-time sampling, yet direct empirical comparisons of such methods––i.e., experimenter-led versus participant-led approaches––and their impact on data quality and listener experience are remain lacking. To address these gaps, the present study systematically compared three experience-sampling methodologies (probe-caught, self-caught, and a retrospective control) using participants’ own smartphones during an 18-minute video of a classical music performance. While the control group yielded significantly fewer thoughts, both experimental groups (probe- and self-caught) reported a comparable total number of thoughts. The probe-caught method exhibited greater inter-participant stability and generated significantly more detailed qualitative descriptions. Importantly, participants’ subjective perceived interference on their listening experience was low and did not differ across groups, confirming that real-time thought reporting did not disrupt the natural listening experience compared with traditional retrospective reporting. By validating the efficiency, stability, and minimal invasiveness of the probe-caught method, this study provides an empirical foundation for future research investigating real-time subjective experiences across diverse listening environments.

articles_hidden.title: Sentiment Analysis of Clinical Interviews Identifies Language Markers of Identity Diffusion in Adolescents with Personality Disorder
articles_hidden.authors: Katarina Lodrant; Filip Melinscak; Ayse Nur Beris; Valentin Schneider; Klara Czernin; Anselm Bründlmayer; Paul Plener; Frank Scharnowski; David Steyrl; Clarissa Laczkovics
articles_hidden.abstract:
Identity diffusion – a fragmented sense of self and others maintained by splitting-based defenses – is a core feature of impaired personality functioning, theorized to involve heightened negative affectivity and affective instability. Evidence from other psychopathologies suggests that markers of affective disturbances can be automatically extracted from spontaneous speech, yet the linguistic correlates of identity diffusion have rarely been examined – particularly in adolescents, the age group in which personality pathology assessment is most challenging but also most consequential for early intervention.
Transcripts of the Structured Interview of Personality Organization (STIPO) for adolescents were analyzed in a sample of 72 German-speaking participants (50 patients, 22 healthy controls) spanning the full spectrum from consolidated identity to severe identity diffusion. An interpretable lexicon-based sentiment analysis framework combined word frequency measures (LIWC) with continuous word-level valence indices (VADER), capturing both the prevalence and the dynamics of emotional tone.
Greater identity diffusion was associated with higher affective variability (r = .48–.55), a more negative overall affective orientation (strongest effect: r = −.62), more frequent negative affective language, and more extreme negative expression, with weaker evidence for reduced positive language. Measures of positive extremes, affective expressiveness, and verbosity showed no significant associations.
Identity diffusion in adolescents is thus associated with a distinctive affective language profile, detectable from clinical interview transcripts using sentiment analysis. The results are consistent with psychodynamic accounts of splitting and affective dysregulation, and support the potential of automated language analysis as a reproducible, scalable complement to clinical assessment.

articles_hidden.title: NICE’s 2026 Consultation Draft Guideline for OCD and BDD (GID-NG10435): A Critical Appraisal with Secondary Analysis of NICE’s Published Data
articles_hidden.authors: Himanshu Tyagi; Mark Paramlall
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background. In September 2026 the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) opened consultation on the first batch of its update to the 2005 guideline for obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) and body dysmorphic disorder (BDD) (GID-NG10435). The draft replaces stepped care with matched care and reviews first-line treatment.

Methods. We appraised the draft and its supporting documents against six questions informed by selected AGREE II domains, analysing NICE’s published effect estimates, sample sizes, sensitivity analyses and economic results descriptively; every value was checked against its source document. Comparison guidelines were identified by a documented search.

Results. The adult OCD review included 82 randomised controlled trials and the BDD review 13 studies. The committee cited small samples and wide credible intervals when it did not recommend metacognitive therapy (52 participants) or eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing (EMDR; 59 participants). Self-administered cognitive behavioural therapy with therapist support, the second adult option, rests on 61 participants, with a wider credible interval than EMDR’s, and was recommended on other documented grounds. The top-ranked adult option had a probability of 0.17 of being the most cost-effective. The first-listed BDD option ranked fifth of nine in the network meta-analysis. The draft gives no drug-specific dose targets, no consolidated definition of an adequate trial and no primary severity measure for allocation or response. Treatment after non-response to an adequate trial is outside the scope of Batch 1; on the assumptions in NHS England’s 2013 specification, a cascade beginning with 48 million adults in England and Wales yields approximately 48,000 people not responding to a serotonin reuptake inhibitor followed by local graduated exposure. All six selected multimodal OCD comparison guidelines address augmentation; none provides a treatment pathway for BDD.

Conclusions. The draft rests on a substantial evidence synthesis. The published rationale does not fully explain why small samples and imprecision precluded recommendations for some treatments but not others; several operational parameters are not specified; and further-line treatment is outside the first batch.

articles_hidden.title: Item-dropping to improve in-sample Cronbach's alpha can harm true reliability: A Monte Carlo simulation
articles_hidden.authors: Ze Freeman; Ian Hussey
articles_hidden.abstract: Cronbach’s alpha is the most commonly reported metric of reliability in psychological measurement, and statistical software encourages a common post hoc revision: dropping the item whose removal most improves in-sample alpha. A Monte Carlo simulation examined what this practice does to true reliability, varying items per scale (5 to 40) and sample size (20 to 1,000), with item pools generated from a loading distribution fitted to 3,783 factor loadings from real psychological scales. Two strategies, always dropping the nominated item or dropping only when in-sample alpha improves, were evaluated against the population alpha and true reliability of the retained items. The bias in the reported alpha itself was modest, overstating true reliability only in short scales at small samples and understating it elsewhere. The decision was another matter: at the smallest scale and sample size, dropping reduced true reliability in 46.7% of the replications in which the conditional rule acted, despite requiring an apparent improvement, and almost the entire apparent gain was selection optimism. Stricter decision rules helped only in large samples: with N of 200 or more, acting only on apparent gains above .02 kept the probability of harming the scale at or below 7%, whereas at N = 20 no threshold examined made the decision safe. Because this risk depends on scale length and sample size, given loadings typical of trait scales, it is knowable before data are collected, whereas nothing inside the alpha-if-item-removed table distinguishes a genuinely weak item from a sampling artefact.

articles_hidden.title: A multidimensional normative database of experiential ratings for German nouns
articles_hidden.authors: Cristina Cara; Christian Bellebaum; Laura Bechtold; Marta Ghio
articles_hidden.abstract: Theories of semantic representation propose that concepts are grounded in multiple forms of experience, yet normative resources capturing this multidimensionality remain scarce, especially in German. We present a database of experiential ratings for 1,985 German nouns, with particularly broad coverage of abstract concepts (a 3:1 ratio of abstract to concrete nouns). In total, 354 native German speakers rated the extent to which the meaning of each word is associated with 16 experiential dimensions spanning perceptual, motor, affective, cognitive, social and magnitude-related domains, complemented by concreteness and familiarity ratings. The database additionally provides the dominant experiential dimension of each word and an exclusivity score quantifying how strongly its profile is dominated by a single dimension relative to the others. Cross-database validation against existing German norms showed strong convergence with our concreteness, valence, and arousal ratings.
