Longitudinal test-retest assessment of all experiential dimensions, as well as concreteness and familiarity, in a subsample of 36 participants showed moderate to high temporal stability across ratings. To characterize the multidimensional structure captured by the database, we further applied exploratory factor analysis followed by hierarchical clustering in the factor-derived semantic space. These analyses identified three broad factors interpreted as socioemotional, perceptual, and magnitude-related, and four clusters of words with distinct experiential profiles. Summary-level and participant-level data are freely available through the project website, which also provides an interactive interface for exploring the norms. The database provides a resource for research on conceptual representation in psycholinguistics, cognitive neuroscience, and computational semantics.

articles_hidden.title: Questionable mediated effect of police work stress on life satisfaction: A comment on Qiu et al. (2026)
articles_hidden.authors: Kimmo Sorjonen
articles_hidden.abstract: Drawing on the covariance matrix reported by Qiu et al., I reassessed the empirical basis of their mediation model linking police work stress to decreased life satisfaction. I demonstrate that the observed covariance structure can be reproduced by a theoretically different latent-variable model that does not rely on the directional mechanism proposed in the original article. In this alternative account, self-reported police work stress, perceived social support, sleep disturbance, and life satisfaction are conceptualized as indicators of a broader construct, core self-evaluation. The results illustrate a broader inferential problem in psychological research: multiple theoretically plausible models may provide equally adequate explanations of the same correlational pattern. Consequently, observational associations alone offer limited grounds for preferring one explanation over competing alternatives. Researchers should therefore routinely evaluate alternative models when drawing inferences about psychological mechanisms from nonexperimental data.

articles_hidden.title: Health care practitioners’ knowledge, attitudes and perceptions of psychedelic treatments for mental disorders: A scoping review
articles_hidden.authors: Jacqueline Samantha Womersley; Gabriela Iacovou; Yumna Kathrada; Marnus Janse van Vuuren; Hannah Lukic; Soraya Seedat
articles_hidden.abstract: Interest in psychedelic treatments for mental health conditions is growing. Health care professionals will be key in the implementation, recommendation, and administration of psychedelic-assisted therapy (PAT) if and when it is approved for clinical use, making their knowledge, attitudes, and perceptions (KAPs) central to successful translation into practice. We conducted a scoping review of health care professionals’ KAPs toward the psychedelic treatment of mental health conditions. Thirty-nine studies, comprising both quantitative and qualitative investigations, were included. The number of studies, and range of health care professionals surveyed, increased over time, though research remained concentrated in North America, Europe, and Australia. Participants mostly performed well on objective knowledge assessments, but this did not necessarily align with subjective knowledge, which indicated lower self-reported confidence in PAT theory and practice. Attitudes toward psychedelics’ therapeutic potential, safety, and legalisation were generally favourable, although concerns included potential misuse, risk of precipitating subsequent psychiatric disorders, and cognitive impairment. Participants generally perceived psychiatrists and specialised facilities as most suitable for PAT administration, and the need for further research was strongly supported. A lack of trained personnel and resources, and cost, side effect, and misuse concerns, were the most frequently endorsed barriers to implementation. Research into health care professionals' KAPs regarding psychedelic treatment is maturing, but important gaps remain: granular insight into KAPs toward specific compound-disorder combinations is lacking, and geographic coverage does not reflect the global burden of mental illness. Addressing these gaps will be important as PAT moves closer to clinical implementation.

articles_hidden.title: Intentions to Help Friends Across Cultural Groups: The Role of Emotional Connectedness
articles_hidden.authors: Arzu Karakulak; Michael Bender
articles_hidden.abstract: Across five studies (N = 1,859), we examined cross-cultural variation in emotional connectedness and intentions to help a family member, a friend, and a stranger. Samples included a nationally representative Dutch panel (Study 1), Turkish and Dutch students (Study 2), Turkish and German working adults (Study 3), culturally primed Turkish-German biculturals (Study 4), and bilingual Turkish students (Study 5). Contrary to the traditional view that collectivists prioritize in-group ties more strongly than individualists, we hypothesized greater intentions to help friends among participants from relatively individualistic contexts or primed with an individualistic cultural frame. Results consistently supported the hypothesized differences for intentions to help friends, while differences in intentions to help a family member and a stranger were less consistent and generally not reliable. Study 1 further suggested that emotional connectedness statistically accounted for group differences in intentions to help friends, and Study 5 provided tentative converging evidence that an English-language prime was associated with greater connectedness with friends than a Turkish-language prime. Together, these findings suggest that considering the role of particular relational targets within their cultural context may provide a more differentiated account of cross-cultural variation in helping than broad individualism–collectivism or in-group–out-group classifications alone.

articles_hidden.title: Vocal Evaluation of Classical Singing in a Concert Hall: Perceptual and Acoustic Associations with Overall Scores in Male and Female Singers
articles_hidden.authors: Haruka Kondo; Sotaro Kondoh; Shinya Fujii
articles_hidden.abstract:
Introduction. In classical vocal competitions, judges reduce a performance to a single overall score, yet what that score reflects is unclear. Research has separately identified the perceptual attributes experts use and the acoustic features of trained singers. Few studies link these to expert evaluation, and those that do have used playback of sound-treated recordings and rarely tested for sex differences. Yet classical singing is judged live in halls, and male and female voices differ acoustically. We asked which attributes and acoustic features are associated with the overall score in a concert hall, and whether they differ by sex.
Methods. Twenty-two classical singers (10 males, 12 females) performed Caro mio ben a cappella in a concert hall. Five singer-instructors rated each performance on a 100-point overall score and 7-point scales for six vocal attributes. Singing power ratio (SPR), loudness units full scale (LUFS), vibrato rate (VR), and vibrato extent (VE) were computed from annotated vowel segments of close-microphone recordings. Linear mixed-effects models related the overall score to the ratings or acoustic features, with sex interactions and a random judge intercept.
Results. Higher ratings of vibrato, resonance, and expressiveness were associated with higher overall scores, whereas timbre, diction, and intonation were not. Higher SPR, greater VE, and lower VR were associated with higher overall scores, whereas LUFS was not. Sex interacted with VE and VR but not with SPR or LUFS: the VE association was stronger in females, the VR association in males.
Conclusion. Overall scores were associated with perceived vibrato, resonance, and expressiveness, and with spectral prominence at 2–4 kHz. Vibrato associations were sex-dependent: a faster rate accompanied lower scores in males, a greater extent higher scores in females. These findings give expert evaluation a measurable basis under realistic conditions and indicate that vibrato should be interpreted with reference to singer sex.

articles_hidden.title: Divided attention during encoding constrains the benefits of interim testing for subsequent learning
articles_hidden.authors: Bernhard Pastötter; Karl-Heinz Bäuml
articles_hidden.abstract: Retrieval practice can enhance learning of subsequently studied target information, a phenomenon known as the forward testing effect or test-potentiated new learning. The present study examined whether this effect depends on attentional engagement during encoding. In two experiments, participants studied three lists of unrelated words (Experiment 1) or three educationally relevant prose passages (Experiment 2). After the first two learning blocks, they either restudied the material or were tested on it. Attention during encoding of the final target material was manipulated by a concurrent secondary task. Under full attention, interim testing enhanced recall of the final target material in both experiments and improved performance on a final knowledge transfer test in Experiment 2. Under divided attention, these effects were reduced in Experiment 1 and eliminated in Experiment 2. The findings indicate that the beneficial effect of interim testing depends critically on attention during encoding of the latter studied information.

articles_hidden.title: Questionable mediated effect of family functioning on college students’ differentiation of the self: A comment on Luo et al. (2026)
articles_hidden.authors: Kimmo Sorjonen
articles_hidden.abstract: Drawing on the covariance matrix reported by Luo et al., I reassessed the empirical basis of their mediation model linking family malfunctioning to decreased differentiation of self. I demonstrate that the observed covariance structure can be reproduced by a theoretically different latent-variable model that does not rely on the directional mechanism proposed in the original article. In this alternative account, self-reported family malfunctioning, loneliness, psychological security, and differentiation of self are conceptualized as indicators of a broader construct, core self-evaluation. The results illustrate a broader inferential problem in psychological research: multiple theoretically plausible models may provide equally adequate explanations of the same correlational pattern. Consequently, observational associations alone offer limited grounds for preferring one explanation over competing alternatives. Researchers should therefore routinely evaluate alternative models when drawing inferences about psychological mechanisms from nonexperimental data.

articles_hidden.title: Choosing Stimuli Wisely by Using Individual Differences: A Step-by-Step Tutorial for the One-Stimulus-Per-Factor Principle in Vision Science and Optometric Assessment
articles_hidden.authors: David Henry Peterzell
articles_hidden.abstract: Given that data collection time in vision research and clinical assessment is limited, investigators and clinicians must select stimuli that maximize diagnostic information with minimum redundancy. This article proposes that analyzing individual differences—through factor analysis (FA), principal component analysis (PCA), and multidimensional scaling (MDS)—offers a principled approach. The covariance structure of individual variation reveals the minimum number of independent factors underlying a visual function, and therefore the minimum number of stimuli needed for efficient, non-redundant characterization. I term this the One-Stimulus-Per-Factor Principle: one well-chosen stimulus per factor is both necessary and sufficient. A complementary rule governs discovery: at least two to three stimuli per expected factor are needed to establish the factor structure. Converging evidence from luminance and chromatic contrast sensitivity, stereoscopic disparity, motion, hue scaling, face recognition, perceptual organization, and other domains shows that the dimensionality of individual variation is often lower than dense sampling suggests—and sometimes higher than sparse clinical testing captures. The approach also tests construct validity, revealing whether behavioral measures index the mechanisms investigators assume. These findings carry implications for clinical instruments across contrast sensitivity, color vision, stereopsis, and visual field assessment, many of which either oversample a single factor or undersample the full factor space. The same framework clarifies psychiatric applications—including contrast-sensitivity changes in depression, schizophrenia, and ADHD—by separating retinal-neural deficits from optical contributions such as higher-order aberrations and from attentional lapses, and it extends to oculomotor biomarkers. The article develops the Principle as a step-by-step tutorial, with a worked example.

articles_hidden.title: Musical Groove as Stabilization of Coordinated Movement: A Dynamical and Embodied Approach to Musical Rhythm
articles_hidden.authors: Ji Chul Kim
articles_hidden.abstract: Research has shown that the bodily experience of pleasurable urge to move to music, called groove, is the strongest for rhythms with an intermediate level of syncopation. Current theories explain groove in terms of predictive processes in the brain, as an active inference which resolves prediction errors caused by syncopation. Here we present an alternative explanation of groove from a new dynamical and embodied approach to music perception and action. The new theory, called embodied dynamics of music (EDM), describes musical rhythm as a dynamic pattern of coordinated movement distributed in the brain and the body and governed by the principles and constraints of coordination dynamics. Specifically, beat-based rhythm is described as a coordinative structure in which beat-carrying oscillatory movements provide anchor points for coordinating discrete movements corresponding to individual rhythmic events. In this view, syncopation is a potentially destabilizing force in the coordinative structure, and groove is an active engagement that stabilizes the coordinative structure by reinforcing beat-carrying oscillation with body movement. We support this theory with an analysis of coordination dynamics and a minimal dynamical model of groove which stabilizes syncopated coordination with a metronome by amplifying its self-sustained oscillation.

articles_hidden.title: Identity Centrality and Trauma- and Stressor-related Psychopathology: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Kari Ellen James; Blake M McKimmie; Fiona Maccallum
articles_hidden.abstract: Over the past two decades there has been growing interest in how events, roles, or relationships that are central to an individual’s identity relate to trauma- and stressor-related psychopathology. However, the field lacks a systematic review to synthesize current knowledge across various facets of identity centrality and guide future research in meaningful ways. This systematic review and meta-analysis of the relationship between identity centrality and trauma- and stressor-related psychopathology identified 154 studies (96.1% traumatic stress, 9.7% prolonged grief) representing 66,371 individual participants. Three constructs were identified: event centrality (96% of studies), role centrality (1.9% of studies), and relationship centrality (2.6% of studies). Meta-analysis of 124 studies examining event centrality (k = 249) revealed a medium to large positive association between measures of centrality and severity of traumatic stress and prolonged grief symptoms (mean effect size of r = .446). However, heterogeneity was high. Moderators of outcomes included event type and cultural background. Notably, most studies were cross-sectional (86.4%), precluding causal conclusions. However, emerging evidence indicates that identity centrality and symptom severity may follow independent trajectories over time, raising questions about whether centrality represents a cause or consequence of distress, or a distinct process, and about the role of associated appraisals. Further, the literature is dominated by studies from WEIRD countries. The field would benefit from systematic reporting of key study characteristics such as time since index event, and studies designed to examine causal relationships. Further, most attention has been paid to event centrality, yet this is only one form of identity centrality. Constructs such as role centrality and relationship centrality should be further investigated where theoretically indicated.

articles_hidden.title: Where, Not How Far: Gender-Diverse Pronoun Use and the Ideal Singing Voice
articles_hidden.authors: Logan Barrett
articles_hidden.abstract: Many transgender and gender-diverse (TGD) people want their voices to change, but how pronoun use, a public expression of gender that only partly overlaps with identity labels, relates to the voice people want is unknown. In an online survey (N = 2,536), participants placed their current and ideal singing voices on a 5-point masculine–feminine scale. In exploratory analyses, participants who used they/them pronouns, alone or with she or he (n = 130), wanted larger changes than binary-pronoun users (n = 2,272; d = 0.84, 95% CI [0.66, 1.02]). The difference was robust to age and sex assigned at birth and was attenuated but still present after adjustment for gender identity and recruitment cohort. Among TGD participants, however, the two pronoun groups wanted changes of similar size (d = 0.11 [−0.16, 0.37]), so the full-sample contrast largely reflected comparison with cisgender binary-pronoun users. Pronoun use instead distinguished the destination of change: among TGD participants, 48.1% of gender-diverse pronoun users placed their ideal at the gender-neutral midpoint, compared with 18.3% of binary-pronoun users, whose ideals more often lay at a masculine or feminine pole. A moderation pattern in which singing-related gender incongruence strengthened the link between desired change and the acoustics of a chosen model singer did not replicate in a held-out test set and is not supported. Pronoun use appears to index where, more than how far, people want their singing voices to go; vocal goals and the scales that measure them should accommodate gender-neutral targets.

articles_hidden.title: One Gender Axis, Two Vocabularies: How People Conceptualize Gendered Speaking and Singing Voices
articles_hidden.authors: Logan Barrett
articles_hidden.abstract: Gender-affirming voice care is organized around speech, yet many people also want to change how they sing. Whether the two rest on one concept of vocal gender is unknown. Participants (N = 2,536) described what makes a speaking voice and a singing voice sound feminine and masculine, rated their current and ideal voices in each modality, and named people whose speaking and singing voices they would like to have. I embedded the descriptions with a sentence encoder and analyzed them, together with word frequencies, in exploratory analyses. The feminine–masculine direction in speaking descriptions was nearly identical to the direction in singing descriptions (cosine = .967), and a classifier trained on one modality separated the other with almost no loss (area under the curve = .960 and .979). The shared direction was carried by register, softness, and depth words; singing descriptions added range, notes, and power, and speaking descriptions added softness, roughness, and monotony. Individuals’ own contrasts aligned only modestly across modalities (mean cosine = .362). Wanting a more feminine speaking voice predicted choosing a female singer but not a more acoustically feminine singer within gender category. Vocal gender appears to be a shared, category-level abstraction expressed in modality-specific vocabulary.

articles_hidden.title: Willpower or Choice? A Within-Country, Cross-Linguistic Comparison of Free Will Judgments
articles_hidden.authors: Alison Oliver; Paulius Rimkevičius; Renato Cesar Cardoso; Marcel Brass; Uri Maoz
articles_hidden.abstract: Does the language we speak influence how we think about free will? Previous work has often compared free will judgments across linguistic and cultural groups without isolating language from broader cultural differences. More recent work has found cross-cultural variation, but these designs could not determine whether language itself contributed to that variation. Here we report two exploratory studies in which language was varied while culture was held relatively constant. In Study 1, monolingual English- and French-speaking Canadians rated comics depicting choice and willpower on whether they represent free will. The English phrase free will makes will, and so willpower, salient; the French phrase libre arbitre makes choice salient (as in “to arbitrate”). If language shapes the concept, English-speakers should associate free will relatively more with willpower, and French-speakers relatively more with choice. They did not: the two groups showed almost exactly the same preference for choice, and equivalence testing rules out anythingbeyond a small difference. Study 2 asked why choice comics were favored. Participants rated thesame comics on choice, willpower, doing what one wants, and absence of constraints. Across thenine comics, free will judgments closely tracked ratings of doing what one wants and of choice, but tracked absence of constraints less closely. Free will might therefore be associated most closely with choice and doing what one wants.

articles_hidden.title: Wrong Note, Wrong Time: Age and Musicianship-Related Influences on Rhythmic and Melodic Timing
articles_hidden.authors: Logan Barrett; Sarah Anne Sauvé; Andrea Rita Halpern; Benjamin Zendel
articles_hidden.abstract: Musical expectancy theory posits that listeners anticipate both the pitch that will occur and when it will occur; however, the interaction between these dimensions across age and expertise is less understood. In this study, 175 adults (ages 18–82; musicians and non-musicians) rated the final note of short monophonic melodies on its melodic and temporal fit. Endings were systematically manipulated in terms of pitch (tonal, chromatic, or atonal) and timing deviations. Results showed a strong effect of melodic expectancy: pitch deviations substantially reduced goodness-of-fit ratings, whereas timing shifts had comparatively weak effects. Musicians gave lower ratings overall, indicating heightened sensitivity to expectancy violations, whereas non-musicians were more lenient. Although age alone did not predict ratings, an age × musician interaction emerged: older musicians diverged most strongly from older non-musician peers, suggesting that expertise sharpens expectancy sensitivity across the lifespan. These findings demonstrate that pitch dominates expectancy judgments, while also revealing how aging and musicianship jointly influence the perception of musical errors—an area that remains underexplored in music cognition.

articles_hidden.title: Evaluating Large Language Models on Clinical Risk Judgement: An Example from Alcohol Use Disorder
articles_hidden.authors: Charles M. Bolton; Kiwon Song; Katelyn A Wasson; Clintin P Davis-Stober; Konstantina Sokratous
articles_hidden.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are being explored for medical risk assessment, yet performance on standardized benchmarks does not necessarily establish clinical competency. The present study evaluated whether LLM-generated Alcohol Use Disorder (AUD) risk judgments aligned with epidemiological evidence and remained consistent as clinical and demographic context changed. Three LLMs—GPT-5.5, LLaMA-2-70B, and MEDITRON-70B—completed four pairwise-comparison experiments involving DSM-5 AUD criteria, demographic characteristics, criteria paired with demographic characteristics, and narrative clinical vignettes. LLM-implied rankings were compared with epidemiological benchmarks derived from the National Epidemiological Survey on Alcohol and Related Conditions, Wave Three (NESARC-III). Our results show that none of the LLMs reproduced the implied severity ordering of the AUD criteria. Demographic cues consistently influenced AUD risk judgments, although the direction and magnitude of these effects varied across LLMs, demographic attributes, and clinical contexts. Demographic rankings also showed only partial stability as contextual information changed. LLMs differed substantially in decisiveness, with GPT-5.5 assigning substantially higher probability to selected responses than LLaMA-2-70B or MEDITRON-70B. These findings demonstrate a gap in current LLM risk-assessment capabilities and highlight the importance of evaluating the direction, magnitude, stability, and certainty of LLM judgments alongside accuracy.

articles_hidden.title: Subjective and Behavioral Difficulties in Social Contexts: Unique and Interacting Effects on Social Dysfunction Transdiagnostically
articles_hidden.authors: Kathryn Kemp; Carly A Lasagna; Scott D. Blain; Cynthia Z. Burton; Costanza Colombi; Aubrey M Moe; Ivy Fei Tso
articles_hidden.abstract: Prior research indicates that social functioning is impacted by both social engagement and subjective experience regarding social interactions. The goal of this study was to examine the extent to which each component, as well as their interaction, contributes to social dysfunction in a combined nonclinical and transdiagnostic psychiatric sample. A sample of young adults (n=193) spanning the social dysfunction spectrum completed measures that capture different forms of psychopathology relevant to social dysfunction, from which two dimensions – Subjective Psychosocial Difficulties (SPD) and Observed Social Difficulties (OSD) – were extracted using Principal Components Analysis. Participants additionally completed a variety of clinician-rated and self-reported social functioning measures that were aggregated into one overall social functioning score. Hierarchical regression was used to examine the unique contribution of SPD and OSD and their interaction on overall social functioning. SPD and OSD explained unique variance (Δr2=61.0%), indicating that elevated SPD and OSD levels predicted worse social functioning. The SPD-by-OSD interaction was positive and explained significant additional amounts of variance (Δr2=1.9%), indicating a less-than-additive effect on social dysfunction. The findings suggest that examining observable social behaviors and subjective psychosocial experience simultaneously is important for understanding social functional outcomes in clinical populations.

articles_hidden.title: In need of adaptation:  The intersecting role of adaptive capacity and demands during the Menopausal Transition on psycho-cognitive wellbeing.
articles_hidden.authors: Laetitia Bruno; Guillaume T. Vallet; Annie Duchesne
articles_hidden.abstract: The menopause transition involves physiological changes that may intersect with changes in identity, social roles, and relationships, as well as pressures related to ageism and sexism. These interacting demands provide a basis for considering cognitive and emotional experiences through the relationship between adaptive demands and available resources. We propose adaptive capacity as an organizing framework encompassing the physiological, psychological, interpersonal, and contextual resources that individuals may mobilize or access during this transition. This framework recognizes diverse menopausal experiences and considers how accumulating or persistent demands may give rise to different adaptive needs. It also draws attention to the resources required to engage with existing treatments and health-related behaviors. We discuss two complementary candidate processes: vagal regulation, relevant to physiological regulation and recovery, and future time perspective, relevant to perceived future opportunities, motivation, and goal-directed action. Breathing-based approaches and interventions supporting future opportunities and planning may offer ways to strengthen resources alongside existing care. Longitudinal and intervention studies are needed to establish their contribution to adaptation during the menopause transition. This framework supports integrated, person-centered, and empowerment-oriented care that combines individualized support with attention to the social and structural conditions shaping access to adaptive resources.

articles_hidden.title: From Named Voice to Measured Sound: A Recording-to-Representation Pipeline and a Leakage-Safe Protocol for Repeated-Stimulus Designs
articles_hidden.authors: Logan Barrett
articles_hidden.abstract: People routinely name a singer they would ideally sound like. Turning that named exemplar into a measurable acoustic target, and asking whether a person’s verbal concept of a gendered voice predicts the sound they select, requires a reproducible bridge from catalog metadata to validated vocal acoustics and an evaluation protocol that cannot be satisfied by memorizing which artists appear in training. I describe both. A recording-to-representation pipeline (exemplar resolution, preview retrieval, vocal-stem isolation, eGeMAPS and singing-specific feature extraction, and artist-mean aggregation with reliability filtering) yielded acoustic profiles for 113 artists from 1,690 tracks, linked to 1,546 of 2,536 participants. In a discovery, confirmation, and hold-out design specified in a dated analysis plan, the desired direction of vocal change predicted the acoustic gender profile of the chosen singer, but its generalization to artists never seen in training did not meet the plan-specified criterion once a leakage step was corrected (retention 67.2%, 95% CI [.23, .88]), whereas participants’ specific verbal descriptions added no acoustic information beyond gender category and popularity (a bounded null). A contrastive two-tower model, retrained under a corrected protocol, also recovered no structure beyond that category. I provide the protocol in reusable form: blocking by the repeating stimulus, a retention ratio that diagnoses memorization, a chance-corrected retrieval metric, a leakage audit, and a runnable worked example.

articles_hidden.title: Does collective identification with moral convictions explain intolerance? Not just “us” versus “them”
articles_hidden.authors: Pierce D. Ekstrom; Lindsay Novak
articles_hidden.abstract: Although people often tolerate disagreement in attitude domains that concern matters of personal taste or social convention, they are much less tolerant of disagreement about moral convictions—attitudes that they construe as matters of right and wrong. The current studies test a novel theory that this ostensibly unique intolerance for moral disagreement is simply a special case of identity-based prejudice. This theory holds that moral convictions are identity-central components of the collective self, and that intolerance for moral disagreement can be explained by a tendency to use moral convictions to distinguish a moral “us” from an immoral “them.” Consistent with this theory, we found that moral conviction was associated with both self-report and reaction-time measures of identity centrality with remarkable consistency, suggesting that relatively moralized attitudes are almost always at least relatively central to the self-concept. We also found (using a recall-based task of social categorization) that participants were more likely to use their moral convictions to categorize others to the extent that participants identified with those convictions. Inconsistent with our theory, however, we found that political and social intolerance for moral disagreement were unrelated to social categorization processes; moreover, participants’ collective identification with the group of people who shared their moral convictions accounted for little if any of the link between attitude-level moral conviction and intolerance for dissimilar others. We conclude that although moral convictions are very often central to identity and invoke collectives of like-minded others, moral disagreement is not just a matter of “us” versus “them.”

articles_hidden.title: Toward process-level decoding of cognition with cross-domain transfer
articles_hidden.authors: Soroush Mirjalili; Dobromir Rahnev; Audrey Duarte
articles_hidden.abstract: Higher-order cognition emerges from the interaction of multiple cognitive processes (e.g., perception, attention, inhibition). Yet, these processes remain difficult to measure during ongoing task performance. Traditionally, researchers have studied each cognitive domain in isolation. In contrast, emerging studies have used multiple-task designs from multiple cognitive domains to better understand the relationship between different cognitive processes. These studies, spanning across humans, non-human animals, and artificial neural networks, suggest that cognition is compositional — built from abstract neural representations that generalize across tasks to support flexible behavior. These findings suggest that, with appropriate experimental design, neural signatures associated with a specific cognitive process can be decoded in one task and tested for transfer to another.  We term this approach ‘cross-domain transfer.’ Here, we explore the possibility that cognition's compositional architecture, instantiated through abstract neural representations, provides a basis for understanding how reusable cognitive processes can flexibly combine across tasks and contexts. We place cross-domain transfer within the broader evolution of cognitive decoding methods, discuss its theoretical foundations, and synthesize emerging evidence across cognitive domains. Through systematic task selection and validation, this framework provides a way to test competing theories of cognition and develop more interpretable, process-level approaches to measuring and predicting behavior.

articles_hidden.title: Stress and Work Performance among Doctors in Clinical Settings: A Cross-Sectional Study
articles_hidden.authors: Tuba Kalam
articles_hidden.abstract:
The present study examined the relationship between perceived stress and work performance among doctors working in clinical settings across India, including government hospitals, private hospitals, and clinics. Doctors frequently operate under demanding conditions involving heavy workloads, long working hours, emotional pressure, and continuous responsibility for patient care, which may affect psychological well-being and professional functioning. A quantitative correlational research design was employed with a sample of 50 doctors selected through convenience sampling. Data were collected using offline and online methods and assessed using the Perceived Stress Scale (PSS-10) and an adapted version of the Individual Work Performance Questionnaire (IWPQ). Descriptive statistics and Pearson’s product-moment correlation were used for data analysis. Most participants reported moderate levels of perceived stress and moderate-to-high levels of work performance. Pearson’s correlation revealed a statistically significant negative relationship between perceived stress and work performance (r = -0.599, p < 0.01), indicating that higher perceived stress was associated with lower work performance in the present sample. These findings highlight the importance of addressing occupational stress and promoting physician well-being through supportive workplace practices and appropriate stress-management interventions.
Keywords: Perceived Stress, Work Performance, Doctors, Occupational Stress, Clinical Settings

articles_hidden.title: When Humor Lands or Flops: Exploring Positive and Negative Aspects of Dad Joke Experiences
articles_hidden.authors: Paul Joseph Silvia; Vi Bui
articles_hidden.abstract: What do people experience when they encounter jokes? Feelings of comic amusement—finding something funny—are the heart of effective humor, but emotional reactions to humor can be complex, as studies of sexual, disparaging, dark, and cringe humor have found. The present research explored a range of experiences to dad jokes, a joke genre marked by clean, affable content and comedic devices founded on wordplay, particularly puns and literalism. A sample of adults (n = 541) read 24 jokes from a large pool and rated each one on several dimensions (funny, interesting, irritating, boring, and confusing). Individual differences in these joke experiences formed two factors related to appeal and aversion, and stable lasso models found that people who found the jokes more appealing were distinguished by demographic features (having children and being more educated, religious, and subjectively affluent), humor self-concepts (identifying as a funny person and having a background in humor), and personality traits (being higher in agreeableness and lower in openness to experience). No stable predictors were found for joke aversiveness. The findings support the 3-WD model of humor, which proposes funniness and aversiveness as general dimensions of humor experience, and illustrate the value of studying specific joke genres instead of an abstract category of verbal humor.

articles_hidden.title: Exploring Equivalence Testing with the Updated TOSTER R Package
articles_hidden.authors: Aaron R Caldwell
articles_hidden.abstract: Despite decades of methodological guidance, researchers continue to misinterpret non-significant results as evidence for the absence of an effect. Equivalence testing via two one-sided tests (TOST) provides a principled alternative, but adoption remains limited by software accessibility and lack of training. The TOSTER R package, originally developed by Lakens (2017), made TOST accessible to experimental psychologists. This paper describes a major update to the package that expands its scope with (1) a unified t-test interface supporting both equivalence and minimal effect testing, (2) a simplified hypothesis testing interface returning standard R objects, (3) tools for computing and testing standardized effect sizes and correlations, (4) robust and resampling-based alternatives including bootstrap and permutation tests, (5) equivalence testing for ANOVAs, and (6) power analysis and sample size planning. Each capability is demonstrated with worked examples. TOSTER is also available as a jamovi module for researchers who prefer a graphical interface.

articles_hidden.title: The Semantic Shift in Autobiographical Memory and Aging: Do Retrieval Goals Contribute to Age-Related Memory Differences?
articles_hidden.authors: Daniel Eric Cohen; Vannia Alexandra Puig Rivera; Jessica R. Andrews-Hanna; Matthew D. Grilli
articles_hidden.abstract: Relative to young adults, cognitively healthy older adults typically include more semantic details when narrating remembered, personal events. This age difference in autobiographical memory is mostly interpreted in the literature as a sign of cognitive and brain decline, and the consequences are largely assumed to be negative. Complementing decline-based accounts, the current perspective builds on a recent proposal that developmental changes in memory-guiding motives may help shape how and why older adults reflect on their personal past (Grilli & Sheldon, 2022). We identify theoretical support and accumulating empirical evidence suggesting that young and older adults may pursue distinct goals when retrieving autobiographical memories. A closer examination of these goals raises the possibility that young adults’ goals may be especially well served by episodically specific memories, whereas older adults’ goals may be better aligned with semantic autobiographical knowledge. Although experimentally causal evidence remains limited and an important direction for future research, the reviewed literature identifies age-related changes in retrieval goals as a plausible contributor to the semantic shift and yields testable predictions for distinguishing this account from decline-based explanations.

articles_hidden.title: The Hierarchical Structure of Antagonism as a Predictor of Suicidal Thoughts and Behaviors
articles_hidden.authors: Timothy Allen; Michelle M. Berry; Shreya Sheth; Aliona Tsypes; Alexandre Dombrovski
articles_hidden.abstract:
Antagonism is a transdiagnostic dimension of psychopathology associated with interpersonal dysfunction, a central feature of theories of suicide risk. However, little work has evaluated how antagonism or its lower-order components relate to suicidal thoughts and behaviors (STB). We examined the hierarchical structure and external validity of antagonism in 496 adults enrolled in a longitudinal study enriched for personality pathology and suicide risk. Hierarchical factor analysis recovered five lower-order facets—dishonesty, grandiosity, callousness, aggression, and hostile distrust—closely replicating prior structural work. We tested associations of higher-order antagonism and these facets with lifetime and prospective suicide attempts, attempt lethality, and prospective suicidal ideation. Higher-order antagonism was associated with lifetime attempt history but no other outcomes. At the facet level, hostile distrust was associated with lifetime attempt history and greater likelihood and severity of prospective ideation; dishonesty predicted greater attempt lethality, whereas
callousness predicted lower lethality. Contrary to expectations, aggression was associated with lower lifetime and prospective attempt risk. Controlling for neuroticism attenuated several associations, including those of higher-order antagonism and hostile distrust with lifetime attempt history. These findings support a reproducible lower-order structure of antagonism and demonstrate that associations between the antagonism
domain and STB are modest, and in some cases, reflective of shared variance with negative emotionality.

articles_hidden.title: Macrostructural Determinants and Social Oppression Forces in Latin American Youth Alcoholism: A Three-Level Model Third-Order Secondary Analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Carlos Fernando Pantoja-Muñoz
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objective: to execute a meta-synthesis grounded in third-order interpretations to critically deconstruct the distal determinants and social oppression forces driving problematic youth alcohol consumption in Latin America. This study analyzes a curated documentary corpus of 18 studies encompassing 21 countries indexed between 2015 and 2020, aiming to transcend dominant individualistic and Eurocentric reductionism in contemporary literature.
Methods: a critical secondary analysis was developed using a third-order interpretive framework. The secondary corpus was derived from a prior systematic review conducted under the PRISMA statement. From an initial screening of n = 16,921 records (Google Scholar, Redalyc, SciELO), a strict analytical sample of 18 empirical investigations was selected (aggregate sample of N = 5,253 adolescents). Qualitative data were processed using structured thematic content analysis and axial coding within a personal, familial, and macrostructural relational model.
Result: epistemological re-analysis identified five latent macrostructural dimensions operating asymmetrically across geographical regions: (1) socioeconomic inequality, (2) traditional consumption norms, (3) public health infrastructure deficiencies, (4) localized historical traumas, and (5) systemic violence. Furthermore, findings demonstrate that conventional scientific literature systematically omits these macrostructural determinants within direct empirical research designs.
Conclusions: the findings elucidate a mechanism of social determination wherein economic macrostructures exert top-down oppressive violence, severely constraining micro-familial systems. These forces generate unsustainable pressure driving alcohol consumption and subsequent molecular damage as an adaptive somatic response that modulates gene expression in reaction to biopolitical traps. For social health research, these outcomes underscore the urgent need for an epistemic paradigm shift toward public policies targeting structural environmental interventions.

Keywords: biopolitics, youth alcoholism, third-order secondary analysis, social determinants of health, macrostructural approach, epistemic violence.

articles_hidden.title: Non-commitment in mental imagery is distinct from perceptual inattention, and supports hierarchical scene construction
articles_hidden.authors: Yichen Li; Veronika Hammond; Tomer David Ullman
articles_hidden.abstract: When calling an image before the mind's eye, people often do not include basic properties of the mental scene. For example, when imagining a person knocking a ball off a table, people may neglect to consider the color of the ball. This "non-commitment" in imagery has been part of ongoing debates on the nature of mental imagery in philosophy and cognitive science, but the central question of its origin remains open. It is possible that this lack of detail in the imagination reflects actual non-commitment, as one constructs a hierarchical mental scene. But it is also possible that people do form highly detailed mental images, but fail to notice, encode, or recall properties of the image, for the same reasons that they do not notice, encode, or recall details of real scenes in direct perception. We tested these contrasting hypotheses across three experiments (N=3,895 total). First, we compared non-commitment patterns in mental imagery with the details that participants failed to notice in briefly presented real images. We found no correlation between properties that were non-committed to in the imagination, and those missed under rapid perception, indicating that non-commitment does not simply arise from perceptual noise. Next, we examined the temporal unfolding of mental imagery, and found consistent evidence of a hierarchical pattern: core entities and spatial relations, then physical properties, then surface details like color and texture. Attempts to interrupt or constrain scene construction did not change the hierarchical ordering. We suggest the results support a hierarchical partial-scene construction account of mental imagery.

articles_hidden.title: A Transcultural, Digital, and Global Perspective: Beyond Family Risk Environments in Adolescent Alcohol Use Disorders
articles_hidden.authors: Carlos Fernando Pantoja-Muñoz
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background and Aims: high-resource Western models restrict adolescent alcohol use disorders (AUD) to static micro-environmental or behavioral variables. This study aims to refute conventional linear predictive frameworks and validate the Global Multidimensional Paradigm against contemporary restrictive models.
Design and Setting: A systematic methodology based on the PRISMA statement was employed to contrast transnational linear parameters against structural evidence derived from an epidemiological screening across 21 Latin American countries.
Participants and Measurements: a pre-pandemic (2015–2020) screening of 16,921 epidemiological records was conducted, extracting data from 18 included studies to consolidate a total aggregated sample of 5,253 adolescents. Transnational profiles from the World Bank and WHO (cellular toxicity, acute intoxication, and immunosuppression) were analyzed alongside macro-structural variables.
Findings: comparative analysis demonstrates that traditional Anglo-Saxon models fail by omitting global macro-structural forces highlighted by the Lancet Commission. The proposed paradigm reveals that alcohol use disorders are determined by a three-dimensional interaction intersecting the micro-family environment with 21st-century digital dynamics (algorithmic marketing on TikTok and Instagram, e-commerce, and systemic violence), validating Krieger’s eco-social theory of embodiment (2024).
Conclusions: by displacing linear biomedical approaches, this study establishes that adolescent alcohol use disorders constitute the literal biological embodiment of macro-structural inequalities, offering an indispensable new conceptual standard for international epidemiology. 

Keywords: adolescence, alcohol use disorders, multidimensional model, biological embodiment, digital networks.

articles_hidden.title: A modality-general bias towards meaning, not enhanced prior knowledge, is linked to hallucination-proneness in the general population
articles_hidden.authors: Freya Hammers; Xiaoran Wu; Ben Alderson-Day; Chelsi Clarke; Eamon Blake; Samuel Evans
articles_hidden.abstract: Predictive processing theories propose that hallucinations arise from excessive influence of prior expectations on perception. Although these theories implicitly generalise across modalities, previous findings suggest potentially different mechanisms in vision and audition. In this study, we tested predictive processing accounts in the visual and auditory modalities in 177 healthy adults using well-matched prior knowledge tasks. Participants discriminated degraded meaningful targets from control stimuli before and after exposure to clear template stimuli, providing explicit prior knowledge. Signal detection analyses quantified pre-exposure response bias (criterion, C) and improvements in discrimination sensitivity (d′) following exposure. Hallucination-proneness was measured using the Cardiff Anomalous Perceptions Scale (CAPS). Prior knowledge improved discrimination equally across modalities, but individual differences in this benefit were unrelated to hallucination-proneness, with Bayesian analyses supporting the null hypothesis. Instead, hallucination-proneness was associated with a more liberal pre-exposure response bias in both modalities. When entered together in regression models, response bias was a stronger predictor of hallucination-proneness than prior knowledge benefit in both modalities. These findings suggest that hallucination-proneness is characterised by a modality-general bias towards meaningful interpretations of ambiguous sensory input, rather than enhanced directed use of prior knowledge.

articles_hidden.title: Event segmentation aligns emotional learning and episodic memory
articles_hidden.authors: Patrick Laing; Josh Cisler; Joseph E. Dunsmoor
articles_hidden.abstract: Emotion prioritizes not only what was significant, but when it was significant. When temporal structure is insufficient to bind emotional relevance to distinct episodes, emotional experiences can lead to overgeneralization and source confusion. Here, we tested whether event boundaries serve as a control mechanism that allows emotional prioritization in memory to reset and re-bind as relevance changes over time. Participants completed a preregistered two-day Pavlovian category-conditioning in which category-shock associations reversed across multiple learning phases. In one group, each reversal phase was preceded by a brief but explicit event boundary signaling an associative transition; in the other group, reversals occurred continuously without an explicit boundary. Episodic recognition memory for trial-unique conditioned stimuli, tested 24-hours later, showed selective enhancement for threat-predictive items in the segmentation group—most prominently during early and final learning epochs—whereas continuous encoding produced flatter, less selective memory profiles that failed to fully track changing emotional contingencies. Individual differences in learning dynamics during encoding predicted selective episodic memory at 24hrs, with event segmentation shifting this learning-memory coupling to the most recent threat reversal rather than the earliest one. Overall, event boundaries promoted tighter alignment between episodic memory and emotional relevance at the time of experience. These findings suggest that event segmentation supports adaptive memory prioritization by binding emotional significance to what is most relevant in the moment.

articles_hidden.title: Estimand or estimator? Comparing vowel overlap measures against a known ground truth
articles_hidden.authors: Grant M Berry
articles_hidden.abstract: Deciding how much two vowel categories overlap is a core problem in laboratory phonology and sociophonetics, and the field has proposed several metrics to quantify overlap: the Pillai trace, Bhattacharyya distance, and Euclidean distance, among others. Researchers rarely compute multiple metrics on the same data, and what look like distinct overlap definitions are sometimes different estimates of the same quantity. I introduce Phontrast, an open-source R toolkit that computes multiple overlap metrics on the same tokens, and I simulate distributions with known overlap to disentangle each measure's estimator from its estimand. Two public vowel corpora show how measures behave on real data, in F1 × F2 space and thirteen-dimensional MFCC space. Mean- or Gaussian-based measures are precise but unresponsive to separation in higher moments. Kernel estimates are biased and bandwidth-dependent, but within the simulation's operating region they recover the ordering on average, whatever the mechanism. Pillai is the most precise for small samples and whenever separation is driven by means. Since this is rarely known a priori, I foreground Jensen–Shannon distance, a distribution-free distance between the two vowels' probability distributions that registers separation however it arises, for ordering speakers and contrasts—with Pillai beside it to show movement in category means.

articles_hidden.title: Unconscious Archetypal Selection Bias in Professional Ice Hockey: A Multivariate Positional Analysis of Astrological Ephemeris Data and the Relative Age Effect
articles_hidden.authors: David R. Juillet; Jorge M. Rodrigues; Joanne V. Longtin
articles_hidden.abstract: This study investigates whether unconscious scouting bias exists in National Hockey League (NHL) talent acquisition, driven by psychological and behavioral archetypes. Analyzing a dataset of 777 players across all 32 NHL rosters, the research quantifies standard physical maturity biases, such as the Relative Age Effect (RAE), against independent lunar variables (Sign, Element, Modality) mapped to emotional typologies. Utilizing exact binomial tests, Cohen’s h effect sizes, and Savage-Dickey Bayes Factors (B10), 4,864 distinct positional configurations were evaluated. Results indicate no archetypal solar advantage capable of overcoming the RAE physical penalty. However, when evaluating independent lunar placements across specific positional subgroups (e.g., Centers, Left Wings, Right Wings, Defensemen), extreme localized scouting biases emerge. Front offices consistently filter players through highly distinct, positional psychological profiles, with 13 franchises exhibiting three or more concurrent statistical anomalies, indicating that human evaluation networks unconsciously draft for specific behavioral mechanics.

articles_hidden.title: Domain-Specific or Domain-General? An Examination of Patterns of Mathematics Performance Across Achievement Groups
articles_hidden.authors: Hillary Mastarciyan; Michael Slipenkyj; Lien Peters; Alyssa Counsell; H Moriah Sokolowski
articles_hidden.abstract: Many children experience persistent difficulties in mathematics throughout elementary school. However, relatively little is known about whether patterns of mathematical performance differ in children whose low achievement is specific to mathematics compared to those whose low achievement extends across academic domains and to typically achieving children. Curriculum-based educational assessments, which evaluate multiple aspects of mathematics achievement, provide a unique opportunity to compare patterns of performance across mathematics domains in population-based samples. The present study examined whether children with low mathematics achievement, low general achievement and typical achievement exhibit distinct patterns of performance across five mathematics curriculum strands in Grades 3 and 6. Data were drawn from three cohorts of children who completed a province-wide math assessment in Canada, yielding a population-based sample of 2,968 elementary school students who were identified as belonging to one of three achievement groups. Analyses compared patterns of strand-level mathematics performance across the three achievement groups in Grades 3 and 6. Children with low math and low general achievement demonstrated strikingly similar patterns of performance across strands, which differed from those of typically achieving children. These findings provide new evidence that children with low mathematics achievement and low general achievement share similar patterns of curriculum-based mathematics performance, informing theories of domain-specific and domain-general academic achievement.

articles_hidden.title: The samplr package: A tool for modeling human cognition with sampling algorithms
articles_hidden.authors: Lucas Castillo; Yun-Xiao Li; Adam N Sanborn
articles_hidden.abstract:
Many models of cognition have sampling as a central component. These have been used to explain human performance across a wide range of tasks, involving perception, probability reasoning, and choice. 
One family of these models takes inspiration from sampling approaches developed in statistics, either by adjusting samples with prior beliefs or by implementing a sampling algorithm that overcomes the difficulty of independent samples at the expense of autocorrelation. 
While these models have been successful in modeling human behavior, their adoption has been slowed by the technical difficulties in applying them. 
Here, we introduce the samplr package, which includes a variety of these algorithms and cognitive models built upon them. We show how models in this package can match qualitative patterns found in human data, and walk readers through an example of how to compare these models quantitatively to human data. This tool aims to make these methods accessible to many more researchers.

articles_hidden.title: Engaging residents in district heating retrofit:  A qualitative evaluation of a mine water heat network project in the United Kingdom
articles_hidden.authors: Michael A. Smith; Faye Doughty; Danielle Goldring; Helen Simmons
articles_hidden.abstract: The expansion of district heat networks (DHNs) is central to achieving net zero heating targets, yet social acceptance remains a major barrier to large-scale domestic retrofit. Although resident engagement is widely recognised as critical to addressing these barriers, there is little empirical evidence evaluating how engagement strategies operate during live retrofit projects. This study addresses this gap through a qualitative evaluation of the resident support and engagement approach employed during the connection of 16 existing low-rise homes to a mine water DHN in the United Kingdom. Data were collected from 18 stakeholders, including residents, local authority officers and construction contractors. The findings demonstrate that effective engagement extends beyond the provision of information. Social acceptance was strengthened through opportunities to build trusting relationships, meaningful resident involvement in decision-making, early engagement, and adaptations that responded to residents' accessibility needs. Participants also highlighted the importance of organisational coordination, accessible communication materials, clear points of contact, and the use of trusted community networks and lived experience to enhance the credibility of project information. These findings suggest that successful DHN retrofit depends not only on technical delivery but also on engagement processes that foster trust, agency and equitable participation. The present study provides the first qualitative evaluation of resident engagement during a live mine water DHN retrofit project and offers practical recommendations for engaging residents during the design and delivery of future DHN projects.

articles_hidden.title: Testing Alternative Approaches to Manipulation of Environmental Self-Identity: Behavior Recall, Anchoring, and Category-Range Manipulations
articles_hidden.authors: Jan Urban; Štěpán Bahník; Markéta Braun Kohlová
articles_hidden.abstract: Environmental self-identity, defined as the extent to which an individual sees themselves as an environmentally friendly person, has become an important concept in environmental psychology. One of the reasons for the prominence of environmental self-identity is that it has been proposed as one of the causal factors of pro-environmental behavior. Experimental studies of environmental self-identity have relied on a recall manipulation that alters the frequency scales on which people report their past pro- and anti-environmental behaviors, thus making past pro- or anti-environmental behaviors more salient. In the current study, we tested two additional alternative approaches to experimental manipulation of environmental self-identity. These rely on two powerful strategies of changing the perception of one’s past behavior, namely anchoring manipulation and category-range manipulation. We conducted a high-power web-based study (N = 4,139) to assess and compare the efficacy of the behavioral-recall manipulation and the two alternative approaches of manipulating environmental self-identity and affecting pro-environmental intention. We found substantial evidence that the three manipulations altered people's self-reports of their past pro-environmental behavior, but this did not change environmental self-identity. Evidence also favored no effect on environmental intention for the recall and anchoring manipulations, whereas evidence for the category-range manipulation was inconclusive. Other manipulations of environmental self-identity that do not rely on self-perception theory are needed for experimental research on environmental self-identity. Practical interventions are unlikely to influence pro-environmental behavior merely by highlighting or changing people's records of their past behavior.

articles_hidden.title: Dissociable neural oscillations track subjective value under risk and ambiguity
articles_hidden.authors: Shuting Mei; Leyou Deng; Gökhan Aydogan; Christian Carl Ruff; Ya Zheng
articles_hidden.abstract: How the brain values uncertain prospects and translates them into choices is a central question in decision neuroscience. Current accounts propose that decisions under risk and ambiguity share a valuation process that integrates outcome with probability information, with ambiguity additionally requiring evaluation of the uncertainty about the probabilities themselves. Here we used computational modeling to estimate trial-wise subjective value and tested whether it was tracked by shared or distinct neural dynamics under risk and ambiguity. Participants accepted or rejected risky and ambiguous monetary gambles while we recorded neural activity using electroencephalography (Experiment 1) and magnetoencephalography (Experiment 2). Across both experiments, alpha-band (9–14 Hz) activity localized to the precuneus and superior parietal cortex tracked subjective value under both risk and ambiguity. By contrast, delta-band (1–3 Hz) activity localized to the ventromedial prefrontal and anterior cingulate cortices tracked subjective value only under ambiguity. These findings reveal dissociable neural signatures for the two forms of uncertainty and suggest that the brain resolves ambiguity by combining a shared valuation process indexed by alpha activity with an additional process indexed by delta activity that may reflect the motivational salience of options with ambiguous outcome probabilities.

articles_hidden.title: ‘The difference between us is that I am an optimist and you are a pessimist.’ An autoethnographic study on suppression of critical scholarship
articles_hidden.authors: P. Matthijs Bal; Mehmet A. Orhan; Yvonne van Rossenberg
articles_hidden.abstract: Critical scholarship constitutes an important part of business and management research, including related fields such as work psychology. However, critical work is also often met with resistance from colleagues and gatekeepers within the discipline. Yet, there is little insight into how this resistance manifests in daily academic practice. This autoethnographic study by multiple critical scholars in work and organizational psychology analyzed 34 events whereby their critical work was suppressed and silenced. Thematic analysis of the events revealed ten different mechanisms through which critical work is suppressed, which could be ordered within four sequential stages of suppression: closing space, discrediting work, discrediting research(-ers), and disciplinary control. Jointly, these stages represent an escalating process of how alternative perspectives, including critical work, are suppressed and silenced in hegemonic fields. The paper contributes to existing critical scholarship by being the first to empirically elucidate how and through which strategies critical work is silenced. The study has important implications not only for the development of critical perspectives within scientific fields, but also for academia more widely, as political and societal forces that undermine academic freedom call for a better understanding of how critical work is suppressed, and how it could be nurtured for a more dignified, equal, and democratic society.

articles_hidden.title: Charting the ontogeny of mnemonic processes in childhood: the COMIC dataset
articles_hidden.authors: Tydings McClary; Elisa Buchberger; Ann-Kathrin Joechner; Ulman Lindenberger; Chi T. Ngo; Markus Werkle-Bergner
articles_hidden.abstract: The human memory system balances two complementary functions: generalization, which involves extracting regularities across experiences, and specificity, which involves retaining the unique details of individual events. Understanding how this balance develops can benefit from a neurocomputational perspective in which three core computations, pattern categorization, pattern separation, and pattern completion, differentially support generalization and memory specificity. Guided by this framework, we present a dataset from 180 children aged 4–8 years who completed four age-appropriate memory tasks that provide behavioral indices of these computations. Children additionally completed three standardized intelligence subtests. Alongside the dataset, we describe a semi-automated data-cleaning pipeline designed for developmental behavioral data, which can serve as a template for identifying and resolving common data-quality issues in studies with young children. In sum, this dataset provides a resource for investigating the development of memory computations supporting adaptive functioning across early and middle childhood.

articles_hidden.title: Affect and Words: An Instrument for the Quantitative Analysis of Emotional Vocabulary in Open-ended Responses.
articles_hidden.authors: Nigel Manchini; Óliver Jiménez; Natalia Sylvia Ramos Díaz; Daniel Trias
articles_hidden.abstract: In a context where emotions play a central role in discussions on psychology and education, the availability of various techniques and resources to assess emotional experience becomes essential. Quantitative language analysis provides a window to emotional experiences, rarely used in Spanish-speaking contexts. This study develops and cross-culturally validates an annotated dictionary of explicit emotional vocabulary, a tool for analyzing affective variables from texts and open-ended responses. A systematic protocol and expert judgment were used to select and annotate 1,041 lexical families (3,051 lemmas and 18,934 words), and pre-recorded hypotheses about the validity of the instrument were tested. Participants, adolescents from Uruguay (n = 1,208, 59% female, age M = 14.4) and Spain (n = 596, 41% female, age M = 15.7), completed Subjective Well-Being (SWB) scales and wrote about their emotional experiences in an open-ended response. The dictionary showed convergence with other instruments and acceptable inter-rater reliability. When applied to open-ended responses, it captured a substantial proportion of the words written by participants and showed significant correlations with SWB in both the Uruguayan and Spanish samples. These results suggest that quantitative analysis of open-ended responses allows the exploration of well-being, and that this freely available instrument is a valid resource for doing so, serving as a complement to quantitative and qualitative approaches for research or intervention purposes.

articles_hidden.title: Labvanced Eye Tracking 2.0: validation of webcam eye tracking with 494 unsupervised online participants
articles_hidden.authors: Caspar Goeke
articles_hidden.abstract: Webcam eye tracking has already become a powerful tool for online behavioral research, and the first generation of Labvanced's system was validated against an EyeLink 1000 in the laboratory at an accuracy of about 1.4° of visual angle (Kaduk et al., 2023). Several questions remained open. How much of that accuracy survives the uncontrolled conditions of a real online study? Why do some participants deliver far worse data than others, and can they be identified before a researcher pays for them? Can the calibration be shortened to make it more practical in ordinary online studies? And what should happen to participants who do not pass it, or otherwise do not qualify? Here we show how we improved eye-tracking accuracy, while simultaneously shortening the calibration, simplifying the setup, and optimizing the whole procedure for real online data collection with our partner Prolific. We then validated the system in seven recording batches with about 500 completed participants of a 45-target accuracy task, and publish their anonymized data so that every result can be verified. With our new standard calibration (about 2 minutes) and balanced screening, the median participant's error was 5.2 % of the screen diagonal, 1.8° of visual angle on a laptop at 60 cm. And with the 5 minute calibration and very strict screening, the median accuracy of online participants reached 4 % of the screen diagonal, which is equal to 1.4° of visual angle at a standard distance. In summary, with this release of Eye Tracking 2.0, we show that the accuracy reported in our peer-reviewed laboratory comparison can be replicated online

articles_hidden.title: From Mortality Salience to Existential Reflection: A Four-Level Model of Reflecting Upon Personal, Human, Biotic, and Cosmic Finitude
articles_hidden.authors: JianHui Zhang; Yixin He; Michel Ferrari; Chao S. Hu
articles_hidden.abstract: Death-related thought can shape emotional responses, meaning-making, health decisions, and social responses to loss. Mortality-salience research has made death-related cognition experimentally testable. Yet a mortality-salience induction does not establish that a person has reflected on death in a sustained or personally consequential way. We propose a Four-Level Model of Existential Reflection. The model distinguishes reflecting upon personal finitude, shared human finitude, the finitude of living beings, and cosmic finitude. These levels identify different objects of thought, not a universal developmental sequence. People may engage with one or more levels in different orders. Culture, spirituality, scientific worldviews, relationships, and life circumstances shape the felt significance of these forms of reflection. The model generates hypotheses about long-term-perspective activities, death-thought accessibility (DTA), movement among levels, and their psychological consequences. It links laboratory mortality-salience research with lived experiences of death, care, meaning, and growth.

articles_hidden.title: Understanding age-related changes in choice stepping responses using the diffusion decision model
articles_hidden.authors: Sarah Anne Kemp; Niek Stevenson; Marlee Jay Wells; Rebecca Healey; Daina L Sturnieks; Stephen R Lord; Mark R. Hinder; Andrew Heathcote; Rebecca Jane St George
articles_hidden.abstract: Stepping responses slow markedly with age, posing a significant risk for falls, yet the cognitive and motor mechanisms driving this slowing remain poorly understood. The diffusion decision model (DDM), which jointly accounts for response times and accuracy, has been used to disentangle the cognitive, sensorimotor and strategic contributors to age-related slowing in upper-limb tasks. We extended this approach to a choice reaction time task with three response conditions: finger (button press), foot (seated foot tap), and step (forward step initiation from quiet standing) to determine if the reasons for age-related slowing differ across upper- and lower-limb responses and stepping responses involving the additional complexity of postural control. Healthy older adults (n = 54) responded more slowly than younger adults (n = 28) across all response conditions. DDM analysis indicated that older adults showed slower evidence accumulation rates and longer non-decision times than younger adults, reflecting less efficient information processing and slower motor execution, respectively. Younger adults also required more evidence than older adults to trigger a decision during stepping, but not in the finger or foot responses. Together, these findings indicate that age-related slowing of choice stepping is driven primarily by reduced information-processing efficiency and prolonged non-decision processes, rather than by increased response caution during action selection. More broadly, these findings demonstrate that cognitive modelling can be extended beyond traditional upper-limb tasks and applied to postural decision making in older adults to characterise the mechanisms contributing to slowed stepping, offering a foundation for targeted therapeutic interventions.

articles_hidden.title: Induced sad mood biases responses to sad and neutral faces under low visibility: behavioral and ERP evidence
articles_hidden.authors: Xueqiao Li; Elisa Vuoriainen; Elina Kangas; Piia Astikainen
articles_hidden.abstract: Facial expression recognition is shaped by both stimulus properties and the perceiver’s affective state. Research on emotional face processing under backward masking has largely focused on threatening expressions, and few studies have examined how an observer's mood influences recognition of non-threatening facial expressions under limited visibility. The present study investigated how experimentally induced sad versus neutral mood modulates behavioral and neural responses to sad and neutral facial expressions under low (10 ms) and high visibility (200 ms) backward masking conditions. Participants underwent sad and neutral mood induction on separate days and performed a facial expression categorization task while electroencephalography was recorded. Behavioral and event-related potential (ERP) analyses included 25 and 20 participants, respectively. Behaviorally, a mood effect on response criterion was observed in the low visibility condition: the criterion was lower in sad than neutral mood, reflecting a reduced tendency to categorize faces as neutral. Discrimination sensitivity was higher under high than low visibility but was not significantly affected by mood. Facial expressions modulated N170, P2, and P3 amplitudes under high visibility, and N170 and P2 under low visibility. P2 amplitude in the low visibility condition showed an interaction effect between mood and facial expression. In neutral mood, sad faces elicited larger P2 amplitudes than neutral faces, whereas in sad mood, the relation was the opposite. These findings highlight the influence of the observer’s affective state on behavioral and neural responses to facial expressions under limited visibility, extending previous findings beyond threat-related expressions to sadness.

articles_hidden.title: Playing at scale: a long-term population perspective on the relationship between play and innovation
articles_hidden.authors: Elena Miu; Marc; Iulia Badescu; Cedric Boeckx; Camilla Cenni; Jean Baptiste Leca; Sheina Lew-Levy; Elodie Lepauldier; Luseadra Joy McKerracher; Mathilde Vestergaard Meyer
articles_hidden.abstract: The multifaceted relationship between play and innovation has long fascinated scholars across disciplines. Yet, we lack robust empirical evidence regarding the causal pathways that may connect these two behavioural concepts. While much work has revolved around how play might drive innovation in childhood, there has been little focus on how play might contribute to transformative societal innovation. Studies investigating play and innovation have taken a short-term synchronic perspective to innovation and have focused mainly on invention (i.e. the first instance of a novel behaviour), interested in how play might increase behavioural flexibility and problem-solving skills. Although these approaches cannot speak to population-level innovation (i.e. novel information that spreads across groups), evidence from such studies is often marshalled to support claims about the role of play for societal innovation dynamics over time. Here we propose that the link between play and population innovation has not been robustly demonstrated because of 1. a lack of precise specification of the causal pathways linking the two and 2. a mismatch between the scale on which play is measured and the scale on which population-level innovation operates. We narrow in on a specific kind of play (object play), a specific life history period (childhood), and a specific kind of innovation (population-level), and introduce a causal framework highlighting long-term processes to understand the state-of-the-art knowledge landscape and to guide future work. We synthesise three mechanistic pathways linking the children’s play and population-level innovation: exploration, development, and cultural evolution. We design formal causal diagrams that link children’s play and population-level innovation via the three mechanisms we identified, and consider potential confounds relevant to each. Our explicit long-term populational perspective on the link between play and innovation sheds light on productive means to move the field forward.

articles_hidden.title: “Puzzling, Yet So Refreshing”: Experiencing the Value of Neurodiversity Within an Inclusive Choir
articles_hidden.authors: Nicolas Petit; Géraldine Dessertenne; Fanny Aprile; Lucie Jurek
articles_hidden.abstract: The social challenges encountered by autistic people are increasingly understood as a double empathy problem: a mutual misunderstanding between autistic and non-autistic individuals, rather than an autistic deficit. This paradigm highlights a need for inclusive spaces that foster mutual understanding, yet this remains challenging, especially in the French sociocultural context which is less familiar with the social model of disability developed in the anglophone world. As this model stresses that the majority largely shapes the social environment, finding ways to influence the general population’s attitudes toward autism is critical. Choral singing offers a promising medium to do so and facilitate cross-neurotype dynamics, as it is thought to have evolved as a biological mechanism to foster social bonding. Accordingly, this qualitative study explored how 12 general population choristers experienced a 6-month neurodiverse choir shared with 8 autistic adolescents and 3 autism specialists.
