Jarak yang secara fisik memisahkan pasangan tidak menjadi penghalang bagi keluarga pernikahan jarak jauh untuk membangun hubungan secara maksimal seperti keluarga lainnya.

articles_hidden.title: When do intentions predict action? The temporal dynamics of the intention–action gap
articles_hidden.authors: Peiyuan Zhang; Luisa Leonelli; Yijun Lin; Wei Ji Ma
articles_hidden.abstract: Procrastination is defined as voluntarily delaying an intended course of action, yet the gap between intention and action is rarely measured directly, and little is known about how it unfolds over time. We gave 127 adults seven days to complete 180 units of a self-paced online reading task and recorded the timestamp of every completed unit. Before the task began, 67 of them reported how many units they intended to complete on each of the seven days, so that intended and actual work were expressed in the same units on the same days. Among those who finished, work was concentrated 0.59 days later than intended, although the day people finished did not differ from the day they had planned. The gap widened through Day 4, stopped growing on Day 5, and narrowed over the final two days. Intentions predicted when people started but not when they finished, and their influence faded after the first half of the task. Trait procrastination showed the opposite pattern, predicting actual but not intended work and shaping the timing of work throughout the task, most strongly in the middle.

articles_hidden.title: Old Test, New Tricks: Using Large Language Models to Generate New Divergent Thinking Test Items
articles_hidden.authors: Averie Elizabeth Linnell; Simone A Luchini; Austin Swanson; Roni Reiter-Palmon; Roger Beaty; Antonio Laverghetta
articles_hidden.abstract: Automated item generation (AIG) using large language models (LLMs) is emerging as a promising solution for scalable creativity assessments, yet the potential of AIG to create psychometrically rigorous creativity items has thus far received little attention. In the present study, we evaluated the psychometric properties of LLM-generated items for the classic Consequences task of divergent thinking, comparing them to human-written items. A sample of 192 undergraduates completed six Consequences tasks—two human-written, two standard LLM-generated, and two genre-inspired LLM-generated, drawing on sci-fi and fantasy themes—along with measures of personality, cognitive ability, and creative behavior. We found that LLM-generated items elicited significantly higher fluency and flexibility. Genre-inspired items (fantasy and sci-fi) additionally elicited higher originality, enjoyment, and positive valence ratings; LLM-generated items were similar to human-written items. Genre-inspired items did not unfairly advantage participants with more exposure to genre content, demonstrating measurement invariance. Together, these findings suggest that LLMs can generate consequences items with psychometric properties comparable to those of human-written items. We discuss the implications for creativity assessment, item bank development, and best practices for AIG in creativity research, and we provide the prompts we used for item generation to enable researchers to generate new Consequences items at scale.

articles_hidden.title: Shared and Divergent Multisensory Emotion Perception Deficits across Mild Cognitive Impairment, Alzheimer’s Disease, and Frontotemporal Dementia: A Systematic Review and Hierarchical Bayesian Meta-Analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Yi Lin; Yangfan Lu; Enze Tang; Yang Zhang
articles_hidden.abstract: The ability to decode others’ emotions from multisensory cues is central to social functioning. However, findings remain inconsistent regarding the extent to which this capacity is compromised in neurodegenerative diseases, leaving the underlying mechanisms unclear. This study aimed to delineate the shared and divergent patterns of multisensory emotion perception (MEP) deficits among clinically distinct populations of individuals with Alzheimer’s disease (AD), frontotemporal dementia (FTD), and mild cognitive impairment (MCI). We conducted a systematic review on 51 studies identified from Web of Science, MEDLINE, PubMed, PsycINFO and PsycARTICLES to synthesize research trends in this field between 2001 and 2025. We applied a hierarchical Bayesian meta-analysis (1,511 patients and 1,151 healthy controls) to quantify the deficits and their moderators. Meta-analytic results demonstrated a differential magnitude of MEP impairment across groups (FTD > AD > MCI), reflecting distinct socio-emotional vulnerabilities rather than a single disease continuum. Moderator analyses of 15 participant- and study-related factors showed that impairment magnitude was more strongly associated with age, sex, education, global cognitive functioning, publication year, and emotion category, and less strongly with region, paradigm, language, and modality. Sensitivity analyses indicated that these patterns remained robust to potential publication bias, though the results were less stable within the FTD cohort. We propose a Hierarchical Socio-Emotional Disintegration and Compensation Framework to explain the dynamic interplay between neurodegeneration-driven deficits and compensatory mechanisms. This framework advances mechanistic insight into the relationship between emotion and cognition, informing future clinical efforts to support the interpersonal well-being of aging populations.

articles.title: Larger, younger, faster, harder: expansion, transformation, and inequality in YouTube’s creator economy (2019–2026)
articles.authors: Bernhard Rieder; Adrian Padilla; Ariadna Matamoros-Fernández; Òscar Coromina
articles.abstract: The growth of YouTube's creator economy raises a question that accounts of individual success and precarity cannot settle: how are the conditions of participation changing across the platform? Comparing two population-scale crawls from 2019 and 2026, we examine expansion, changes in production, and the distribution of attention across millions of channels. The population above the 1,000-subscriber threshold for advertising monetization grew from 4.4 million to 24.5 million, while its video catalogues grew ninefold. Expansion was strongest in South, Southeast, and East Asia, with India's share of channels declaring a country rising from 10 to 27 percent. This growth accompanied substantial turnover: most channels recorded in 2019 had no recent upload in 2026, and continued participation differed sharply by prior standing. Production also changed fundamentally. Median video duration fell from 247 to 60 seconds, with shortening across every content category and channel size. Among channels above 100,000 subscribers, new entrants accounted for most of the shift toward short form, while most continuing incumbents also shortened their output. Attention became more concentrated even among the same channels observed at both dates, and advertising revenue grew more slowly than the population meeting the subscriber threshold. These findings show how the output imperative extends from producing more to adapting what is produced, while sustained participation remains sharply unequal. They also place the increasingly Asian geography of the creator economy at the center of questions about platform labor, opportunity, and precarity.

articles.title: Beyond the Joke: A Thematic Content Analysis of Russian-Linked Meme Pages Targeting Azerbaijan
articles.authors: Gudrat Guluyev
articles.abstract: As internet memes evolved from mere entertainment into a tool of digital propaganda, their role in modern warfare has become increasingly significant. This study examines their role in the case of Russian-linked information operations targeting the Azerbaijani audience on Facebook.  While the existing literature on meme-based Russian propaganda focuses heavily on the United States and Ukraine, the South Caucasus, one of the important regions of Russia’s “near abroad” policy, remains overlooked. The research addresses this critical gap by analyzing how these strategies are adapted to Azerbaijan's specific cultural and political context. The study relies on qualitative, multimodal analysis and emergent coding of 78 memes from nine Russian-linked Facebook pages targeting Azerbaijan between January 2023 and December 2024. The analysis identifies four consistent themes (the negative othering of the West, the discrediting of Western leaders, the reframing of the Nagorno-Karabakh Conflict, and the promotion of Azerbaijani sovereignty) and various propaganda techniques that have already been revealed in existing studies. The research paper concludes that these pages conduct a systematic influence campaign that sophisticatedly blends pro-Russian narratives with culturally conservative and patriotic domestic sentiments to resonate with the local audience.

articles.title: Did local authorities lose revenue following banning unhealthy food advertising?
articles.authors: Mark Alan Green; Emma Boyland
articles.abstract: UK local authorities are increasingly exploring restrictions for the advertising of unhealthy foods on their estates to promote healthier food environments. Concerns about effects on revenue can be a barrier to progress. In this study, we provide preliminary evidence that these policies did not negatively affect total advertising revenue across four local authorities in North West England. In some cases, we found that revenue increased post-implementation.

articles.title: Conceptualizing Political Consumerism in the Attention Economy
articles.authors: Christopher Starke; Claes de Vreese; Natali Helberger
articles.abstract: Social media platforms increasingly become targets of politically and ethically motivated user protest, yet existing approaches do not sufficiently explain how deliberate platform use can operate as political participation. This conceptual paper extends the established concept of political consumerism to the attention economy, defining it as individuals’ market-oriented behaviors to punish or reward social media platforms on political or ethical grounds. It argues that three main factors constrain political consumerism on social media platforms: opaque value extraction, limited ethical alternatives, and high switching costs. Because political consumerism can take many forms, the paper suggests distinguishing user actions by their economic impact and whether they signal user preferences to the platform company. It further explains how social media literacy and regulation can improve the legibility and actionability of these practices. Finally, it outlines methodological implications for studying political consumerism through mixed-method designs that combine user motivations with behavioral data.

articles.title: Resilience in a Discordant Security Culture: Georgia between Institutional Continuity and Political Realignment
articles.authors: Mariam Bibilashvili
articles.abstract: Challenging the common understanding in the relevant literature, this study reconceptualizes resilience to hybrid threats as a politically mediated process rather than purely a matter of institutional capacity-building. To examine how policy frameworks and political rhetoric interact to shape resilience, it traces Georgia’s security culture in the aftermath of the Russo-Georgian war. Through intertextual discourse analysis, the article cross-examines the institutional architecture of digital resilience, encompassing cybersecurity (systemic), media regulation (protective) and media literacy (empowerment) measures, with the government’s shifting rhetoric (2023–2025), while interview data provide contextual insights. The analysis reveals a discordant security culture manifested in fragmented governance and discursive struggle over resilience. Although formal policy frameworks normatively align with the West and consistently identify Russia as the principal security threat, governmental rhetoric portrays the same Western actors as sources of foreign interference and prioritizes political autonomy over cooperation while still invoking commitments to the constitutionally enshrined Euro-Atlantic trajectory. This dichotomy between institutional design and political discourse results in strategic ambiguity. It suggests that in hybrid regimes formal frameworks may function symbolically to signal external alignment, while practice is determined by short-term political calculations and discretionary authority, leaving institutions and societies vulnerable to evolving forms of foreign interference.

articles.title: Speed-Quality Tradeoffs Shape the Structure of Decision-Making Collectives
articles.authors: Chanuwas Aswamenakul; Tyler Marghetis; Paul E. Smaldino
articles.abstract: Many human groups employ hierarchical decision-making, in which only a few individuals hold the power to make decisions for the collective. A common explanation for the prevalence of hierarchical decision-making is that it provides group-level benefits by speeding up the decision-making process. However, groups can often do better by taking more time to explore a problem space or generate ideas. These contrasting accounts suggest that hierarchical or egalitarian decision structures may emerge under different circumstances. To more clearly distinguish between these circumstances, we studied an evolutionary model of group decision-making that includes both intra-group and inter-group dynamics. We show that the emergent social structure depends critically on the trade-off between speed and decision quality: scenarios that demand rapid decisions favor the evolution of skewed, hierarchical structures, while scenarios that reward extended deliberation favor the evolution of flat, egalitarian structures. Our results suggest that, instead of inevitably becoming centralized and hierarchical, groups and organizations are likely to evolve social structures that reflect the relationship between the speed and the quality of decisions they collectively make.

articles.title: “AI” as gaslighting – Considering the affordances of stochastic generative systems in relation to anthropo-centered epistemic operations
articles.authors: Daniel Cardoso
articles.abstract:
This paper mobilizes the notion of ‘AI’ as a carcinogen, as developed by Berman, to then inquire and analyze what is the possible human impact that results from the democratization of the use of Large Language Models and Generative Pretrained Transformers, from the perspective of how epistemic frameworks are mobilized as a core component of sociability.
It then advances the proposal that we understand ‘AI’ as a case of the ‘Thomas Theorem’, and that, as such, LLMs and GPTs can effectively operate as systems of non-targeted, non-intentional, gaslighting.
From that approach, the paper follows up with a materially-grounded analysis of how the operations performed on data for the creation and usage of LLMs and GPTs mean that these technologies have the affordance of being episteme-fixative, and that such an affordance (as defined here) is specific to these technologies, in a way that allows for non-essentialist and non-deterministic analysis that considers both changes and continuities in both media systems and our everyday engagement with them.
It concludes by suggesting venues of inquiry that are made easier by the previous conclusions, and returns to capitalism’s uptake of technology, rather than to any immanent aspect of technology, as a central aspect to consider in evaluating the epistemic harms that might come out of these affordances.

articles.title: “Safe for now?” Boundary work and tensions of AI Adoption in Sign Language Interpreting and Speech-to-Text Reporting in Belgium and the Netherlands
articles.authors: Maartje De Meulder; Karolien Gebruers; Deborah Giustini
articles.abstract:
Abstract
This article examines how sign language interpreters (SLIs) and speech-to-text reporters (STTRs) in Belgium (Flanders) and the Netherlands understand and navigate artificial intelligence (AI)-driven language technologies in their professional lives. While speech-to-text reporting already faces displacement by automated transcription, sign language interpreting remains partly sheltered by the limited AI training data for Flemish and Dutch Sign Language. Drawing on an online survey (N = 134) conducted in 2025, and theorized through  boundary work, we identify three tensions structuring practitioners' accounts: a temporality tension, in which anticipated disruption coexists with present stability; an access tension, in which AI expands available options while enabling institutions to narrow the definition of "sufficient access"; and a professional identity tension, in which the technology threatening practitioners' livelihoods may simultaneously advance the profession's own emancipatory ideal. Respondents describe AI as a new third actor in interpreted interaction, shifting some practitioners toward editing and quality-control roles that lack institutional recognition. We argue that AI in language access is actively produced through practitioners’ ongoing boundary work and calls for recognizing them — alongside deaf consumers — as epistemic actors in governing just technological transitions.

articles.title: Associations between content and engagement vary across social media communities
articles.authors: Alberto Acerbi
articles.abstract: Research on social media engagement often seeks general content features that are associated with online success. However, social media platforms contain communities with different audiences, topics, and norms, and the same features may have different associations with engagement within different communities. This research considers 1,078,044 items from 587 communities in five corpora spanning Reddit, Stack Exchange, X, and YouTube. For each corpus, negativity, moralization, arousal, and in-group versus out-group language were measured. Their relationships with engagement were compared using multilevel models imposing one within-community slope per feature with models allowing slopes to vary across communities. Varying-slope models fit the data better in all five corpora. The estimated community slopes varied substantially in magnitude and, frequently, direction. Nevertheless, the average slopes from the varying-slope models remained small. The improved fit therefore reflects heterogeneity across communities rather than stronger average associations. These findings show that a weak average association can conceal stronger but opposing associations across communities. General claims about the content associated with social media engagement need to account for the specific communities in which that content appears.

articles.title: Attribute Relevance in Conjoint Analysis
articles.authors: Lukas Stoetzer; Asya Magazinnik
articles.abstract: Researchers often rely on conjoint analysis to understand which attributes drive respondents' decisionmaking, yet standard estimands are not designed to measure attribute relevance. We introduce a novel approach to measuring attribute relevance in conjoint analysis by drawing on causal attribution methods. Our proposed estimand, the average probability of necessary and sufficient causation (APNS), captures the probability that swapping two profiles' levels on an attribute would change a respondent's choice. We establish nonparametric identification under assumptions related to preference heterogeneity, and provide simple difference-in-means estimators that can be applied to existing conjoint data structures. Two empirical applications illustrate the method. A candidate choice experiment in Germany reveals significant preference heterogeneity that leads standard estimands to mask relevance, while under the right assumptions the APNS recovers it. By contrast, in a replication of a prominent refugee experiment, we find that assuming preference homogeneity is unproblematic for many attributes of asylum-seekers.

articles.title: An Empirical Model of Mobile App Competition: The Role of the Revenue-Source Channel
articles.authors: Kohei Kawaguchi; Susumu Sato; Toshifumi Kuroda
articles.abstract: Mobile apps can earn revenue from download fees, in-app purchases, and in-app advertising, and mixed business models coexist within a market, unlike in many familiar markets where firms rely primarily on a single price per product. Because developers choose these revenue sources jointly, a shock to one source can induce adjustments in the others, including the activation or shutdown of a source, a mechanism we call the revenue-source channel. We develop an empirical model of app competition in download prices, usage prices, and advertising intensities, in which developers endogenously determine their business models. The model admits a competition-in-utility formulation that yields a tractable equilibrium characterization and a unified measure of disutility that applies to zero-priced apps. We estimate the model using data on roleplaying apps in the Japanese Google Play market during 2015–2017 and use it to assess how horizontal mergers, changes in platform transaction fees, and changes in advertisement prices affect app developers and consumers. In a merger of a paid app and a free app, a cost synergy at the free app is not passed through to consumers, whereas a quality synergy raises consumer surplus. A lower platform transaction fee can raise the average download price when previously free apps begin charging, while consumer surplus still rises. A higher advertisement price raises advertising intensity and slightly lowers usage prices, while modestly increasing consumer surplus, app profit, and platform revenue. These results demonstrate the importance of zero-priced apps and the revenue-source channel in markets where multiple revenue sources coexist.

articles.title: An age-old advantage: Evidence for a consistent survival advantage for children of long-lived parents in Sweden 1880-2022
articles.authors: Ingrid K van Dijk; Niels van den Berg
articles.abstract: The average lifespan has increased strongly in the past decades, but not everyone has benefited equally. Establishing the degree of intergenerational persistence of survival generates insights into broad inequalities between individuals and families in their likelihood to live to high ages. Using established register-type data for two regions in Northern and Southern Sweden 1880-2022 linked to historical records, we show that even before the rise of the modern social gradient in health in the 1960ies, mortality is lower among descendants from long-lived parents (top survivors of their birth cohort). This shared survival advantage between parents and children persists over time even after considering SES. Mortality among the descendants of top survivors is lower in lifestyle-related causes of death, suggesting that behavioral factors could be a significant factor in explaining the survival advantage. Overall, we find that mortality concentrates in families in patterns that go beyond the influence of SES alone. Similarities between relatives in health and mortality therefore provide an important lens into inequalities in survival and health over time.

articles.title: Scrutiny, sanctions, and attacks on scholars: Public acceptance and perceived deservingness in Switzerland
articles.authors: Niels G. Mede; Julia Metag; Mike S. Schäfer
articles.abstract: Different forms of critical and hostile public engagement with science have been documented worldwide. They range from valuable scrutiny to public protests, support for funding cuts, and attacks. Whether people accept such engagement, and whether they consider it deserved, has rarely been studied with representative data. Using a preregistered, nationally representative survey from Switzerland (n = 698), we examine acceptance of public scrutiny, support for sanctions, and attacks on scholars and their perceived deservingness when scholars speak out politically. We find that acceptance follows a graded hierarchy: Most respondents accept scrutiny, fewer accept sanctions, and hardly anyone accepts attacks. Two thirds consider criticism of politically outspoken scholars deserved, whereas attacks are largely rejected, although noteworthy minorities consider them deserved. Acceptance of attacks is associated with science-related populist attitudes, right-leaning views, younger age, lower income, and active online engagement. Moreover, perceived political distance from scholars is associated with acceptance of scrutiny.

articles.title: Resilience through Pathway Specificity for Managing Climate Shocks. A Review of Evidence from East Africa.
articles.authors: Mohamed Abdirahman Ibrahim
articles.abstract:
The study systematically reviews and synthesizes 74 empirical studies from East Africa, covering Ethiopia, Kenya, Somalia, and Somaliland. Using study-level, asset-based thresholds and other complementary indicators, the findings identify that household resilience is non-linear and requires targeted, specific programming. The Pathway-Specific Resilience Framework (PSRF), which the paper validates, divides the target populations into two groups: a resource-deficient group that needs asset assistance and external safety nets (socially supported livelihood resilience pathway) and an asset-based cohort that prioritizes asset protection and market-based interventions. The study found that households with constrained resources face limitations in asset accumulation, which leave them more vulnerable to persistent poverty traps. PSRF proposes poverty graduation that balances immediate protection with long-term resilience through a sequence of protocols. The first “Protocol “A” protects resource-poor (Socially supported pathway) households to prioritize consumption, direct transfers (e.g., assets), and human capital. Once households transition to “Protocol B”, the shift is from survival assistance to access to market, finance, and index-based insurance. Additionally, the PSRF integrates other cross-cutting measures to sustain immediate gains from the protocols and prevent relapses brought by climate shocks. These include basic infrastructure like access to water, healthcare, and education; Connectivity and information such as early warning systems, transport, telecommunications, and adaptation measures including climate-smart technologies. 
Key words: Pathway-Specific Resilience Framework (PSRF), Drought resilience, livelihood pathways, Social protection, East Africa

articles.title: Tricky Trade-Offs on a Transparency Spectrum: How the Financial Times Approaches Transparency about AI Use in News
articles.authors: Liz Lohn; Felix M. Simon
articles.abstract: As news organisations adopt artificial intelligence (AI), they face growing pressure to be transparent about when and how it is used – yet practical approaches remain uneven. This paper examines AI transparency through an in-depth case study of the Financial Times (FT). Drawing on 13 semi-structured interviews with 12 senior managers across editorial, product, data science, and communications, together with internal documents, we show that the FT approaches transparency as a hybrid of policy, process, and practice, framed by a desire to safeguard both internal and external trust. Transparency is calibrated to context: internally, AI use is signposted in tools and reinforced through training and personal accountability; externally, the prominence of disclosure scales with system autonomy and editorial oversight, with stronger labelling for no-human-in-the-loop features than for AI-assisted, journalist-edited outputs. We identify nine factors that shape audience-facing disclosure – legal/provider requirements, industry benchmarking, nature of the task, human oversight, system novelty, audience expectations, perceived risk, commercial sensitivities, and design constraints – and five crosscutting challenges, including site-wide consistency (especially on mobile) and potential “transparency backfire.” Conceptually, our analysis links AI transparency to isomorphic pressures and to intersecting institutional logics. We argue that AI transparency in news is best understood as a spectrum, evolving with technological advancements, commercial, professional and ethical considerations and shifting audience attitudes.

articles.title: Doubly Preferential: The Treatment of Contested Experts in News Media
articles.authors: François Claveau; Jacob Hamel-Mottiez; Léon Gatien; Olivier Santerre
articles.abstract: This article contributes to the characterization of media bias by analyzing how Canadian news media select and contextualize messages originating from think tanks, an influential yet ideologically marked form of expertise. Drawing on a large media corpus (2017–2021), this article shows that Canadian journalists make relatively limited use of textual indicators of credibility, but that these indicators systematically reflect the ideological preferences already evident in their source selection. Think tanks that are more frequently solicited thus benefit from more favorable contextualization, corroborating the hypothesis of a doubly preferential treatment. The study concludes by discussing the normative implications of these practices for journalistic standards, such as impartiality, in the face of contested expertise.

articles.title: Commercial video games improve species-related knowledge, perceptions, and action
articles.authors: Katie Blake; Paul J Johnson; Diogo Veríssimo
articles.abstract: Digital media often mediates human-wildlife interactions. It is feared that overexposure to virtual animals will distort public awareness and valuation of real-world species. This is alarming given the current rate of extinction. Commercial video games have attracted much attention for their capacity to engage players with biodiversity and conservation. Yet their impact for this is unclear. We use an online experiment to explore whether this medium can improve species-related knowledge, perceptions, and actions, as well as test assumptions that digitised wildlife are favoured by players over real-world counterparts. Our findings are based on a sample of 272 players and 273 non-players of Planet Zoo, using species that feature in this title. We found that both gameplay hours and recency of playing Planet Zoo are positively linked to: more accurately identifying species’ names and conservation status; how much the species are liked; threat appraisals about the likelihood and impact of species loss; and increased donations. Players donated nearly twice as much to species protection as non-players on average (£7.16 versus £4.68), and they allocated the maximum possible donation value of £20 three times as often. Furthermore, we did not observe any detrimental outcomes for digitised wildlife on responses compared to real versions, and we found that any positive effects from experience with Planet Zoo tended to be greater for reptiles than mammals. Our findings do not support concerns that digital media necessarily has harmful implications for public engagement with biodiversity and conservation. Rather, we show that commercial video games might provide an avenue for players to better understand the natural world and take action to protect it, and they might even be particularly beneficial for less desirable taxa. We challenge more game studios to bridge the gap between virtual and real nature where appropriate, joining efforts to ensure that wildlife can also persist beyond digital spaces. We encourage more researchers to pursue this line of inquiry. Given the rapid loss of biodiversity, we cannot continue to overlook how these platforms with global reach might be leveraged to drive conservation action.

articles.title: ‘Building the Internationalist City from Below’: The Role of the Czechoslovak Industrial Cooperative “Interhelpo” in Forging Urbanity in early-Soviet Bishkek
articles.authors: David Leupold
articles.abstract:
Abstract
The paper explores the historical trajectory of Interhelpo, an industrial cooperative from Czechoslovakia, and its role in forging urbanization “from below” in early-Soviet town of Pishpek (now Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan). In light of scarce literature available on the success and failures of Western internationalist communes in the early Soviet period, this paper draws from intensive field work in Kyrgyzstan and understudied sources in Czech, Kyrgyz, Slovak and Russian to offer a novel, bottom-up narrative on the socialist city in Central Asia.

Founded 1924 by Czech, Slovak, Hungarian, German internationalists and Ido-learners around the mountaineer and Bolshevik Rudolf Pavlovič Mareček in the Czechoslovakian town Žilina, the cooperative actively shaped urbanization in what would be become known as the capital of Soviet Kyrgyzstan. From 1925 until its liquidation during WWII, the cooperative built from scratch a whole district including the first electric power station of the city, textile and furniture factories, workshops for tailors, shoemakers and joiners, a school, a kindergarten, a tannery, a brewery as well as unique residential district. In the process, the cooperative forged an organic patchwork language referred to as spontánne esperanto to secure translocal collaboration between internationalists from Central Europe, on the one hand, and a heterogeneous mix of workers including Armenians, Kyrgyz, Dungans, Uygurs, Uzbeks, Russians and Ukrainians, on the other.

Transcending a purely historical analysis, the paper ultimately turns to the urban landscape of present-day Bishkek. There it argues that while the district built by Interhelpo corresponds today to an exiled site dislocated by the hegemonic ethno-national memory regime, its materiality harbors relicts of another future capable of mobilizing alternative narratives on the city and her socialist and multi-ethnic past.

articles.title: The Illusion of Precision: Interpreting International Rankings Within Their Measurement Limits
articles.authors: Milos Kankaras
articles.abstract: International rankings publish precise country positions. We ask which comparisons the evidence behind five of them supports, by reproducing published tables, optimising weights, applying multiplicity-adjusted rank inference and two source checks, within a framework separating invalid measurement, insufficient validation, normative trade-offs, underrepresentation of uncertainty and misleading communication. In every programme the adjacent ordering is unsupported, each for a different reason: Report Card 19 trades off dimensions in all 35 adjacent pairs; World Happiness Report countries move a median of 30 places when affect replaces life evaluation; 23 of 38 countries can lead the Better Life Index under unrestricted weights; retrospective rescoring moves Global Health Security Index countries a median of seven places within one year; only 4 of 80 adjacent PISA pairs are distinguishable. Broad contrasts survive throughout. Two unrepresented uncertainties are documented: rotated administration behind Report Card 19's social-skills indicator, and unlinked assessment vintages behind the Human Capital Index.

articles.title: Rethinking Revictimization
articles.authors: Joyce Mok
articles.abstract: Survivors of childhood abuse have a heightened risk of experiencing adulthood interpersonal violence. Existing theories explain revictimization through the victim’s deficits and past experiences of violence. These theories fail to explain the causes of revictimization, can lead to ineffective interventions, and can harm victims. This article presents a secondary analysis of the qualitative literature inspired by Eve Tuck’s formulation of desire-based research, which originally aimed to address similar narratives in the fields of education research and Indigenous studies. This analysis shows the benefits of a theoretical approach that situates the individual’s motivations within an interpersonal, social, and cultural context.

articles.title: A Productivity Fixated World in the Age of AI: Investigating The Purpose of Human Art
articles.authors: Bruce Tan
articles.abstract: Modern society increasingly prioritizes final products over the creative process, a trend exacerbated by the rapid adoption of generative AI. This study aims to explore the impact of AI integration into the creative process on subjective well-being and fulfillment, and to determine whether these effects differ between individuals creating for leisure versus those creating for a profession. Within this research, a quantitative-focused survey was conducted with 200 adults, categorized using a 2x2 design: acting as either a hobbyist or a professional illustrator, and either utilizing or not utilizing AI. The data reveals a consistent drop in a person’s well-being across both hobbyist and professional groups when AI is utilized. The differences in fulfillment between hobbyist and professional groups were not statistically significant. While a positive correlation was found between a product-focused mindset and satisfaction among professionals using AI, the overall satisfaction for AI users across the board remained significantly lower than for those who didn’t use AI. These findings suggest that AI integration into creative tasks carries measurable psychological costs by separating the creator from the intrinsically beneficial creative process, along with social costs that taint the creator-audience relationship. These findings underscore the value of human creation, suggesting that the ongoing conversation surrounding AI adoption must extend beyond efficiency to account for value within the human process. An avenue for further research lies within AI use in other fields less traditionally considered a “creative” discipline, such as STEM, which show evidence of having similar psychological benefits arising from the process.

articles.title: Do Chatbots Sound Equally Sure in French and in Arabic? A Pilot Audit of Expressed Certainty in ChatGPT and Gemini
articles.authors: Houda Es-sqalli
articles.abstract: People increasingly ask chatbots about health and public services and pass the answers on to others. Whether they check first may depend on how sure an answer sounds. This pilot audit asks whether the certainty cues that chatbots give change with the language of the question. Ten questions on public health and public services in Morocco were asked once in French and once in Modern Standard Arabic to ChatGPT and Gemini (40 answers). Answers were scored with a bilingual lexicon of hedges and boosters. Both chatbots hedged less in Arabic than in French, and the pattern held under two alternative versions of the lexicon. A model-assisted second coding of 10 answers showed that the lexicon captured boosters well but missed about a third of hedges. With 10 questions and one run each, these results are a first look, not a finding. They motivate a larger audit with repeated runs and human validation.

articles.title: Do polls underestimate support for right-wing parties? Assessing variation in polling error by party family
articles.authors: Stuart Perrett; Will Jennings; Jonathan Mellon; Christopher Prosser; Christopher Wlezien
articles.abstract: Pollsters have underestimated support for notable right-wing electoral outcomes, including Donald Trump’s vote share in 2016, 2020, and 2024, the UK Conservative Party in 2015 and 2024, and Leave in the 2016 EU referendum. Do these outcomes reflect isolated polling failures, or a persistent partisan asymmetry in polling error across democracies? We provide the first comparative analysis of partisan polling error. Drawing on over 38,500 election-poll-party observations across 32 countries and 372 elections between 1945 and 2025, we use a Bayesian hierarchical modeling framework to estimate latent election-party polling error. We find that, on average, support for parties on the left is overestimated, while support for parties on the right is underestimated. This pattern is evident across countries, party classifications, and vote intention polling dating to the 1940s. In spotlighting persistent partisan asymmetries, our findings contribute to understanding institutional and contextual correlates of pre-election polling accuracy.

articles.title: Answering without disclosing: How officials under scrutiny compress what they say
articles.authors: Nasrul Ismail; William S. Harvey
articles.abstract: How do organisational actors withhold information while continuing to answer under scrutiny? Research on organisational silence has largely treated withholding as a question of whether actors speak. This article examines variation within speech through 1 781 question-and-answer exchanges from 102 recorded interview encounters with senior officials in prison health governance across three studies conducted between 2016 and 2023. Narrative absence was coded across six features and response timing was derived from audio and validated against blinded listener judgements. Higher narrative absence was associated with substantially shorter answers within encounters, and this association held across all robustness checks. Changes in response onset were much smaller, while pausing supported no independent association, and the automated measure of fillers and repairs failed validation. The findings identify controlled compression as a response form through which disclosure contracts while interactional responsiveness continues. Separating responsiveness from disclosure matters because organisational accountability is routinely assessed through visible responsiveness even though meaningful accountability depends on disclosure. An actor may therefore satisfy every observable requirement of cooperation while narrowing what is made available. The article shows that where speaking is expected, withholding does not cease but relocates into the answers themselves.

articles.title: Public Safety and Electoral Competition in Cities
articles.authors: Jeyhun Alizade
articles.abstract: Cities in advanced democracies are often seen as cosmopolitan strongholds of the left. I argue that public safety can create an electoral opening for the right within these otherwise progressive electorates. Focusing on Germany, I first show that residents of cities, including those with more cosmopolitan attitudes, report greater fear of crime and crime victimization than those living elsewhere. I then analyze more than 35,000 Facebook ads and find that the center right places greater emphasis on public safety in cities than elsewhere, a pattern that does not emerge among parties of the left. Finally, a conjoint experiment shows that more restrictive law-and-order positions can induce progressive urban voters to defect to the center right, including those with more cosmopolitan attitudes. The findings show how public safety can cut across the cultural attitudes that sustain progressive urban coalitions and create opportunities for the right in cities long regarded as unfavorable electoral terrain.

articles.title: Fairness Perception and Trust Erosion in Competitive Mobile Gaming: A Five-Year Longitudinal Study of a Persian-Language Backgammon Platform
articles.authors: Hanieh Hatefi Yousefi
articles.abstract:
Fairness perception is a critical yet understudied dimension of player experience in competitive mobile games. This paper presents findings from a five-year longitudinal qualitative study (2022–2026) examining how players construct, reinforce, and communicate beliefs about unfairness in a competitive mobile gaming environment. Using Inductive Thematic Analysis (ITA), we analysed a corpus of more than 52,000 player reviews collected across multiple mobile app marketplaces, supplemented by anonymised customer support interaction transcripts obtained through a research collaboration agreement.
Data were collected using a longitudinal sampling design that examined the same calendar month across five consecutive years, enabling the identification of long-term trends while reducing seasonal effects. Analysis identified seven operational themes describing players’ fairness-related beliefs and behaviours, which were subsequently consolidated into three higher-order meta-themes: Perceived Agency (the belief that game systems determine outcomes independently of player skill), Trust Erosion (the progressive reinforcement of manipulation beliefs through negative experiences and platform interactions), and Statistical Misinterpretation (the attribution of probabilistic outcomes to intentional system design). The proportion of 1-star reviews citing fairness-related concerns increased from 3% in 2022 to 18% in 2026, indicating a substantial decline in player trust over the study period.
The study further proposes a ten-stage Player Journey of Distrust, mapping the cognitive and emotional progression from initial doubt to entrenched beliefs about manipulation. Findings suggest that fairness complaints are often better understood as expressions of deteriorating trust rather than perceptions of technical malfunction. The paper discusses implications for transparency design, player communication strategies, support systems, and the broader study of trust in digital gaming environments.
Keywords: fairness perception; player experience; trust erosion; mobile gaming; thematic analysis; player psychology; app store reviews; cognitive bias; longitudinal qualitative research; trust in digital systems

articles.title: Doubly Preferential: The Treatment of Contested Experts in News Media
articles.authors: François Claveau; Jacob Hamel-Mottiez; Léon Gatien; Olivier Santerre
articles.abstract: This article contributes to the characterization of media bias by analyzing how Canadian news media select and contextualize messages originating from think tanks, an influential yet ideologically marked form of expertise. Drawing on a large media corpus (2017–2021), this article shows that Canadian journalists make relatively limited use of textual indicators of credibility, but that these indicators systematically reflect the ideological preferences already evident in their source selection. Think tanks that are more frequently solicited thus benefit from more favorable contextualization, corroborating the hypothesis of a doubly preferential treatment. The study concludes by discussing the normative implications of these practices for journalistic standards, such as impartiality, in the face of contested expertise.

articles.title: Self-Constructed Recovery from Cognitive Collapse: An analytic autoethnography
articles.authors: Xin Sun
articles.abstract: Severe childhood maltreatment is known to impair brain development. However, this retrospective single-case autoethnography illustrates that an individual with extreme developmental trauma can achieve functional recovery without formal intervention. This study covers the participant’s life from birth to age 28, and the core recovery period begins with cognitive collapse at age 14 and ends with high functional recovery at age 28. This recovery is marked by the participant‑researcher’s ability to produce this manuscript. Consequently, this case shapes a distinct recovery trajectory that existing models do not capture.

articles.title: Fertility, Affiliation Transmission, and Religious Reproduction in Germany
articles.authors: Gordey Yastrebov
articles.abstract: Religious groups reproduce across generations through childbearing and the transmission of affiliation. I examine how these processes jointly shape religious composition in Germany. A pseudo-prospective design combines repeated cross-sectional surveys of women’s affiliation and fertility with retrospective information on maternal affiliation and adult offspring affiliations from the German Socio-Economic Panel. I reconstruct five-group distributions for women born in 1931-1950 and their offspring, including childless women in the starting population. Under the assumptions linking these sources, fertility differences modify but do not reverse the generational redistribution associated with affiliation transmission. Catholic point estimates indicate partial fertility compensation for transmission losses, whereas Protestant fertility provides little compensation. Lower fertility moderates but does not eliminate unaffiliated gains. Across maternal cohorts, the unaffiliated generational gap narrows as the maternal share rises toward a comparatively stable reconstructed offspring share. Unaffiliated mothers also account for a growing share of unaffiliated offspring. A conditional reconstruction for women born in 1951-1970 yields the same directions in the point estimates under fixed transmission probabilities. The findings quantify the limited extent of fertility compensation in the reconstructed religious reproduction of these cohorts.

articles.title: Hate speech against scientists can backfire – but so can counterspeech: Evidence from a four-country experiment
articles.authors: Niels G. Mede; Lena Frischlich
articles.abstract: Hate speech against scientists can harm their well-being and undermine knowledge-based societies, and counterspeech by bystanders is often proposed as a remedy. But comparative evidence on how bystanders perceive hate speech targeting scientists and on whether counterspeech helps is lacking. In a preregistered experiment with quota samples weighted to national population margins from Denmark, Germany, the United Kingdom, and the United States (N = 2,769), participants saw a fictitious social media post by a scientist either alone, with a hateful comment, or with a hateful comment plus a counterspeech reply. Hate speech backfired: Participants rated the scientist’s post more positively in both comment conditions. Counterspeech had mixed effects: It increased participants’ intentions to speak up themselves, but in Germany and the United Kingdom it made the hateful comment appear more acceptable. Our findings advance research on attacks against epistemic authorities and demonstrate the value of comparative, multi-outcome designs.

articles.title: From Water Scarcity to Paceklik: Ecological Memory in Banyumas Literary and Expressive Traditions
articles.authors: Dwi Scativana Isnaeni
articles.abstract:
Abstract
Water is more than a physical necessity in communities whose everyday life has historically been closely connected with agriculture, seasonal rainfall, and the availability of water. It can become an object of desire, ritual expectation, narrative valuation, social celebration, and material anxiety. This article examines how such relationships are articulated across four Banyumasan literary and expressive traditions: Banyu Emas, Cowongan, Ricik-Ricik, and Ahmad Tohari’s Ronggeng Dukuh Paruk. The study employs qualitative comparative interpretation within an ecocritical framework and uses the concept of ecological memory in a deliberately bounded cultural sense. Rather than treating ecological memory as proof of a population’s psychological recollection of particular environmental events, the article defines it as the recurrent cultural articulation of human–environment relationships through forms in which environmental experience can be represented, performed, retained, and reinterpreted. The analysis finds that the four corpus units do not constitute a single environmental narrative or a continuous chain of cultural transmission. Their significance lies instead in the different ways cultural form transforms environmental experience. Banyu Emas renders water scarcity as a condition that gives water extraordinary value; Cowongan turns uncertainty over rainfall into ritual supplication and collective anticipation; Ricik-Ricik constructs the arrival of drizzle or rain as an occasion of happiness, humor, sociability, and play; while Ronggeng Dukuh Paruk connects drought with agricultural disruption, paceklik, food scarcity, and bodily vulnerability. The comparison extends ecological-memory discussion by demonstrating that environmental memory can encompass positive affect as well as crisis, including happiness, relief, humor, and anticipation. It also suggests that recurrence should not be confused with transmission and that continuity may occur through transformation rather than preservation. Ecological memory, in this formulation, persists because environmental relationships remain culturally productive even when the forms and meanings through which they are expressed change.

articles.title: AI Systems for Filmmaking: A Survey of HCI Research from a Labor-Centered Perspective
articles.authors: YUYING TANG; Lin Gao; Haotian Li; Baiqiao Zhang; Rebecca Fiebrink; Sebastian Deterding; Xiaojuan Ma; Huamin Qu
articles.abstract: Artificial intelligence is integrated into filmmaking and has attracted attention in human-computer interaction (HCI). Existing studies have primarily characterized AI systems for filmmaking by their capabilities and supported tasks, with limited attention to the organisation of filmmaking labor during system use. We review 31 HCI system papers and develop a three-layer taxonomy of labor sites, labor types, and human-AI allocation, examining where AI systems are positioned, what types of labor are involved during system use, and how those labor types are allocated between humans and AI. Our analysis reveals a concentration on individual below-the-line contexts, increasing attention to structural and meaning-making labor beyond execution, comparatively limited relational labor, and substantial variation in human-AI allocation across labor types. We further identify opportunities for the design and evaluation of AI systems that account for the broader organization of filmmaking labor. This review provides a labor-centered taxonomy for synthesizing AI systems for filmmaking and a basis for examining how AI may become involved in broader organizations of creative labor.

articles.title: Platform visibility and protest recirculation in the Cockroach Janta Party movement
articles.authors: Nitesh Kumar yadav
articles.abstract:
This paper examines how the Cockroach Janta Party connected digital communication and street
protest in India between May and July 2026. I draw on nineteen public documentary records and a
separate retrospective account of my participation. I follow calls to attend demonstrations, a
request to share protest photographs and videos, Sonam Wangchuk's involvement, and disputes
over platform access. In my early visits, I remember small gatherings, people who stayed only
briefly, and volunteers who hoped the protest would grow but were unsure how far it would spread.
These observations make it difficult to assume that online popularity leads to sustained
participation. I use a visibility-action-recirculation framework to examine how gatherings produce
material that returns to digital circulation. A limited comparison with Nepal's September 2025
protests considers how people maintain communication when services are restricted. The evidence
documents deliberate organizing and reported interruptions. It does not establish how
recommendation systems, emotional appeals or recirculated material affected attendance.

Keywords: Cockroach Janta Party; platform visibility; digital protest; recirculation; platform governance;
India; Nepal

articles.title: Exploring the Intersection of Language and Literacy in a Young Person with Autism, Learning Disability and Minimal Speech.
articles.authors: Barbara Rose Clogg
articles.abstract: It is argued that language and literacy are inseparable for users of alternative and augmentative communication, and that literacy can offer a route to the acquisition of fully functioning language for non-verbal individuals with autistic spectrum disorder. This applied linguistics project explores the intersection of language and literacy in a young person with autism, learning disability and minimal speech. By use of multimodal conversation analysis, it reveals the range of everyday literacy practices used by the young person and how these literacy practices are drawn upon to make meaning in interaction. It finds that literacy practices constitute a significant part of their multimodal communicative repertoire and offer affordances as a mode of communication that breaks the limitations posed by their disabilities and the forms of AAC available to them.

articles.title: Artificial Intelligence in Agriculture: Enhancing Yield and Sustainable Farming Practices among Farmers in India
articles.authors: Seema Wankhade; Subhash Patil
articles.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being applied across sectors, including agriculture. In India, agriculture remains central to employment, rural livelihoods, and national food security. Rising population pressure, climate change, declining land availability, pest and disease risks, labour shortages, and resource constraints have intensified the need for more productive and sustainable farming systems. This paper uses secondary data to examine how AI can enhance agricultural yield and support sustainable farming practices among farmers in India. It reviews applications such as precision agriculture, drones, crop disease detection, digital advisory services, market information systems, and resource optimisation tools. The paper also analyses the major barriers to AI adoption, including weak rural connectivity, high initial investment, limited digital literacy, and the need for localised solutions. The study concludes that AI has strong potential to improve productivity and sustainability in Indian agriculture, provided that adoption is supported through public investment, affordable access models, local-language advisory systems, farmer training, and public- private partnerships.

articles.title: A golden era for open-ended questions? Using LLMs to scale the qualitative coding of open-ended survey responses
articles.authors: Ansgar Hudde; Shannon Taflinger
articles.abstract: Open-text questions in quantitative surveys can yield rich information from large samples, but analysing and coding these data using qualitative text analysis is resource-intensive. Large Language Models (LLMs) are a promising tool for scaling up such analyses, reducing time and costs. We first use thematic qualitative text analysis to create a typology of responses; we then let LLMs code texts based on our typology and instructions and compare their coding accuracy with that of student assistants, defining accuracy as agreement with a researcher-coded benchmark dataset. We assess performance on an interpretive coding task: applying a 15-category typology to approximately 1,400 open-ended responses from young US Americans about dating across party-political lines. We evaluate models from OpenAI, Anthropic, and Mistral, with and without training data. The most advanced models outperform student assistants, and performance further increases with training data. This study contributes by applying LLMs to a use case with great analytical potential, namely open-ended survey responses, and testing whether the resulting codes support the same substantive conclusions as hand-coded data. We offer applied social scientists practical recommendations for a division of labour in which researchers retain conceptualisation and codebook construction and delegate the standardised coding to an LLM.

articles.title: “I wouldn’t trust her with my life but...” - Exploring trust in voice-based assistants through user-generated content
articles.authors: Katharina Frehmann; Jana Peters
articles.abstract: Investigating trust in conversational AI, such as voice-based assistants (VBAs), is increasingly important for understanding their rising popularity and the tasks users entrust to them. Howev-er, since VBAs are technical devices perceived as human-like and sometimes serving as infor-mation sources, it is unclear what forms trust in them takes. Technical, interpersonal, and media trust approaches may all be relevant, yet previous studies have not fully considered this poten-tial multidimensionality of trust in AI, especially regarding the inclusion of media trust. Fur-thermore, research on VBAs lacks qualitative studies that provide insights into users’ perspec-tives. This study therefore pursues two objectives: First, to develop a more comprehensive theo-retical perspective on trust in VBAs by integrating technical, interpersonal, and media trust ap-proaches. Second, to empirically explore signs of trust in VBAs in German user-generated online content. To this end, we conducted a qualitative content analysis of 169 postings about Alexa, Siri, and Google Assistant found on marketplaces, under media coverage, and on dis-cussion platforms. The results show that users evaluate typical and new technical, interpersonal, and media trustworthiness indicators for VBAs and sometimes combine these dimensions when discussing AI capabilities. When explicitly speaking of trust, users mostly refer to the parent company in high-risk situations rather than to the VBA itself. Users also discuss aspects that may represent consequences, processes, and external factors of trust. Based on these findings, the paper proposes a preliminary model of hybrid trust in VBAs that can inform future research on trust in conversational AI.

articles.title: A comment on “A Mother's Voice: Impacts of Spousal Communication Training on Child Health Investments”
articles.authors: Evan Veer; Lenka Fiala
articles.abstract: Björkman Nyqvist et al. (2024) evaluate a randomized experiment in rural Uganda that studies whether strengthening women’s communication skills within marriage can shift household decisions toward greater investment in child health. All treatments provide health and nutrition training, varying whether mothers or fathers are involved, while one additional treatment incorporates a communication skills curriculum for mothers, allowing the authors to isolate the effect of communication. The authors report five core findings: First, women offered communication training report improved relationship quality. Second, the communication treatment increases the frequency of discussions between spouses about health and finances, but does not improve men’s health knowledge, indicating limited information transmission. Third, communication training does not increase the adoption of health-promoting behaviors beyond the gains from women’s health training alone. Fourth, the communication training shifts household spending, particularly on meat and fish. Fifth, none of the treatments improves the study's primary child health outcomes. We successfully computationally reproduce the paper's main claims, and show that the results are robust to corrections for multiple hypothesis testing, inclusion of control variables in analyses, and an alternative definition of relationship quality measure.

articles.title: Rethinking methods for studying online information and health decision-making: a participant-centred approach
articles.authors: NIHR Policy Research Unit in Reproductive Health; Elena Proffitt; Nicola Merrett; Lois Harvey-Pescott; Jennifer Hall; Abigail McNiven; Abimbola Ayorinde; Kamilla Abdullayev; Rebecca French; Kelly Dickson
articles.abstract:
Online information, accessed through social media, websites, apps and artificial intelligence, is frequently described as shaping health attitudes and decision-making.  Many methodological approaches to understanding how online information influences decisions provide important insights into online content, information exposure, or user perspectives, but often struggle to capture the personalised and algorithmically curated digital environments people encounter, how they engage with information as it appears in their everyday lives, and how such encounters intersect with wider social, cultural and personal contexts to shape decision making. New methodological approaches are needed that can generate meaningful evidence about the varied realities of navigating online health information and the role it plays in decision-making.  

Drawing on reproductive justice and feminist principles that privilege participant expertise and lived experience and informed by literature and collaboration with lived and learnt experts, we co-designed a participant-centred longitudinal content-oriented study exploring the influence of online information on contraceptive decision-making. Inspired by Photovoice approaches, participants documented in real time the online information they encountered over a one-month period, capturing content presented through their own tailored digital environments. Interviews conducted before and after the collection period explored contraceptive experiences, attitudes, decision-making and reflections on the role of online information. By combining real-time documentation with in-depth interviews, this approach enabled interpretations of participants lived encounters with online information, including algorithmic changes, emerging trends, current events, and the types of content that resonated with them. Collaborators with lived experience were involved throughout the methodological development and interpretation and analysis of findings.  

This participant-selected content-oriented longitudinal design demonstrates the value of methodologies that capture and generate evidence on lived digital and offline realities as they unfold in real time. Understanding how online information shapes health decision-making requires moving beyond approaches that treat the internet as an isolated and static influence on behaviours. Online information is not a singular, stable object of inquiry but dynamic, personalised, algorithmically mediated and embedded within broader social, cultural, and political contexts. Methodologies that recognise this complexity are essential for generating evidence capable of informing empathetic and meaningful health care and support and care for people prioritising their needs and navigating complex health decisions.

articles.title: Workplace Mental Health and Psychological Safety: A Systematic Review of Interventions and Outcomes
articles.authors: Sarah Khairunnisa Budiyanto
articles.abstract:
Background. Workplace mental health and psychological safety are critical determinants of employee wellbeing, organizational performance, and public health. Despite growing recognition of their importance, evidence on effective interventions across occupational sectors remains fragmented, and the moderating role of psychosocial safety climate (PSC) is underexplored in existing syntheses.
Objective. This systematic review synthesizes global evidence on individual- and organizational-level workplace mental health interventions, with particular attention to psychological safety climate as a moderating construct and the differential effectiveness of universal versus targeted delivery models.
Methods. A comprehensive, PRISMA 2020-compliant search was conducted across  PubMed and Google Scholar databases, covering publications from 2011 to 2026. Ninety-seven records were identified; following removal of four duplicates, 93 deduplicated records were retained, encompassing systematic reviews, meta-analyses, umbrella reviews, and qualitative syntheses. Quality appraisal employed ROBINS-I, QATQS, AXIS, Downs and Black, GRADE, and EPHPP tools.
Results. Individual-level digital interventions demonstrated the strongest measurable short-term effects: mindfulness-based eHealth programs (Hedge’s g = 0.60) outperformed cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT; g = 0.15) and stress management programs (g = 0.17). Web-based interventions improved psychological wellbeing (g = 0.37) and work effectiveness (g = 0.25), with effects sustained at follow-up (g = 0.23). Targeted delivery yielded markedly larger effects for stress management (g = 0.64–0.69) compared to universal delivery (g = 0.00). Universal CBT reduced depression across the general workforce (SMD = 0.16). Manager training significantly increased mental health knowledge (SMD = 0.73). Among healthcare workers during the COVID-19 pandemic, pooled disorder prevalence reached 36% for depression, 37% for PTSD, 27% for stress, 47% for anxiety, and 49% for insomnia. Organizational-level interventions showed mixed results with high heterogeneity.
Conclusions. Effective workplace mental health promotion requires multi-layered strategies that combine scalable digital tools with organizational structural changes and manager capability building. Future research should prioritize longitudinal designs, under-represented worker populations, cost-effectiveness analyses, and the integration of PSC measurement into intervention frameworks.

articles.title: From “Robs to Riches”: Scandal Constructivation, Democratic Ambivalence, and Pagsasaayos in the Philippines
articles.authors: Karl Patrick Regala Mendoza
articles.abstract: This research note examines Philippine corruption scandals from the dual vantage of citizen and scholar. Building on my concept of scandal constructivation, I argue that scandals are not simply signs of democratic defect but communicative events that dramatize democracy’s ambivalence. The DPWH flood control scandal illustrates this: outrage turned comic in the “robs to riches” quip, while blame extended to contractors’ children, exposing relational accountability. Local publics—through gossip, assemblies, and social media—oscillated between vigilance and cynicism. In the Global South, scandals disrupt structures yet provoke repair, serving as resources for rethinking public engagement, legitimacy, and democracy.

articles.title: Regressive Restoration: A Process Model of Belief Rigidity Under Epistemic Destabilization
articles.authors: Mitchell Sanders
articles.abstract: Beliefs do more than represent the world; they can also regulate uncertainty, affect, identity, and significance. This article introduces regressive restoration as a temporal regulatory process in which epistemic destabilization increases reliance on coherence-restoring beliefs, the immediate stabilizing effects of those beliefs reinforce commitment, and that commitment subsequently reduces epistemic flexibility. Epistemic destabilization refers to conditions in which cues for determining what is credible, coherent, or socially shared become fragmented, overloaded, unreliable, or contested. The model proposes that available integrative resources– the momentary attentional, affective, and uncertainty-tolerance resources needed to remain engaged with conflicting information– moderate whether destabilization promotes adaptive accommodation or regressive restoration. The model distinguishes short-term stabilization from maladaptive rigidity. Coherence restoration is context-sensitive and may be functional, whereas rigidity is indicated when closure-oriented responses resist correction or persist across contexts in which reflective integration is possible. Regressive restoration is defined as a process rather than a trait or latent factor, and identity consolidation is treated as an important but nonessential amplifier. Five propositions specify the model’s distinctive predictions concerning regulatory function, temporal ordering, motivational amplification, correction resistance, and cross-context generalization. A focused empirical agenda is proposed to test whether immediate coherence, affective relief, or significance restoration predicts later belief rigidity beyond established informational and motivational mechanisms.

articles.title: A Middle Way proposal towards an equitable open access publishing model
articles.authors: Diogo Provete
articles.abstract: Open access promised to widen participation in science, but the article-processing charge (APC) that funds much of gold open access has shifted the cost of publishing onto authors, reproducing rather than removing exclusion for the Global South. Writing as a journal editor based in Brazil, I argue that the instruments now relied upon, namely fee waivers, purchasing-power-parity pricing and transformative agreements, are each useful but insufficient, because each treats a structural problem as a matter of discounting. Latin America's non-commercial diamond model, exemplified by SciELO, has shown that affordable open access is achievable at roughly a tenth of the cost of a commercial APC, yet it remains constrained by limited global visibility. I propose a “Middle Way”: a public–private model in which national governments fund and own the core publishing infrastructure as a public good, as Brazil is now doing through the nationalisation of SciELO, while commercial firms are contracted, on transparent and unbundled terms, for the services they perform better, chiefly discoverability and global distribution. Ownership stays public, and the commercial sector becomes a contracted supplier rather than the owner of the venue. The proposal's scope condition is ownership: it fits systems where the publishing venue is, or can become, publicly or institutionally owned.

articles.title: Are EU Kidding Me? Notes from a Poorly Drafted Social Media Ban
articles.authors: Michael Veale
articles.abstract: In September 2026, the European Commission published a proposed EU KIDS Act, responding to the demand for restrictions and further design obligations applying to digital services accessible to children, including social media. This Article argues that regardless of what one believes about the merits of this policy direction, the EU KIDS Act is not the legislative text we need. The scope and drafting are little short of chaotic, full of holes, enormous ambiguities, and unintended consequences. Recitals contradict articles. The use of scope borrowed from other pieces of legislation not designed for this purpose brings services into scope that should not be subject to the relevant provisions, like book-recommendation websites, music services, or exercise trackers. The infrastructural requirement for assurance of age and parental responsibility attestation simply omits enormous issues of complex families and childhoods. Complex design obligations are written in ways that can be plausibly interpreted as implicitly prohibiting entire swathes of products, such as voice assistants. This Article outlines these issues, and many more. The Commission should withdraw this proposal and reissue a workable and realistic text.

articles.title: Youth physical activity in transitioning subsistence societies varies by biological maturity and market integration
articles.authors: Lee Gettler; Vidrige Kandza; Jessica K. Hlay; Haneul Jang; Rahul C. Oka; Francy Kiabiya Ntamboudila; Derlan Brenez Bihoundou Mouketou; Chelvin Destin Siassia Vindou; Evrahd Ngalekandza; Brel Koubemba
articles.abstract: Background: Physical activity patterns across childhood and adolescence help shape long-term health and contribute to the allocation of limited resources among growth, maintenance, and reproduction during maturation. The vast majority of data on youth physical activity comes from post/industrial societies. We know relatively little about youth physical activity in smaller-scale subsistence contexts where youth routinely contribute to production and household tasks under energetically demanding conditions. Methods: Using wearable technology, we measured moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (MVPA) and sedentary behavior among BaYaka forager and Bantu fisher-farmer youth (N=206; obs. days=798) in the Congo Basin. These communities live under energetically-demanding conditions and varying degrees of early market integration. Results: Youth were highly physically active, averaging 4.07 hours of daily MVPA. Forager females had the highest routine MVPA, although foragers were more sedentary than farmers. Developmentally, youth who were more pubertally advanced engaged in a lower percentage of daily MVPA, and older youth were more sedentary. Youth residing in the most market-integrated village engaged in a lower percentage of daily MVPA compared to the least-integrated village. Conclusions: Our findings suggest that youth facultatively adjust their activity levels as they biologically mature and that physical activity is lower with incipient market integration. The routinely high levels of youth physical activity in these communities underscore the gap between subsistence lifestyles in energetically-demanding environments and physical activity in post/industrialized societies. From a global public health perspective, our findings highlight a crucial window during early economic transitions for public health interventions aimed at preventing physical inactivity and the chronic disease burden associated with lifestyle shifts.

articles.title: Between resistance and negotiation. Intellectual property as a survival strategy for media facing AI and digital platforms
articles.authors: Javier Díaz-Noci; Javier Odriozola-Chéné; Rosa Pérez Arozamena; Koldobika Meso-Ayerdi; Simón Peña-Fernández
articles.abstract:
Introduction. Generative AI has intensified tensions between news organisations and technology platforms over intellectual property, audience traffic and journalism’s economic sustainability. The report examines how leading Spanish digital media have framed AI since ChatGPT’s emergence, while considering the subsequent disruption caused by Google AI Overviews and AI Mode.

Methods. The study combines quantitative content analysis with legal and industry analysis. It examines 242 AI-related articles published between January 2022 and December 2024 by leading Spanish digital-native and legacy outlets, selected according to GfK DAM audience data. Frequency distributions and contingency tables assess thematic frames and editorial positions.

Results. Intellectual property emerges as the central underlying conflict. Coverage concentrates on authorship (68%), ethics and legal liability (45%), business models and licensing (32%), and employment (21%). Legacy media generally frame AI as a threat to journalistic assets, whereas digital-native outlets emphasise efficiency and commercial opportunities. Civil society and journalists themselves remain marginal in the debate. Google’s AI-generated summaries further intensify concerns by retaining users within the platform and reducing referral traffic.

Discussion. Intellectual property is becoming both a defensive right and a bargaining asset. The sector is consequently shifting from litigation towards licensing, collective negotiation and technological adaptation, although confidential agreements may strengthen major publishers while marginalising smaller outlets.

articles.title: Citizens’ Support for EU AI Sovereignty Policy
articles.authors: Pascal König; B.J.A. Leidorf-Tidå
articles.abstract: This article examines EU citizens’ support for EU policy to attain digital sovereignty regarding Artificial intelligence (AI). Promoting domestic industries in AI is crucially important for attaining AI sovereignty. Yet, AI sovereignty policy ultimately hinges on support by the European public, and protective policy intervening in the EU AI market may be felt directly – and negatively – by citizens. Using survey data from Lithuania, the Netherlands, Romania, and Sweden, we examine how much citizens support AI sovereignty policy even if this comes with costs and study how political and AI attitudes are associated with this trade-off evaluation. The analysis shows that EU-centrism is positively associated with support for AI sovereignty policy whereas positive attitudes toward AI and higher trust in US and Chinese tech companies show negative associations. The results have important consequences for the EU’s possibilities to garner public support for an AI sovereignty policy agenda.
