articles.title: Citizen Trust in AI Regulatory Regimes in Four EU Countries
articles.authors: B.J.A. Leidorf-Tidå; Pascal König
articles.abstract: Trust in artificial intelligence (AI) applications is deemed crucial for uptake of the technology and the development of an AI market. In the present article, we argue that the institutional design of regulatory regimes matters for whether citizens trust AI systems. We study how trust in AI systems depends on who the responsible regulator is, the scope of the regulator’s scrutiny of AI systems, and the involvement of external stakeholders in regulatory oversight. Based on a conjoint design, we examine how respondents value these institutional design choices for the case of high-risk AI systems used in health care. Using samples from Lithuania, Romania, Sweden, and the Netherlands, with 4001 respondents overall, the pre-registered experiment shows that citizens have more trust in AI systems if vendors, civil society and especially independent researchers are involved in oversight, and if regulators actively scrutinize AI systems rather than relying solely on self-reporting. At least in two countries, citizens also seem to have more trust in AI systems if the sectoral health care regulator is the responsible regulator instead of a cross-sectoral regulator such as the national Data Protection Authority or a specific AI regulator.

articles.title: Industrializing Eastern Slovakia and Its Post- Socialist Legacy: The Cases of the East Slovak Ironworks in Košice and the Metal Working Factory in Medzev
articles.authors: Tereza Juhászová
articles.abstract:
This article explores patterns of post-socialist reindustrialization in Eastern Slovakia—a region
deeply shaped by heavy socialist industrialization and subsequently exposed to the tumultuous
“manager’s privatization” of the 1990s. Bridging social and economic history, it argues that
inherited industrial legacies—in know-how, infrastructure, workforce, and export orientation—
persisted even after a sharp decline in the first decade following the fall of socialism. Through
two case studies—the “giant” East Slovak Ironworks near the regional capital Košice and a
smaller metalworking factory in the nearby town of Medzev—the article shows how foreign
investment, limited state intervention, and local agency jointly enabled the partial revitalization
of regionally significant industries, despite the absence of a coherent industrial policy and the
dismantling of state coordination after 1989. Drawing on archival records, contemporary press,
and biographical interviews, the study traces the long-term trajectories of these sites within both
socialist development agendas and post-socialist restructuring. By demonstrating how
industrial continuity and reactivation emerged largely in the absence of strategic governance
and industrial policy, the article contributes to broader debates on post-socialist varieties of
capitalism, state capacity, and the uneven geography of industrial transformation. By
foregrounding continuity and reinvention, this nuanced perspective challenges binary accounts
of post-socialist change.

articles.title: Digital Civic Activism and Configurations of Social-Identity Factors: Protest Campaigns in Gaming Communities on Reddit
articles.authors: Gudzenko Vladislav; Anastasia Poretskova
articles.abstract:
This study examines the conditions associated with successful digital protest campaigns in online video-game consumer communities. The theoretical framework combines the Social Identity Model of Collective Action (SIMCA) with research on digital political consumerism. The analysis covers 20 campaigns coordinated on Reddit between 2019 and 2024 and includes five conditions: discursive indicators of collective efficacy (EFFIC), group identification (IDENT), and group-based anger (ANGER), as well as the share of new/low-karma accounts (ANON) and the concentration of activity among the most active participants (LEAD). The empirical corpus contains 312,816 comments; an additional 8,055 comments were manually coded for validation and comparison with automated annotation. Fuzzy-set Qualitative Comparative Analysis (fsQCA) is used to identify configurations associated with outcomes.
None of the five conditions is necessary for a concession by the campaign target. The parsimonious solution contains three alternative configurations, but the most robust result is the combination of high group-based anger and low concentration of activity among the most active participants (ANGER × ~LEAD). This path survives most sensitivity checks and indicates that concessions in this sample are associated with mass, emotionally salient, and relatively decentralized mobilization. At the same time, cases of intense mobilization without concessions show that community-level characteristics are insufficient to explain outcomes without considering the cost of concession, the type of demand, and the position of the target organization.
Artificial-intelligence tools were used in the research process and in preparing this manuscript. A pretrained CardiffNLP model was used for emotion classification; Gemini was used for automated EFFIC and IDENT annotation; Claude models assisted with the development and checking of replication code; and ChatGPT was used to translate the manuscript. The research question, case selection, operationalization, calibration decisions, result validation, and substantive interpretation were performed by the researcher.

articles.title: From Berberism to Kabyle-Nationalism. Historical Analysis of Berberism in Algeria between 1930 and  2005.
articles.authors: Christoph Novak
articles.abstract: This article examines the historical development of Berberism in Algeria from the emergence of Algerian nationalist movements in the 1930s to the aftermath of the Black Spring of 2001. It argues that Berberism should not be understood as a stable political ideology with a fixed substantive meaning, but rather as a changing political practice through which the idea of a distinctive Berber identity has been mobilised in response to particular political contexts. The analysis distinguishes three phases in the development of Berber activism. The first, exemplified by the Berber Crisis of 1948–49, was largely an elite struggle within the Algerian nationalist movement over the definition of the Algerian nation and the recognition of its linguistic and cultural plurality. The second, crystallised in the Berber Spring of 1980, transformed Berberism into a broader social movement centred on cultural recognition, linguistic rights and opposition to state Arabisation. During the subsequent period of political liberalisation and civil war, Berber activism became increasingly institutionalised through political parties, social movements and transnational networks. The third phase, associated with the Black Spring of 2001, marked a significant reorientation. The declining legitimacy of established Berberist parties and the emergence of the Citizens’ Movement shifted political mobilisation toward territorial, socio-economic and increasingly Kabylia-centred claims. Drawing on concepts of political identity, recognition, nationalism and imagined communities, the article argues that this development contributed to the emergence of a specifically Kabyle nationalism. Whereas Berberism provided a broader cultural and transnational identity, it lacked a clearly defined territorial project capable of consolidating a common political community. The post-2001 mobilisation in Kabylia, by contrast, increasingly linked cultural identity to a specific homeland, territorial political structures and demands for autonomy. The article therefore conceptualises the transition from Berberism to Kabyle nationalism not as a linear transformation, but as a reconfiguration of political actors, strategies, territorial imaginaries and claims to collective self-determination. The article was written in 2012.

articles.title: The distinctive nature of non-partisanship: How independents pursue and prioritize political information
articles.authors: Stuart Perrett; Delia Baldassarri
articles.abstract: The two major parties present American voters with increasingly stark electoral alternatives. How do independents make political decisions in this era of heightened partisanship? Prevailing accounts portray independents either as inattentive, low-information voters or as "undercover" partisans whose behavior mirrors that of Democrats and Republicans. We challenge both characterizations. Drawing on novel survey experiments, we compare the information-seeking behavior of independents and partisans by examining the importance they attach to different candidate attributes and the quantity of information they seek before choosing between candidates. We find that independents and partisans rank candidate attributes in similar ways, with both groups prioritizing issue positions over socio-demographic characteristics. Yet, independents rely less on candidate partisanship and acquire more information than partisans across a variety of hypothetical electoral conditions. These differences persist across levels of political knowledge, suggesting that independents and partisans use distinct decision rules when evaluating political candidates.

articles.title: Contagion or substitution? Experimental evidence on spillovers in trust between legislative and judicial institutions
articles.authors: Michal Ovadek; Stuart Perrett
articles.abstract: Does information about one branch of government affect trust in another? We show that institutional trust is neither institution-specific nor uniformly system-wide. In a survey experiment embedded in the British Election Study Internet Panel, respondents received information about the UK Parliament, the UK Supreme Court, and the European Court of Human Rights that varied the policy content of decisions, party framing of these decisions, and the conduct of individual officeholders. Policy decisions conflicting with respondents' preferences reduce trust well beyond the institution responsible, while congruent decisions leave trust unchanged. Spillovers are strongly asymmetric: parliamentary decisions depress trust in the courts more than in Parliament itself, whereas court decisions produce little spillover beyond the judicial domain. Criticism from parties offsets rather than deepens the penalty, regardless of how much respondents like the cueing party. Information about conduct of officeholders moves trust neither within nor across institutions. We conclude that institutional trust is selectively contagious, shaped above all by the policy decisions institutions make.

articles.title: Distributional Validity of a Korean Synthetic Persona Panel: Evidence From the Korea Media Panel Survey
articles.authors: Howard Kim; Keun Tae Cho
articles.abstract: Large language model (LLM) personas are proposed as survey respondents, yet validation outside English-speaking contexts is scarce. We evaluate how well a Korean synthetic persona panel used to condition Gemini 3.5 Flash and EXAONE reproduces digital and artificial intelligence (AI) service-use distributions of the Korea Media Panel Survey. About 8,000 personas per model answered eight service-use items and eight attitudinal constructs; responses were compared with weighted survey estimates. The overall mean absolute error (MAE) was 14-19 percentage points (pp), with binary item-mean correlations of 0.70-0.91 across waves. Segment error across five axes was 14-18 pp, with between-group signed-error ranges of 49.6/34.7 pp (Gemini/EXAONE; 39.5/31.2 without the non-comparable teen cells). Errors were model-specific: an age stereotype (Gemini) versus an acquiescence-consistent level bias (EXAONE). Generative-AI overestimation was consistent with temporal misalignment; short-form underestimation was framing-sensitive and persisted under randomized order (both shown for Gemini). Post-hoc holdout calibration on 30% of the real data, with the correction form selected inside the calibration set, cut cell MAE from 18.3/15.1 to 4.9/4.4 pp, yet direct estimation from that subsample was more accurate than the calibrated panel (3.6 pp), a synthetic-informed shrinkage estimator beat its real-only counterpart by at most 0.7 pp, and the correction did not transfer competitively across waves. The calibrated panel kept an advantage only below roughly 250-860 real responses (at most 2.3 pp over a real-only shrinkage estimator) or, for one model, on unobserved segments. In this setting, synthetic panels are not survey substitutes; their value is diagnostic.

articles_hidden.title: Research and Impact of Prompt Engineering Nexus on Programming and Routine Tasks: Exploring Future Possible Directions
articles_hidden.authors: Felix Reichel
articles_hidden.abstract:
Prompt engineering has developed as a transformative subfield in artificial intelligence
(AI), enabling humans to enhance AI systems through structured (PROLOG-like) instructions
to perform specific tasks. This paper shines a light on its multi-dimensional impact on
programming, routine tasks and broader AI applications, drawing on insights from recent
studies. By using techniques such as parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT), zero-shot
learning, multi-shot learning and linguistic feature analysis, prompt engineering often is used
to tackle remaining issues in software engineering (SE), language processing (NLP) and AI
safety. The body of literature highlights its role in optimizing AI performance, reducing
computational overhead and reducing biases. Additionally, it highlights critical gaps in 
current methodologies, such as the comparative energy intensity of state-of-art large language
models (LLMs) and the requirements for adaptive and scalable prompt crafting strategies.
Finally, the paper suggests future directions for research, highlighting the importance of
human-centered design and collaboration to advance the field.

articles_hidden.title: Unexpected heat suppresses emigration from the world's poorest countries
articles_hidden.authors: Ashley Vicary
articles_hidden.abstract: Whether climate stress displaces people or traps them in place is unresolved. The common intuition is displacement: crops fail, heat becomes unliveable and people leave. Other work predicts the opposite for poor countries, where migration abroad is expensive and the shock that sharpens the wish to leave can destroy the means to go. Estimates disagree, partly because realized temperature mixes warming that households anticipated with warming they did not. I isolate the unanticipated part with temperature forecast errors, the warmth or cold a forecast missed, and estimate their effect on monthly international migration from countries holding most of the world’s population. Here I show that unexpected warmth does not detectably move migration on average, but that in low-income countries an unexpectedly hot month lowers departures over the following year. No richer income group shows a detectable response. The migration suppression is strongest where incomes depend on agriculture, also appears outside the growing season and leaves in-migration flat, consistent with heat removing the means to move. For the poorest countries, unexpected heat may hold people back rather than push them abroad. Projections and policies built around displacement may overstate departures from these countries and overlook those who cannot afford to leave.

articles_hidden.title: Defaulting to Decarbonization?  Financial Insolvency and the Energy Transition in India’s States
articles_hidden.authors: Johnathan Guy
articles_hidden.abstract:
How do financial constraints shape the energy transition in developing countries? I study this question in India, where electricity procurement is governed at the subnational level. Electoral politics motivates state governments to subsidize electricity consumption, resulting in financial stress for electricity distribution utilities (DISCOMs). Using multiple sources of original data on utility and plant operations, I investigate the relationship between financial distress and decarbonization. I theorize that the effect of utility insolvency depends on the margin considered—dispatch vs. capacity investment—and on institutions. Counterintuitively, but consistent with my theory, I find that financial stress is associated in the short run with greater relative procurement of renewable energy and less procurement of fossil fuels. Mechanism tests suggest that coal dispatch is more sensitive to liquidity constraints, as distressed DISCOMs cut back on coal deliveries while renewable energy remains protected by “must-run” dispatch regulations. In contrast, I find at most weak evidence that insolvency raises challenges for decarbonizing electricity in the long run: insolvency shows no relationship with renewable-energy tendering, only suggestive evidence that it slows renewable capacity investment, and similarly weak evidence that it curtails expansion of transmission lines that renewables need to scale. The results qualify the conventional wisdom that electricity utility
insolvency is a binding constraint on the energy transition.

articles_hidden.title: Explaining historical persistence in Germany's electoral geography across 130 years: a cleavage-perspective on continuity in spatial patterns of party support
articles_hidden.authors: Leon Gawenda
articles_hidden.abstract: This article studies the long-run persistence of electoral geographies. Drawing on cleavage theory, I argue that spatial patterns of party support persist where cleavages remain politically salient and the social groups they mobilise stay in place. I evidence this argument for Germany, combining electoral and census data from the German Empire (1890–1912) and reunified Germany (2002–2021) at the municipality, county and electoral-district level. The spatial analyses reveal substantial continuity in the electoral geographies of the mainstream left and right. The analysis traces both to one source, the persistent spatial distribution of Catholics. Christian democrats continued historical strongholds of the Center Party where Catholics stayed concentrated, while the SPD persists as its mirror image in the non-Catholic space. Persistence therefore rests on the stability of the religious geography and cleavage, not on the class cleavage and the economic geography, which has changed markedly. The findings position cleavage-based persistence as a complement to cultural-transmission accounts of historical legacies, locating continuity in the ongoing mobilisation of stable social groups rather than in transmitted attitudes alone.

articles_hidden.title: Academia as a Mirror of Society: Science in the Age of Capitalist Realism
articles_hidden.authors: Philipp Strasberg
articles_hidden.abstract: Prima facie, the scientific endeavor seems anti-capitalistic par excellence: a collective, non-profit driven effort of humanity to advance its knowledge in which everyone with enough education is free to participate. But a more detailed look reveals that science and its academic system perfectly mirror our late capitalist society: inequality, exclusivity, overproduction, hypercompetition, exploitation, control, self-optimization, burnout and depression are today’s symptoms, here and there. In addition, missing political agency is not only mirrored in academia---it is cultivated there. A common perspective on both, science and society, can offer the chance to change both for good.

articles_hidden.title: Product Market Reform and Enterprise Software Diffusion: Evidence from European Industries
articles_hidden.authors: Frenki Shatku
articles_hidden.abstract: This paper examines whether product-market reforms in upstream network sectors are associated with faster diffusion of enterprise software in downstream European industries. The analysis combines Eurostat data on Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) and Customer Relationship Management (CRM) adoption with OECD ETCR and REGIMPACT indicators for 24 economies and 13 industries over 2010–2021. Reform exposure is constructed using major annual regulatory declines and fixed 2010 US input-output weights, while the empirical specification includes country-by-interval, industry-by-interval and country-industry fixed effects. Industries more exposed to major reforms experience faster growth in the combined ERP-CRM adoption index. At the median nonzero reform exposure, the estimate corresponds to approximately 1.5 percentage points of additional adoption growth. The response is stronger for CRM, while ERP is smaller and less precisely estimated. Minor and moderate regulatory changes show no comparable relationship. The results remain similar across alternative samples, reform thresholds and controls for the initial stage of software diffusion. The findings connect upstream product-market reform to downstream diffusion of organizational technologies.

articles_hidden.title: Living Arrangements, Going Outdoors, and Well-Being Among Older Persons: Examining Their Associations in a Swedish Population
articles_hidden.authors: Jeanette Melin; Marie-Louise Möllerberg; Marit Preuter; Kristofer Årestedt
articles_hidden.abstract:
Aim: This study examined associations between living arrangement, frequency of going outdoors, and well-being among older persons in Sweden, with particular attention to their interaction.
Methods: Community-dwelling older persons (n = 1,727) across nine Swedish municipalities participated in a cross-sectional survey. Well-being was assessed using the Older Persons’ Well-being Scale (OPWELLS). Linear regression models examined associations and interactions.
Results: Living alone was associated with lower well-being compared to cohabiting, whereas going outdoors more frequently was associated with higher well-being. The association between living arrangement and well-being differed by outdoor frequency.
Conclusions: Frequency of going outdoors was strongly associated with well-being irrespective of living arrangement. However, the association between living alone and well-being varied with outdoor frequency. Thus, living alone should not be considered an isolated indicator of lower well-being in older age and highlights the importance of considering living arrangements within the broader context of older persons’ everyday lives.

articles_hidden.title: From Desktop to Spatial Interfaces: UX Design Implications of Evolving Interaction Paradigms
articles_hidden.authors: Hiromu Tsuruta
articles_hidden.abstract:
This study examines how the transition from screen-based interaction paradigms to spatial
interfaces affects established user experience principles and design considerations. The
study is guided by the following research question: How does the transition from
screen-based interaction paradigms to spatial interfaces affect established UX principles and
design considerations? Apple Vision Pro and visionOS are examined as one case. The
corpus consists of 60 selected Human Interface Guidelines pages, 76 WWDC sessions, the
Apple Vision Pro User Guide, and notes from researcher observation. The HIG and WWDC
materials were analyzed qualitatively and coded using four dimensions: consistency,
feedback, affordance, and information architecture.
The analysis suggests that established UX principles remain relevant in spatial interfaces,
although the way they are implemented changes. This study describes that change through
three categories: retention, adaptation, and extension. Some familiar purposes and
structures remain in place, others are adapted through spatial interaction, and some design
concerns expand to include the user’s body and surrounding environment. Familiar
structures such as windows, controls, and navigation remain important, but visionOS adds
gaze, gesture, depth, distance, sound, anchoring, and immersion as additional design
mechanisms. From this pattern, the study proposes selective spatiality: spatial presentation,
immersion, and embodied interaction are most useful when they support the task, not simply
because they are available on the platform.
In the Vision Pro case, effective spatial UX comes from keeping familiar interaction
structures while adding spatial features only where they are useful. Designers must also
consider comfort, attention, accessibility, environmental awareness, and hardware limits.
Because the study examines one platform and does not include independent user testing, its
findings should be interpreted within that scope.

articles_hidden.title: From Public Dominance to Private Expansion: Changes in Hospital Infrastructure in Spain (1986–2018)
articles_hidden.authors: Mauricio Matus-Lopez; Margarita Vega-Rapún
articles_hidden.abstract: In many countries, the growth of the private hospital sector coincides with a decline in beds per inhabitant. Spain is no exception, showing one of the lowest relative bed provisions in the EU. This study offers an exploratory analysis of the evolution of private hospital bed provision in Spain and its Autonomous Communities between 1986 and 2018. Using historical hospital catalogs from the Ministry of Health, we conducted graphical and cluster analyses to examine trends and classify regions by the share of private hospital beds. Results indicate a national trend toward fewer beds and a growing presence of the private, mainly for-profit, sector, with notable regional differences such as the Catalan model. This research provides comparative and long-term evidence on structural changes in Spain’s hospital system.

articles_hidden.title: Using large-scale supermarket transaction data to understand the environmental sustainability and healthiness of food and drink purchases. Policy Insights from the FIO Food Project.
articles_hidden.authors: Emma Wilkins; Mark Alan Green; Mark S Gilthorpe; Alice Rose Kininmonth; Alexandra Johnstone; Michelle Morris
articles_hidden.abstract: A policy brief summarising recommendations for policy from FIO Food work package 2, which uses large-scale retail transaction data to understand the environmental sustainability and healthiness of food and drink purchases.

articles_hidden.title: Occupational class inequality in non-monetary job quality in Europe, 1995-2024
articles_hidden.authors: Edvin Syk
articles_hidden.abstract:
Occupational class is central to research on inequality, but we have limited knowledge about how it structures non-monetary job quality across countries and over time. 
We examine four dimensions of job quality—autonomy, physical working conditions, work intensity, and work time quality—across eight occupational classes in 14 European countries from 1995 to 2024, using the European Working Conditions Survey. 
We compare class profiles over time, decompose variation into within- and between-class components, and benchmark occupational class against country, country-year, and income. 
Most variation in job quality is within occupational classes, but gradients remain pronounced for physical working conditions and autonomy, while work intensity is only weakly structured by class. Cross-national differences are modest on average but substantially larger among lower-skill than higher-skill classes. 
Occupational class thus remains an important source of inequality in some dimensions of job quality, but captures only part of the broader variation in working conditions.

articles_hidden.title: Behavioural Sociology of Humans and Machines
articles_hidden.authors: Taha Yasseri; Hao Cui; Nico Mutzner
articles_hidden.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly participates in communication, decision-making, and collective action, making the social organisation of human–machine interaction central to Hybrid Intelligence (HI). This chapter reviews the behavioural sociology of humans and machines through an HI lens, examining how interaction and feedback shape the combination of human and artificial capabilities. Drawing on sociology, social psychology, human–computer interaction, organisational studies, collective intelligence, and science and technology studies, it traces processes from individual social perception to cooperation in hybrid groups and organisational and institutional arrangements. Particular attention is given to how machine participation alters familiar mechanisms: social categorisation attaches expectations to designed identities, reciprocity may involve unequal social obligations, and algorithmic recommendations acquire authority through organisational practices. The chapter distinguishes observable machine behaviour from human interpretations of intention, understanding, and moral responsibility. It also considers how behavioural effects can extend beyond direct human–machine encounters, while separating established findings from proposed longer-term consequences. It argues that the benefits of HI depend on how roles, incentives, reliance, and accountability are organised, and identifies priorities for empirical research on these evolving sociotechnical arrangements.

articles_hidden.title: BirthClim_IT: A Harmonized Municipality-Level Dataset on Fertility,  Environment, and Territorial Contexts in Italy, 2003–2022
articles_hidden.authors: Chiara Baldan; Anna Giraldo
articles_hidden.abstract:
BACKGROUND
Environmental conditions and climate change, alongside spatial heterogeneity in fertility, have received increasing attention in fertility research. However, research combining these perspectives remains limited, partly due to the lack of data linking fine spatial resolution with detailed demographic, environmental, and socioeconomic information. This is particularly relevant in Italy, where substantial spatial variation in fertility coexists with heterogeneous environmental conditions.
OBJECTIVE
This paper introduces BirthClim_IT, a harmonized longitudinal dataset designed to support research on fertility and its environmental and territorial contexts across Italian municipalities. The dataset description is accompanied by two empirical applications illustrating its use.
METHODS
The BirthClim_IT dataset combines monthly demographic information with environmental, climatic, geographic, and socioeconomic indicators for 7,896 Italian municipalities from January 2003 to December 2022. The dataset contains 126 variables, harmonized to the administrative boundaries in force on January 1, 2024. To address sparsity in monthly birth counts, we also provide a spatially aggregated version comprising 4,936 spatial units and a customizable aggregation procedure. 
RESULTS
The dataset provides both municipality-level and aggregated data, allowing fertility patterns to be examined jointly across space and time. The two descriptive applications illustrate its use in identifying distinct environmental profiles across Italian municipalities and in examining seasonal variation in fertility and environmental conditions.
CONTRIBUTION
Given the growing interest in environmental dimensions of fertility and increasing attention to the spatial dimension of demographic processes, BirthClim_IT provides a new and flexible resource combining fine spatial and temporal resolution with information spanning multiple dimensions of the demographic, environmental, and socioeconomic context.

articles_hidden.title: How Model Choice Obscures Forecast Uncertainty: The Rashomon Effect and the 2026 Senate
articles_hidden.authors: Jack T. Rametta; Christopher Hare
articles_hidden.abstract: Election forecasts report ostensibly precise predictions that depend on modeling choices. These include the size of the incumbency advantage, the weight on state partisan lean, and how strongly national conditions move individual races. We show that the record of Senate elections between 2010 and 2024 is insufficient to adjudicate such choices. While hundreds of Senate races provide information about race-level relationships, the role of shared national conditions must be learned primarily from comparisons across only eight election cycles. Indeed, of 120 plausible models varying these weights, 117 predict past elections similarly well. This “Rashomon set” illustrates how different assumptions can produce comparable predictive performance but distinct substantive findings. Our reference model predicts a 50.6% chance of Democratic control of the 120th Senate with 50.5 expected seats (90% interval 45–56). The 117-model Rashomon set, however, puts the chances of Democratic control anywhere between 43.2% and 57.6%. We recommend reporting this range alongside conventional predictive intervals from a single model.

articles_hidden.title: Survivors' Perspectives and Experiences of Intimate Partner Violence Perpetrator Intervention Programs and Associated Services: A Qualitative Systematic Review
articles_hidden.authors: Alison Stafford; Chae Rose
articles_hidden.abstract:
This qualitative systematic review synthesises survivors’ perspectives of intimate partner 
violence perpetrator interventions and associated support services. Specifically, it examines 
how different relationship structures, such as intact, co-parenting, or separated 
arrangements, shape these experiences and determines which program features are 
perceived as supporting or compromising safety. Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, 
electronic databases were searched for peer-reviewed literature published after 1 July 2016. 
Although 13 studies met the initial inclusion criteria for descriptive mapping, the final 
thematic synthesis integrated 11 primary sources containing the specific contextual data 
required for qualitative analysis. The analysis generated three main analytical themes: the 
intervention environment, perpetrator behaviour patterns, and the survivors’ processing 
journey. Findings indicate that relationship structures influence how survivors experience 
these interventions. While individuals navigating ongoing contact or reconciliation attempts 
often report transactional partner compliance driven by child-access pressures or relationship 
motivations, those seeking complete separation report an environment of persistent 
hypervigilance. Survivors report that specialised advocacy and literacy provided by partner 
contact services support safety by deconstructing mutual-blame frameworks and shifting self
blame. Conversely, interventions are perceived as compromising safety when they rely on 
isolated compliance checks and operate separately from substance use and mental health 
services, creating a false impression of behavioural change. Ultimately, the qualitative 
evidence indicates that measuring progress through mere attendance alone provides a 
misleading indicator of risk, suggesting that future policy should prioritise coordinated 
communication across sectors and elevate survivor-defined safety as the key indicator of 
program success.

articles_hidden.title: Electoral systems shape the entry and entrenchment of extremist parties
articles_hidden.authors: Chanuwas Aswamenakul; Tyler Marghetis; Brad L. LeVeck; Paul E. Smaldino
articles_hidden.abstract: Representative democracies aspire to represent voters’ viewpoints through their elected officials. At the same time, they may try to minimize extremist viewpoints that can destabilize democracy itself. Here we show that electoral systems navigate this tension by trading off between two vulnerabilities: extremist entry and extremist entrenchment. Using computational models, we investigate how electoral systems respond to the emergence of ideological extremism arising either through the introduction of a new party or through the gradual radicalization of an established party. Systems that more accurately represent public opinion are more permissive to new parties, including extremist ones. Conversely, systems that suppress extremist entry can also protect incumbent parties as they drift toward increasingly extreme and unrepresentative positions. Electoral systems therefore differ not only in how well they represent voters or how many parties they sustain, but in the vulnerabilities they create: institutional openness increases the risk of extremist entry, while institutional inertia increases the risk of extremist entrenchment. Democracies thus face a fundamental design challenge: The same institutional features that protect a democracy from one extremist risk also expose it to another.

articles_hidden.title: Social media and the prevention or reduction of harmful gambling: a rapid evidence review with integrated lived experience
articles_hidden.authors: Jenny Sweetman; Liz Littlewood; Patricia Darcy; Greg Forshaw; Amanda Perry; su golder
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background and aims: Research has established a clear link between social media use and harmful gambling. Existing systematic reviews highlight how social media platforms enable and normalise gambling. This rapid evidence review aimed to identify interventions using social media to prevent or reduce harmful gambling. 

Methods: Searches were conducted (January 2026) in MEDLINE, Embase and PsycINFO. Searches of grey literature searches, and backward and forward citations from included references, were also completed. Independent screening, data extraction and quality assessment was undertaken by two independent reviewers. Data were analysed using narrative synthesis methods. An expert by experience group directly informed each stage of the review process.

Results: From 1138 unique records, 10 studies met our inclusion criteria (2 randomised controlled trials, 2 cohort studies, 2 mixed methods studies and 4 qualitative studies). Included studies focused on brief messages, the impact of a social media platform outage, and the use of gambling support forums. Findings highlighted the benefits and potential risks of implementing gambling harm reduction strategies on social media, the role of interaction with others, and opportunities to use social media to better understand the process of recovery from problem gambling.

Discussion and Conclusions: There is some evidence that social media platforms could usefully support the reduction or prevention of harmful gambling. Further research is required, co-designed by those with lived experience to optimise engagement and impact, to better understand how online interventions can support different people and to assess the effectiveness through large high-quality randomised controlled trials.

articles_hidden.title: Stabilizing Without Integrating: Ethnopolitical Cartelization and Power-Sharing in Post-Ohrid Macedonia
articles_hidden.authors: Ognen Vangelov
articles_hidden.abstract: This article examines the long-term effects of Macedonia’s post-conflict power-sharing arrangement, introduced by the Ohrid Framework Agreement (2001), on interethnic integration and democratic accountability. While the consociational model is widely credited with stabilizing the state and ensuring minority inclusion, it has also contributed to the institutional entrenchment of ethnic segmentation, shaping the incentives of political competition and governance. The article introduces the concept of ethnopolitical cartelization to describe how consociational power-sharing facilitates the consolidation of dominant ethnic parties as gatekeepers to state institutions, limiting intra-ethnic pluralism while preserving interethnic parity. Drawing on institutional analysis and empirical evidence, the article argues that key features of the Macedonian model, such as ethnic veto mechanisms, proportionality rules, and decentralized governance, have incentivized the monopolization of political representation within ethnic blocs, most clearly exemplified in the long-standing dominance of DUI within the Albanian political segment. This dynamic has enabled the development of vertically integrated party structures that channel access to state resources through identity-based patronage and informal governance. The result is a form of segmented stability in which public administration, education, and language policy operate through parallel structures. The Macedonian case illustrates the broader limitations of consociational design in deeply divided societies: while formal inclusion is achieved, it may come at the expense of shared civic space, horizontal accountability, and democratic responsiveness. By segmenting political authority and embedding elite brokerage into the structure of governance, the system inadvertently entrenches the very boundaries it was designed to overcome.

articles_hidden.title: The Dataset of World Refugee and Asylum Policies (DWRAP): de jure asylum policy for 205 countries, 1951-2022
articles_hidden.authors: Christopher W. Blair; Guy Grossman; Jeremy Weinstein
articles_hidden.abstract: More than two-thirds of the world's refugees and asylum-seekers are hosted in the developing world, yet the national laws governing their reception have never been measured comprehensively across countries or over time. We introduce the Dataset of World Refugee and Asylum Policies (DWRAP), the most expansive coding of de jure asylum and refugee policy assembled to date. DWRAP records every national law pertinent to forcibly displaced populations in 205 countries from 1951 to 2022---951 legal instruments in all. From the text of each law, we hand-code 54 policy provisions, which we aggregate into 14 strands, five fields---access, services, livelihoods, movement, and participation---and a single index of policy liberality, released in three aggregation forms. The result is a country-year panel of 11,484 observations measuring displacement-policy liberality within and across countries over seven decades. Together, these data open the causes and consequences of refugee-policy change to global, historical analysis. They measure law rather than its enforcement---and so make the distance between the two visible and measurable.

articles_hidden.title: The 128 Paths to Victory - Swing State Math in the U.S. Presidential Elections
articles_hidden.authors: N. Asger Mortensen; Joel D. Cox
articles_hidden.abstract: In U.S. presidential elections, outcomes are often predictable in most states, with variability primarily introduced by a small number of "swing states". While the specific swing states can fluctuate from one election cycle to the next, they collectively play a critical role in determining the overall result. In the 2024 election, seven key swing states contribute a total of 93 delegates to the electoral college. Without considering mutual correlations, each of the 128 potential electoral outcomes has an equal probability of approximately 0.8%. Due to an uneven distribution of "safe" delegates (219 Republican and 226 Democrat), the Democratic candidate holds a slight statistical advantage. Analysing all possible outcomes for the 2024 election suggests an estimated 55% probability for a Democratic win, compared to 42% for a Republican victory. The odds of a tie are approximately 2.3%, while the likelihood of either party achieving a clean sweep of all swing states is 0.8%. A detailed analysis of the 128 possible election outcomes reinforces the widely held view that securing Pennsylvania is crucial to electoral success. Notably, in 4\% of all possible scenarios, victory is achieved by the narrowest possible margin, and in every such case, it hinges on winning Pennsylvania.

articles_hidden.title: Gene-Environment Interactions: Reconciling Scarr-Rowe and Compensatory Advantage Hypotheses
articles_hidden.authors: Sonia Petrini
articles_hidden.abstract:
Note: Version 3 adds a simulation benchmark accounting for SES differences in completion rates. Versions 1 ans 2 interpreted SES gaps in over- and underachievement as support for both the compensation and Scarr–Rowe hypotheses; this version shows that, with few exceptions, these gaps can be explained by baseline differences in completion rates alone.

Research on gene–environment interactions in education focuses on two main hypotheses: compensatory advantage, where genetic disadvantage is less consequential in resource-rich environments; and Scarr–Rowe hypothesis, where resource-rich environments reinforce ge- netic advantage. Although regression approaches frame these as mutually exclusive, the hypotheses concern differences at the extremes of the genetic distribution, as measured by a polygenic index (PGI). Compensation and reinforcing dynamics are here mapped to socioeconomic (SES) differences in the rate of overachievers (low-PGI individuals who at- tain a degree) and underachievers (high-PGI individuals who do not). Results show that in three representative datasets from the US and UK, high-SES students are indeed more likely to overachieve and less likely to underachieve, a pattern seemingly consistent with both hypotheses. Simulation analyses reveal, however, that gaps of the observed magnitude are, with few exceptions, explainable by SES differences in completion rates alone. This study advances the theoretical framing of compensation and Scarr–Rowe dynamics as co- existing rather than competing, while aligning with recent calls for careful interpretation of gene–environment interactions in the presence of baseline environmental differences.

articles_hidden.title: A Pipeline for Extracting Data from Videos of Complex Events
articles_hidden.authors: Mirya Holman; Andreas Kuepfer; Tyler Simko
articles_hidden.abstract: Political scientists now regularly use audio, video, and text data to investigate questions about deliberation, representation, and emotion. However, existing research using multimodal data focuses largely on highly professionalized settings with readily available preprocessed data. Although the availability of data from less standardized environments such as campaign events, court hearings, and local government meetings has increased, using recordings of these events for research poses common measurement challenges, including creating transcripts, identifying speakers, and idiosyncratic production styles. In this paper, we present a streamlined and tested pipeline that uses open source tools to automatically transform raw recordings into data formats needed for political science research. The outputs of our pipeline can then be used for a wide range of substantive analyses. We validate our approach through an examination of thousands of hours of local government meetings and state supreme court hearings, showing how we can accurately segment audio, identify speakers, transcribe speech, and detect gender across varying structures and audio/video quality. The flexible open-source pipeline is publicly available and supports both local machines and computing clusters. As an application, we examine participation by gender in over 1,000 hours of school board meeting videos and US state supreme court hearings.

articles_hidden.title: Patriarchal Norms of Reproductive Behavior as an Adaptation to the Demographic Challenges of the Neolithic Transition
articles_hidden.authors: Maksim Sapozhnikov
articles_hidden.abstract:
This article proposes an evolutionary-materialist hypothesis on the origin of three basic
patriarchal norms of reproductive behavior: restriction of divorce, control over female
sexuality, and parental control over the choice of a spouse, which convergently emerge in
societies transitioning to food production. These norms are viewed as an evolutionary
adaptation to the conditions of the Neolithic transition, having emerged at the social level.
Methodologically, the work is structured as a retrospective analysis of specific
demographic conditions that created pressure in favor of such an adaptation. The starting
mechanism is the reproductive strategy of "sex for resources"—the exchange of male-
provided resources for female reproductive access—which arose in the ancestors of
humans in the Paleolithic (or earlier) and was entrenched by sexual selection.
Retrospective analysis shows that the most likely demographic challenges of the Neolithic
transition, creating pressure in favor of the adaptation of reproductive behavioral strategies
at the social level, were: (1) a manifold increase in population density, facilitating the
switching of marital partners (primarily for men) and creating a threat of resource insecurity
for women with children; (2) the emergence or intensification of awareness of the direct
link between sexual intercourse and childbirth, which could reduce women's motivation for
sexual activity due to awareness of reproductive costs; and (3) the dissociation between
the timing of sexual and social maturation in males, as a result of which female hormonal
mechanisms of partner choice (romantic love) continue to target young men who are not
yet able to provide a family with sufficient resources under the new conditions. The
convergent emergence of patriarchal norms of reproductive behavior in isolated cultures
(Mesopotamia, China, the Aztecs, the Incas, and others) serves as evidence of their
reproductive effectiveness compared to possible alternative adaptations. The hypothesis
explains the specific role of older males (fathers) as the main agents maintaining these
norms. The article is theoretical in nature and provides a foundation for further cross-
cultural empirical research.

articles_hidden.title: "I don't give a shit anymore" – Future-Oriented Career Agency and Precarity at the Postdoc Stage
articles_hidden.authors: Julian Hamann; Kathia Serrano Velarde; Tim Fenkner; Jonas Gottschalk-Rayling; Sven Boniger; Michi Hügel
articles_hidden.abstract: This paper examines how postdoctoral researchers navigate precarious employment conditions and claim career agency during an uncertain career stage. Drawing on a longitudinal qualitative interview panel of 35 postdocs from particle physics and modern history, the study distinguishes between two forms of agency: empowered strategizing and restricted drifting. Strategizing postdocs actively align short- to mid-term career goals with opportunities arising from fixed-term contracts and grant funding cycles, while drifting postdocs prioritize present research activities over long-term planning. Through in-depth interviews conducted in three waves, the analysis reveals how temporal horizons are compressed by the cyclical nature of academic recruitment and funding. The findings highlight the dynamic interplay between structural constraints and different forms of individual agency. This work contributes a processual perspective on career agency and precarity and adds to career research and studies of precarious working conditions.

articles_hidden.title: Research dataset sharing and ethical researcher conduct: A commentary on Ghuge et al. (2026) and Kumar et al. (2026).
articles_hidden.authors: Margaret K. Merga; Saiyidi Mat Roni
articles_hidden.abstract:
This commentary is written for an audience within and beyond academia, as
it concerns a dataset from the international community of school library professionals
(SLPs). After briefly orienting the reader to commentary and data fabrication, we
respond to Ghuge et al. (2026) and Kumar et al. (2026), recent articles with the same
corresponding author. Kumar et al. (2026) strongly imply that amongst other
researchers, there was a fabrication of data in our 2026 article where some SLP
respondents disclosed experiencing significant risk related to their work roles, notably
though not exclusively in the US political context. Kumar et al.’s (2026) “reasonable
evidence” that we fabricated our data is based on our data availability statement and an
opinion poll sent to associates (N=100); this method does not test whether a dataset
exists. Ghuge et al. (2026) cites Kumar et al., (2026) to make a similar though far softer
claim. We consider Kumar et al. (2026) in relation to ethical conduct in research
methods and research respondent risk related to research ecosystem norms. Data
sharing cannot be simply conflated with ethical research conduct. If we cannot
guarantee anonymity where appropriate, at-risk populations will refuse to participate in
social science research.

articles_hidden.title: Evidence from China: A quantitative examination of China's new competition regime for the digital economy
articles_hidden.authors: Leonard Baum; Joanna J. Bryson
articles_hidden.abstract: Growing global concern about the problems associated with concentrated market power in the digital economy is leading to a renewed interest in competition policy. Since the late 2010s, China’s government has squarely confronted the problems of its own ‘Big Tech’ with a new competition regime for digital markets. The ensuing ‘tech crackdown’ of late 2020 provides a rare quasi-natural experiment to study the impact of antitrust regulation. Here we deploy a novel market capitalization approach that builds on the informativeness of China’s financial markets. Harnessing Bloomberg data of 1142 publicly listed firms for the period 2019 to 2022, we find that across China's digital economy, this unprecedented intervention is associated with both reduced market concentration and reduced market-capitalization growth, but no harms to revenue. Employing a difference-in-differences and event-study design, we identify a causal link between China’s new competition regime and a reduction in concentration in the primary markets of China's three most dominant digital platforms — Baidu, Alibaba and Tencent (BATs). Other empirical findings include a negative association between market concentration and the openness of digital markets and a non-relationship between market concentration and profits. Our results indicate that neither profit- nor revenue-based metrics are entirely appropriate for measuring digital market power effectively. We conclude by discussing the relative success of China’s digital competition policy as well as the relevance of these insights for global, including Western regulatory strategies.

articles_hidden.title: University-affiliated sustainability badges: Shared identity, tourist perceptions, and hotel manager receptivity
articles_hidden.authors: Peter Lewin; Danyelle; Anna Kristina Zinn; Sarah MacInnes; Sara Dolnicar
articles_hidden.abstract: Hotel sustainability research shows that pro-environmental behaviour‑change interventions are often effective in field experiments, but widespread adoption by hotels remains limited. One possible explanation is that hotels lack external recognition that would make adopting these measures visible to guests and rewarding to managers. This study investigates whether university-affiliated sustainability badges could serve as a recognition mechanism, testing their effectiveness across two studies drawing on Signalling Theory and Social Identity Theory. In an online experiment (N=975), prospective hotel guests viewed simulated hotel booking pages featuring one of the four badge options, or no badge, across budget, mid-range, and luxury hotel pricing segments. All badge variations increased perceived hotel sustainability and guests’ sense of belonging to a community of environmentally conscious travellers (group identification). Badges did not trigger negative emotions, but the university affiliated logo did not perform better than a generic environmental logo on almost all measures, suggesting these effects are based on the presence of any badge, rather than the university partnership specifically. Semi-structured interviews with ten hotel managers found conditional receptivity to university-affiliated badges, primarily through a sense of shared values and community orientation with the partnering institution (collective values) rather than the badge’s function as a credibility signal. These findings suggest that collective values and shared identities, rather than signalling, may be the more promising mechanism for engaging hotels and guests around sustainability initiatives, and offer an encouraging direction for potential university-hotel partnerships that may translate into the future implementation of pro-environmental behaviour change interventions.

articles_hidden.title: Understanding First Nations Disconnection and Reimagining Connection: A yarn between Aboriginal women.
articles_hidden.authors: Cammi Murrup-Stewart; Tess Ryan
articles_hidden.abstract: Connection and belonging are significant processes concerning cultural identity, and for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples in Australia, it has been at the forefront of discussions around the Social and Emotional Wellbeing of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people. One area that needs more investigation is that of those individuals on the margins of society who may find access to communities a complex practice. Furthermore, there has been an emergence of recent practices that move connection and belonging beyond more traditional ways of being towards modernity, which includes inclusiveness, accessibility and flexibility for those involved. Drawing on existing literature, collaborative yarning with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples and reflective commentary, this article explores the many facets of connection and belonging and the ways in which many Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples navigate between cultural traditions, socio-historical challenges and contemporary realities. We call for a reimagining of community spaces and practices to ensure they are inclusive and responsive to the diversity of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples’ lived experiences.

articles_hidden.title: La voz que no debió contestar: llamadas silenciosas, clonación de voz y la identidad como dato biométrico — de la stipulatio romana al Reglamento General de Protección de Datos, al Reglamento europeo de inteligencia artificial y a la Ley N° 21.719 (con Epicteto sobre las impresiones)
articles_hidden.authors: Andrés Gabriel Varas Quijón
articles_hidden.abstract:
Suena el teléfono, se contesta, nadie habla y la llamada se corta. En septiembre de 2026 una
alerta de ciberseguridad difundida en Chile explicó lo que hay detrás: las llamadas silenciosas sirven para
confirmar que un número está activo, aprender a qué hora responde su dueño y recoger pequeñas muestras
de su voz que, acumuladas con audios de redes sociales, pueden alimentar una imitación por inteligencia
artificial para un fraude posterior. Este trabajo toma ese hecho cotidiano y lo lee con el derecho chileno, el
derecho europeo, el derecho romano y la Estoa. Primero separa lo que la técnica dice de lo que la alarma
exagera: una o dos palabras no bastan para clonar una voz y un «sí» grabado no autoriza jurídicamente nada;
el peligro es la acumulación de muestras y la ingeniería social que viene después. Segundo, muestra la
inversión histórica que el fenómeno revela: en Roma la voz obligaba —la stipulatio nacía de una pregunta y
una respuesta orales— y hoy la voz identifica, lo que la convierte en un dato biométrico que el derecho debe
proteger: así lo hacen el Reglamento General de Protección de Datos (artículos 4.14 y 9), el Tribunal
Europeo de Derechos Humanos desde 2001 —la voz es vida privada, no solo lo que se dice con ella— y, en
Chile, la Ley N° 21.719, que incluye los datos biométricos entre los sensibles y entra en vigor el 1 de
diciembre de 2026, con una prórroga en trámite. Tercero, examina el fraude por voz: la ultrasuplantación
que el Reglamento europeo de inteligencia artificial define y obliga a revelar, el fraude informático del
Convenio de Budapest y de la Ley N° 21.459, y la vieja definición romana del dolo como maquinación.
Cuarto, responde la pregunta que importa a la víctima —quién paga—: en Europa, la PSD2 devuelve al día
siguiente y limita la pérdida del ordenante a cincuenta euros salvo fraude o negligencia grave; en Chile, la
Ley N° 20.009 reformada en 2024 obliga al emisor a restituir hasta 35 UF en diez días hábiles y el exceso en
siete, y solo puede detener la restitución si convence a un juez de policía local de que hubo dolo o culpa
grave — estándar que, con el artículo 44 del Código Civil, no alcanza a quien fue engañado por una
imitación que una persona de poca prudencia tampoco habría detectado. Quinto, analiza el consentimiento
prestado a una voz falsa como consentimiento viciado por dolo o error. Y sexto, propone la regla estoica que
resume toda la prevención: la de Epicteto ante las impresiones —«impresión, espérame un poco; déjame ver
quién eres»—, convertida en protocolo de verificación por canal independiente. La tesis: la voz dejó de ser
el instrumento con que nos obligamos y pasó a ser el rasgo con que nos identifican; protegerla es hoy
La voz que no debió contestar: llamadas silenciosas, voz biométrica y fraude

articles_hidden.title: Measuring the impact of area-based early years support in Wales on children’s social care: Preliminary findings
articles_hidden.authors: Meng Le Zhang; Martin Elliott; Gareth Griffith; Sally Holland
articles_hidden.abstract: Flying Start is an area-based intervention which offers support for families with children under four living in disadvantaged areas in Wales. This study uses a quasi-experiment (Regression Discontinuity Design) and administrative data on children born in Wales between 2012 and 2017 (n = 126,705) to measure the impact of Flying Start eligibility on children’s social care at age 4/5. We find that Flying Start reduces rates of children with care and support plans and children looked after.  These effects are stronger for male infants and mothers who were 21 or younger at childbirth. However, we find no effects on child protection.

articles_hidden.title: Social Origin and the Baccalauréat: Curriculum, Sex, Teachers and Sector in French Upper-Secondary Schools, 2017–2023
articles_hidden.authors: Adrien Dufour
articles_hidden.abstract:
2022–23, an index of the social composition of each school’s pupils. We use these sources, combined into a panel of 2,394 general and technological lycées observed over the seven sessions from 2017 to 2023, to ask how far social origin still determines what pupils obtain at the end of secondary school, and through which parts of the system that determination passes.
At national level, passing the baccalauréat has become close to universal, but the gap between the children of senior managers and the children of manual workers has not narrowed since 1998. Between schools, social composition orders results with considerable force: a ten-point difference in the social index corresponds to about eight percentage points in the share of candidates passing with distinction, and this single relationship accounts for more than half of the variation between establishments. The two pandemic sessions of 2020 and 2021, awarded largely on continuous assessment, temporarily compressed this relationship; it returned to its earlier level after the 2021 reform of the examination.
We then examine four further lines of division. Curricular choice is the strongest: the technological streams are offered where the pupils served are least advantaged, and since the reform replaced the general-track streams with a menu of specialisms, mathematics has become the clearest social marker in the system. Sex produces a second, largely independent segregation that is greater in curricular terms than the social one. Teaching staff are distributed unequally in a way that closely follows pupils’ social origin, but this inequality accounts for little of the outcome gap once pupils’ social origin is held constant. The gap between the public and the subsidised private sector is about half a matter of the pupils each sector serves; the remainder resists every adjustment we can make.
We conclude that the published indicators describe social sorting more than institutional quality, and that the additions needed to change this are known and modest.

articles_hidden.title: A STUDY OF THE EMERGENCE OF WELFARE CLEAVAGES IN SOUTH KOREA
articles_hidden.authors: Jihun Yeo
articles_hidden.abstract:
This study aims to trace the cause of an emerging welfare cleavage under circumstances where discourses on economic growth have been dominant in Korean politics. On the basis of the theories of interaction between changing social structure and social-norm dynamics, this paper explores the causes of an emerging welfare cleavage in the case of South Korea during the late 2000s. To analyze the change of economic structure and public awareness regarding public welfare, I used the data of macro-economic indicators and public opinion polls and utilized press releases to analyze discourses of political actors.
The linked-policies effects of an immature “developmental welfare regime” and neo-liberal economic policies caused social polarization and expansion of the poverty stratum in the course of a slowdown in economic growth in the 1990s and foreign exchange crisis in 1998. The existing norm (i.e., economic growth could solve problems concerning people's livelihood) that had been maintained in the era of rapid economic growth was weakened. A conflict between an education superintendent and the Gyeonggi-do Provincial Council triggered a debate on free meals and welfare in 2009. Civil society groups were organized on a national scale, and they started a discourse struggle to replace individual interests with public interests and to obtain social legitimacy. Political parties gradually accepted the welfare issue as the primary electoral pledge for their political interests after public preference regarding growth and distribution changed when confronted with political crises.
This study draws an implication that general factors affecting Western welfare states (e.g., power alliance and democratic institutions) influence East Asian welfare states by analyzing the case of South Korean welfare politics. It means that studies of East Asian welfare states can use explanatory building blocks partly from existing welfare theories rather than stressing the exceptionalism of East Asian welfare states. However, owing to the different economic and political structures of East Asian states from those of Western countries during the formative stage of welfare states, studies of East Asian welfare states need to consider path dependency in the historical context of East Asian political economy.

articles_hidden.title: Assaults, Self-Harm, and the Allocation of State Resources in English and Welsh Prisons, 2009-2010 to 2024-2025
articles_hidden.authors: Nasrul Ismail
articles_hidden.abstract: Routine prison allocation in England and Wales is based on staffing, occupancy and regime, but does not incorporate assaults or self-harm. Using 1,727 public-sector establishment-years of Ministry of Justice expenditure and safety data from 2009-2010 to 2024-2025, this article examines whether deteriorating conditions were followed by changes in expenditure. Real expenditure per place fell 28.7 per cent by 2016-2017 before recovering, while prisons retained their relative positions. Higher assault rates were associated with increased expenditure in the following year before 2019-2020, but not thereafter; the interaction test did not establish a change between periods. Self-harm showed no statistically detectable association with subsequent expenditure in either period. Routine allocation continued throughout, but did not consistently respond to deteriorating safety conditions.

articles_hidden.title: Навигация по звуку: Картографирование семантических сообществ музыкальной сцены Казахстана
articles_hidden.authors: Alla Kislova
articles_hidden.abstract: Как выглядит музыкальная сцена Казахстана? Сформированная на пересечении двуязычной музыкальной среды, глобализации и сложившейся музыкальной традиции, она описывается через отдельные жанры, языки и рынки, однако значительно меньше известно о том, как различные исполнители располагаются относительно друг друга внутри этого единого культурного пространства. Опираясь на исследования культурных различений, а также теорию культурной всеядности мы рассматриваем музыкальную сцену как единое пространство и реконструируем его на основе корпуса текстов песен музыкальных артистов, не задавая жанровые или другие границы заранее. Кластеризация репертуаров исполнителей выявила три семантических сегмента, которые по содержанию и смыслу можно интерпретировать как казахоязычную эстраду, русско- и англоязычную сцену, а также Q-pop и новую казахоязычную сцену. Русско- и англоязычные исполнители оказываются в одной области, тогда как казахоязычные распределяются между двумя различными сегментами. Наше исследование показывает расположение кластеров относительно друг друга внутри пространства казахстанской сцены, в которой языковая граница является важной, но не единственной для формирования кластеров. Разброс тем внутри репертуара каждого артиста, демонстрирует что наиболее однороден тематически эстрадный кластер, наиболее разнороден русско-англоязычный, новая сцена занимает промежуточное положение. Мы связываем эти различия с условиями производства, а не только с культурной иерархией. Мы демонстрируем как близки или далеки между собой исполнителями внутри единого культурного пространства и показываем, как семантическая структура сцены выявляет различия внутри культурного производства

articles_hidden.title: Reference Observability and Journal Universe Choice in Open Reconstructions of Recursive Journal Metrics
articles_hidden.authors: Utz Weitzel
articles_hidden.abstract: Open reconstructions of recursive journal indicators can differ from a benchmark along two dimensions: reference observability, which determines which citation records enter the calculation, and the recursive journal universe, over which prestige circulates. We analyze the two dimensions separately in a factorial design. First, we reconstruct Clarivate’s 2024 Article Influence Score (AIS) with OpenAlex data as the Article Network Score (ANS) for a JCR-derived universe (J), the Norwegian Register (N), and the OpenAlex journal universe (A), with ANS defined for 21,706, 22,577, and 107,268 journals, respectively. Then, using a common sample of 15,951 journals, we cross the three universes with two treatments: RAW includes all cited-window articles and reviews, whereas REF retains only those for which OpenAlex records at least one reference. REF improves agreement with AIS in every universe: mean error falls and rank agreement rises. An additional component experiment shows that this improvement does not come from changing the ANS denominator alone, but from its joint change with citation-edge eligibility. Across universes, J and N yield similar results, whereas A has consistently higher errors and lower rank agreement. Robustness checks support the main results on larger journal sets, in the Leiden/CWTS core universe, and in 2023.

articles_hidden.title: Empathy-Related Traits and Domain-Specific Self-Rated Creativity: Indirect Associations Through Five C-PETS Dimensions
articles_hidden.authors: Masahiro Yoshida
articles_hidden.abstract: This study examined statistical indirect associations between empathy-related traits and domain-specific self-rated creativity through five dimensions of the Creative Personality and Thinking Styles Scale (C-PETS). An online survey of 359 North American adults assessed Perspective Taking (PT), Fantasy (FS), and Empathic Concern (EC), the five C-PETS dimensions, and five domains of the Kaufman Domains of Creativity Scale (K-DOCS). Parallel multiple mediation models were estimated using 10,000 bootstrap samples and Benjamini-Hochberg false-discovery-rate correction. Significant total indirect effects were found for PT across all five K-DOCS domains, for FS across four domains, and for EC only for Self/Everyday creativity. After correction, significant specific indirect effects were limited to Challenge-Seeking (CS) pathways from PT and FS to all five K-DOCS domains. Because the data were cross-sectional and based on self-report, these results do not establish causal mediation. Instead, they indicate that challenge-seeking is a robust conditional statistical link between perspective-related empathy traits and domain-specific self-rated creativity.

articles_hidden.title: Immigrant wages are lower in immigrant-dense areas, and the limited-English differential is mostly occupational: metropolitan Philadelphia, 2012–2024
articles_hidden.authors: Haobing Liu
articles_hidden.abstract: Immigrants who speak limited English earn less than those who speak it well. On the protective view of residential concentration, that differential should be smaller where immigrants are concentrated, because concentration supplies employers and customers who do not require English. On the isolation view it should be larger. This study tests both views in metropolitan Philadelphia, a former gateway whose immigrant population has grown again, with American Community Survey microdata for 2012 to 2024 and a two-level model of 7,355 foreign-born workers in 48 Public Use Microdata Areas. Hourly wages are about 8 percent lower per standard deviation of area immigrant density for foreign-born workers who speak English well and about 3 percent lower, an estimate not distinguishable from zero, for those who speak it poorly. Native-born workers in the same areas show a gradient of 2 percent, so most of the difference is specific to immigrants. The interaction between density and limited English is 0.049 (standard error 0.029) and disappears once occupation is held constant. The limited-English differential is 21 percent overall and 9 percent within an occupation, so most of it is associated with the occupations limited-English workers hold. An exploratory measure of the density of the worker’s own home language gives a positive interaction of 0.046 (0.022), driven by lower wages for proficient workers rather than higher wages for limited-English workers, and the same specification in the New York metropolitan area gives 0.045 (0.009). Higher earners move from the city to the suburbs.

articles_hidden.title: List and Sequential Attention
articles_hidden.authors: Yunhao Yang
articles_hidden.abstract: This paper studies stochastic choice when both availability and presentation order may vary across choice problems. We characterize a fixed-list sequential attention model for menu choice and a sequential attention model with a common continuation profile for list choice. In the list domain, we further show that, holding preferences fixed, more persistent attention shifts choice probability toward more preferred alternatives.

articles_hidden.title: The shape of NSF openness to newcomers: same share, fewer doors
articles_hidden.authors: Jingwen Zhang; Hengyi Fu; Haining Wang
articles_hidden.abstract: Openness to new investigators is often judged by the share of awards to principal investigators (PIs) without recent funding. We examine it in fiscal year (FY) 2026, when the US National Science Foundation (NSF) made the fewest new grants in four decades. NSF made 30% fewer new research projects than in FY2025, and the number of funded PIs with no NSF award as PI in the previous decade (newcomers) fell nearly as much, yet their share of new projects barely moved (34.5% to 34.3%). CAREER, NSF's main early-career award, added 3.3 percentage points to the newcomer share, offsetting the closure of three early-career programs reserved for institutions outside the Carnegie R1 tier (−3.0 points). The stable share hid a narrowing of reach. Where those programs closed, newcomers fell by 13% at R1 universities and by 66% at institutions below R2, whereas in engineering, which kept its program, newcomers below R2 rose. CAREER's growth went to institutions with more prior NSF projects, and NSF's grant obligations to institutions below R2 fell by 44%, twice the fall at R1 universities, with no offset from other federal research agencies. Per dollar, the closed programs had produced more papers than CAREER or standard grants.

articles_hidden.title: Cruelty Across Substrates: From Animal Cruelty to Embodied AI and the Coming Detection Gap
articles_hidden.authors: Travis Gilly
articles_hidden.abstract:
Childhood cruelty to animals is among the most durable behavioral warning signs of later interpersonal
violence in the forensic and clinical literature. The predictive mechanism does not rest on any settled
answer about the moral status of the target. It rests on what the perpetrator practices, rehearses, and
trains in themselves: desensitization, dominance affect, and the social learning of cruelty as pleasure.
This paper offers a conceptual continuity argument and research agenda. We argue that the substrate
of the target is incidental to that training, with one critical qualification: the configuration of the target
matters. Routine digital destruction in static media (the static video game target, the scripted non player
character) is a categorically different case from the closed loop, contingent emotional response systems
on which the argument turns. As world models, embodied robotics, and closed loop emotional voice
systems converge toward agents that perform distress in ways a user cannot reliably distinguish from a
being in pain, we argue that the dispositional consequences of practiced cruelty against those agents are
likely to recruit sufficiently similar mechanisms to warrant clinical and forensic attention. The paper does
not claim that synthetic agents are moral patients. It claims that the warning signal forensic and clinical
fields have relied upon for fifty years risks migrating to a venue with substantially diminished detection
infrastructure. Existing human robot interaction research already shows that users do not need to believe
a synthetic agent is conscious to respond to it through social, emotional, or dominance based scripts. The
Kantian observation that cruelty corrupts the cruel is sufficient to ground the argument. Conduct disorder
assessment, character evidence frameworks, school counseling protocols, and pre employment screening
for sensitive roles will need to adapt or lose one of the more durable early behavioral indicators available
to forensic and clinical assessment. The paper is offered as agenda setting; the operational protocols it
identifies as necessary are deliberately scoped to a planned companion paper.

articles_hidden.title: ¿Quién decide sobre la digitalización de la escuela? Agencia digital transformadora y toma de decisiones informadas ante la dependencia estructural de las corporaciones tecnológicas
articles_hidden.authors: Pablo Rivera-Vargas
articles_hidden.abstract: La digitalización escolar descansa cada vez más sobre infraestructuras, servicios de datos, sistemas algorítmicos y modelos de inteligencia artificial generativa controlados por corporaciones tecnológicas, lo que desplaza las decisiones sobre la digitalización fuera del alcance de los actores escolares. La literatura sobre agencia digital tiende a asimilarla a la competencia o la alfabetización digital, entendidas como capacidades individuales de uso y adaptación, y no como una alfabetización crítica orientada a la agencia, mientras que los estudios sobre soberanía digital han mapeado la distribución del poder sin articularla necesariamente con la agencia de quienes forman parte de la escuela. Este artículo conceptual se pregunta cómo puede potenciarse la agencia digital de la dirección de los centros, del profesorado y del alumnado para tomar decisiones informadas sobre la digitalización escolar. Caracteriza primero cuatro modos de desplazamiento de las decisiones (externalizadas, heredadas, por defecto y delegadas).
